# Osteopathic Manipulative Treatment: Sacrum

# Introduction

Sacral somatic dysfunctions involve altered biomechanics and restricted mobility of the sacrum, significantly impacting posture, gait, and pelvic stability.  This article outlines the mechanics of sacral motion, diagnostic techniques for identifying dysfunctions, and osteopathic manipulative treatment (OMT) options.

# Anatomy

## Sacral landmarks

The sacrum is composed of 5 fused vertebrae **(S1 through S5)**, with the top of the sacrum (most cephalad region) called the sacral base.  The sacral promontory, located at the sacral base, articulates superiorly with L5; the lowest part of the sacrum (apex) is fused with the coccyx.  The 2 important palpatory landmarks for diagnosing sacral somatic dysfunctions include the:

-   **Sacral sulci**:  Located on the **upper** lateral part of the sacrum (some references use the terms "sacral sulci" and "sacral base" synonymously).
-   **Inferior lateral angles** (ILAs):  Located on the **lower** lateral part of the sacrum.

The sacrum articulates with the innominates (composed of 3 fused bones: ilium, ischium, and pubis bones) via the sacroiliac joint ((Figure 1)).  Stability at this joint is provided by the sacroiliac ligaments.  Additional pelvic ligaments include the sacrotuberous ligament, sacrospinous ligaments (divide the greater and lesser sciatic foramina), and the iliolumbar ligament (commonly the first affected ligament implicated in lumbosacral pain) ((Figure 2)).  The innominates and associated dysfunctions are further discussed in a separate article.

## Pelvic diaphragm and nerves

The sacrum, along with the coccyx, serves as an attachment point for the **pelvic diaphragm** muscles (levator ani and coccygeus muscles).  These muscles are important not only for **pelvic support** but also for working in synchrony with the abdominal diaphragm to **facilitate lymphatic drainage** from the pelvis and perineal regions.

The anterior surface of the sacrum is concave and features 4 pairs of pelvic sacral foramina, through which the ventral rami of the S1-S4 spinal nerves pass, contributing to the sacral plexus.  This plexus provides motor and sensory innervation to the pelvis and lower limbs.  Furthermore, the S2-S4 segments of the spinal cord give rise to parasympathetic preganglionic fibers **(pelvic splanchnic nerves)**, forming the **S2-S4 autonomics** responsible for regulating pelvic visceral functions, including urination, defecation, and sexual function ((Figure 3)).

# Biomechanics

## Sacral movement

Movement at the sacrum occurs at the sacroiliac joints around the following axes ((Figure 4)):

-   **Oblique** axis (left and right):  Engaged during weight bearing (ie, stance phase of gait).  For example, the left oblique axis is engaged when the left leg is in the stance phase.  Movement around an oblique axis involves a "twisting" or rotational motion of the sacrum.  For instance, rotation of the sacrum around the left oblique axis can be described as a rotation of the sacrum on the oblique axis (eg, a left rotation of the sacrum on a left oblique axis).
-   **Superior transverse** axis (**S1** level):  Movement about this axis occurs during respiratory and craniosacral motion.
-   **Middle transverse** axis (**S2** level):  Engaged during postural sacral motion.  Major movements include nutation (anterior movement of the sacral base) and counternutation (posterior movement of the sacral base).
-   **Inferior transverse** axis (**S3** level):  Innominate rotation about the sacrum occurs along this axis, including the walking phase of gait.

## Lumbar movement

Sacral motion is intimately linked to L5 motion:

-   **L5 sidebending** engages the sacral **oblique axis** on that **same side**.  For example, if L5 sidebends to the left, the left sacral oblique axis is engaged.
-   **L5 rotation** causes the sacrum to **rotate** in the **opposite direction** (on an oblique axis).  For example, L5 rotation toward the left is accompanied by sacral rotation toward the right.

Understanding this link between sacral and L5 motion is crucial for diagnosing sacral somatic dysfunctions, particularly sacral torsions.  Diagnostic implications are discussed in further detail later in this article.

# Diagnostic tests for sacral dysfunctions

Sacral diagnosis typically begins with the seated flexion test (SFT), backward bending test, and lumbosacral spring test, which allow narrowing of possible diagnoses.  In addition, noting the positions of the sacral sulcus (upper sacrum) and ILAs (lower sacrum) allows determination of the precise diagnosis.  The broadest categories of sacral dysfunctions include:

-   Symmetric dysfunctions:  Bilateral sacral flexion/extension.
-   Asymmetric dysfunctions:  Unilateral sacral flexion/extension and sacral torsions.  Sacral torsions can be subdivided into forward torsion (left on left or right on right) and backward torsion (left on right or right on left).

Sacral dysfunction terminology is discussed in more detail later in this article.

## Seated flexion test

For the SFT, the patient sits upright while the physician monitors the posterior superior iliac spines (PSISs).  Normally, forward-bending in a seated position primarily reflects forward sacral rotation (sacroiliac joint); the innominate (ilium/ischium/pubis), including the PSISs, does not move significantly.

-   **Positive** SFT = **excessive PSIS motion** superiorly/anteriorly on that side = **dysfunctional sacral sulcus** on that side = asymmetric sacral dysfunction (ie, unilateral sacral flexion/extension, sacral torsion).  The innominate (including PSIS) moves disproportionately to compensate for the dysfunctional sacral sulcus (moved either forward or backward).  The **oblique axis of dysfunction is on the opposite side** of the positive SFT.
-   Negative SFT = no asymmetric sacral dysfunction (or bilateral sacral dysfunctions \[eg, bilateral sacral flexion/extension\]).

Positive SFTs on the right and left are demonstrated in these images ((Figure 5)) ((Figure 6)).  The SFT should not be confused with the standing flexion test, which is abnormal in innominate, not sacral, dysfunctions.

## Backward bending (sphinx) test

To perform the backward bending (sphinx) test, the physician maintains contact with the sacral sulci while the patient lifts the torso off the table while in the prone (sphinx) position, inducing lumbar extension ((Figure 7)).  Lumbar extension normally causes both sacral sulci to move anteriorly.  Patients with asymmetric sacral dysfunctions (ie, sacral torsion or unilateral sacral flexion/extension) have impaired sacral sulcus motion on the dysfunctional side.

-   **Positive** sphinx test:  The sacral sulci move forward (ie, anterior/deep) with lumbar extension, but the **dysfunctional sacral sulcus is "stuck" rotated backward** (ie, posterior/shallow); therefore, sacral sulci asymmetry increases.  This occurs in unilateral sacral extension or **backward sacral torsion** (ie, left on right or right on left).
-   Negative sphinx test:  The sacral sulci move forward (ie, anterior/deep) with lumbar extension, but the dysfunctional sacral sulcus is already "stuck" forward; therefore, sacral sulci asymmetry decreases.  This occurs in forward sacral torsion (ie, left on left or right on right) or unilateral sacral flexion.

## Lumbosacral spring test

The lumbosacral spring test involves applying an anterior force over the sacrum while monitoring for a spring ((Figure 8)).  Normally, applying an anterior force over the lumbosacral junction in a prone patient creates a "springing" movement of the sacrum in relation to L5.  The results of the spring test help determine whether the dysfunctional sacral sulcus/sulci have moved anteriorly/forward or posteriorly/backward.

-   A **positive** spring test (ie, **decreased springing**) indicates that one or both sacral **sulci have moved posteriorly** in relation to L5.  This is seen with the following dysfunctions: **backward torsion**, unilateral extension, and bilateral extension.
-   A negative spring test (ie, springing freely) indicates that the sacral sulci are in a neutral position or have moved anteriorly in relation to L5.  This is seen with the following dysfunctions: forward torsion, unilateral flexion, and bilateral flexion.

# Sacral flexion and extension dysfunctions

## Unilateral sacral flexion

In unilateral sacral flexion, there is anterior displacement of 1 sacral sulcus, with a deeper sulcus and posterior/inferior ILA on the same side.  The SFT is positive (indicating restricted mobility on the dysfunction side), whereas the sphinx and spring tests are negative (indicating adequate anterior motion).

## Unilateral sacral extension

Unilateral sacral extension involves posterior displacement of 1 sacral sulcus, with a shallow sulcus and anterior/superior ILA on the same side.  The SFT, sphinx test, and spring tests are all positive, indicating restricted posterior motion.

## Bilateral sacral flexion

In bilateral sacral flexion dysfunction, both sacral bases are displaced anteriorly, resulting in symmetric deep sacral sulci and symmetric posterior and inferior ILAs bilaterally.  The SFT may appear negative or symmetric because dysfunction is bilateral.  The sphinx and spring tests are typically negative, indicating no resistance to anterior motion.

## Bilateral sacral extension

Bilateral sacral extension dysfunction involves posterior displacement of both sacral bases.  This presents as symmetric shallow sacral sulci and symmetric anterior/superior ILAs bilaterally.  The SFT may be negative or symmetric due to bilateral involvement.  Both the sphinx test and the spring test are positive, highlighting resistance to posterior-to-anterior sacral motion.

# Sacral torsion diagnostic principles

## Nomenclature

Sacral **torsions** are characterized by the upper **(sacral sulci)** and lower **(ILAs)** sacrum **rotating in opposite directions** about a diagonal axis through the sacrum (ie, **oblique axis**).  The nomenclature of sacral torsion is "**direction of rotation" on "oblique axis**."

-   **Forward** torsions (FTs) (**r**ight on **r**ight, **l**eft on **l**eft) involve the sacral sulcus rotating anteriorly about an oblique axis in the same direction, with negative spring test results.  ("Matching letters march forward.")
-   **Backward** torsions (right on left, left on right) involve posterior rotation with the rotation axis in the opposite direction and a positive spring test.  Of note, backward torsions are typically the most painful of the sacral somatic dysfunctions. ("Mismatched letters mosey backward.")

With sacral dysfunctions, the positions of the sacral sulci and ILAs are typically combined with the results of specialized tests (eg, spring test) to name the dysfunction.

The side of the positive-seated FT corresponds to the dysfunctional sacral sulcus; the "direction of rotation" is named for the side with the ILA/sacral sulcus that has moved posterior/shallower, and the "oblique axis" passes through and is named for the sacral sulcus on the side *opposite* the positive-seated FT.  For example, in a right on left sacral torsion:

-   The seated FT is positive on the right, indicating that the right sacral sulcus is dysfunctional (either deep/anterior or shallow/posterior) and that there is a left oblique axis (*opposite* side of positive-seated FT).
-   The right sacral sulcus is shallow/posterior and the left ILA is deep/anterior, indicating right sacral rotation about that left oblique axis.

## L5 shortcut

In sacral torsion, the position of L5 can be used as a shortcut (if provided for examination purposes).  In sacral torsions, **L5 rotates in the opposite direction of the sacrum and sidebends toward the oblique axis**.

For example, in a patient with an L5 that is rotated left and sidebent left, the sacrum must be rotated right (opposite direction to L5 rotation) on a left oblique axis (same side of L5 sidebending).  Therefore, the diagnosis would be a right on left sacral torsion.

The following figure summarizes sacral torsions, which are described in further detail in the subsequent sections ((Figure 9)).

# Specific sacral torsions

## Left on left sacral torsion

In left on left sacral torsion, the sacrum rotates left around a left oblique axis, which runs diagonally from the left superior sacral sulcus to the right ILA.  This rotation drives the right sacral base anteriorly, making the right sacral sulcus deeper, whereas the left ILA becomes posterior and inferior due to the sacrum "twisting" backward on the left.  To maintain spinal equilibrium, L5 compensates by rotating right (opposite the sacral rotation).

The SFT is positive on the left because the left oblique axis restricts sacroiliac motion on that side.  The lumbosacral spring test is negative (springing is present) because the anteriorly rotated right sacral base allows easy recoil.  Findings are summarized in the figure ((Figure 10)).

## Right on left sacral torsion

In right on left sacral torsion, the sacrum rotates right around a left oblique axis.  This posteriorly displaces the right sacral base, causing the right sacral sulcus to become shallow, whereas the left ILA moves anteriorly and superiorly as the sacrum twists forward.  L5 compensates with left rotation to balance the lumbar spine.

The SFT remains positive on the left (side of the axis), reflecting restricted sacroiliac motion.  The lumbosacral spring test is positive (no spring) because the posteriorly rotated sacral base resists anterior pressure.  Findings are summarized in the figure ((Figure 11)).

## Right on right sacral torsion

In right on right sacral torsion, the sacrum rotates right around a right oblique axis, extending from the right superior sacral sulcus to the left ILA.  This anteriorly displaces the left sacral base, deepening the left sacral sulcus, whereas the right ILA becomes posterior and inferior.  L5 compensates by rotating left to align with the rotated sacrum.

The SFT is positive on the right (side of the axis), indicating restricted motion at the right sacroiliac joint.  The lumbosacral spring test is negative (springing is present) because the anterior left sacral base allows smooth recoil.  Findings are summarized in the figure ((Figure 12)).

## Left on right sacral torsion

In left on right sacral torsion, the sacrum rotates left around a right oblique axis.  This posteriorly displaces the left sacral base, making the left sacral sulcus shallow, whereas the right ILA shifts anteriorly and superiorly.  L5 compensates with right rotation.

The SFT is positive on the right (side of the axis), reflecting restricted sacroiliac mobility.  The lumbosacral spring test is positive (no spring) because the posterior sacral base resists anterior pressure.  Findings are summarized in the figure ((Figure 13)).

# Osteopathic manipulative treatment

OMT for sacral dysfunctions aims to restore normal biomechanics, alleviate pain, and improve function.  Various techniques can be chosen based on the specific diagnosis, patient presentation, and physician preference.  The most commonly used techniques are direct muscle energy and high velocity–low amplitude (HVLA).

## Direct muscle energy technique 

Direct muscle energy involves guiding the dysfunctional joint toward its restrictive barrier and then using the patient's own muscle effort (isometric or isotonic contraction) to move the joint through the barrier, often relying on postisometric relaxation.

-   **General principles for sacral torsions**:  The modified Sims position (lateral recumbent with torso rotation) is commonly used.  The goal is to position L5 in a way that encourages the sacrum to move toward correction.  L5 rotates opposite to the sacrum and sidebends toward the engaged oblique axis.
-   **Positioning**:  The patient is typically positioned on the side of the engaged oblique axis.  For example, for a left on left (forward) sacral torsion, the patient would lie on the left side.
-   **Torso rotation**:  The patient's torso is rotated to influence L5 and thereby the sacrum.  A common mnemonic is "forward torsion = face down" (patient's face/torso rotated toward the table) and "backward torsion = back down" (patient's face/torso rotated away from the table).  This rotation helps engage the restrictive barrier at L5, which, in turn, influences the sacrum.
-   For example, in a left on left sacral torsion, positioning the patient on the left side with the torso rotated forward (face down) aims to engage the barrier to L5 left rotation/left sidebending, which would encourage sacral right rotation.
-   **Leg positioning and activation**:  The patient's legs are then positioned to further engage the sacral restrictive barrier (eg, by flexing the hips and allowing the legs to drop off the table to induce a corrective sacral rotation).  With the barrier engaged, the patient is instructed to perform a gentle isometric contraction against the physician's counterforce (eg, attempting to lift the legs toward the ceiling or rotate the pelvis against resistance) for 3-5 seconds.  This is followed by relaxation, during which the physician gently guides the sacrum into the new barrier (ie, postisometric relaxation).

The example of muscle energy for a left on left sacral torsion is shown in the image ((Figure 14)).  Positionings for other sacral torsions are shown in these images ((Figure 15)) ((Figure 16)) ((Figure 17)).

## High velocity–low amplitude technique

HVLA is a direct technique in which a rapid, short, and gentle thrust is applied through a restrictive barrier to restore normal joint motion.

-   **Principle**:  To move a joint beyond its pathologic restrictive barrier.
-   **Patient positioning**:  Commonly, the patient is prone for sacral HVLA.  The specific setup varies based on the dysfunction.  For instance, to correct a posteriorly displaced sacral base on 1 side, the physician might position the patient to localize force to that area.
-   **Application**:  The physician carefully positions the patient to isolate the dysfunctional segment and engage the restrictive barrier.  A quick, precise, and controlled thrust of low amplitude is then delivered.

# Summary

Sacral somatic dysfunctions, characterized by impaired sacral mobility and biomechanics, can significantly affect posture, gait, and pelvic stability.  Anatomically, the sacrum's key landmarks (sacral sulci, inferior lateral angles) and its articulation with L5 and the innominates are important for diagnosis.  Biomechanically, sacral motion occurs around oblique and transverse axes and is intricately linked to L5 mechanics, where L5 sidebending engages the oblique axis on the same side and L5 rotation induces sacral rotation in the opposite direction.

Diagnosis relies on tests, including the seated flexion test (identifies asymmetry), backward bending (sphinx) test (assesses anterior/posterior sacral base movement relative to L5 with extension), and lumbosacral spring test (evaluates posterior restrictions).  Dysfunctions are categorized as symmetric (bilateral flexion/extension) or asymmetric (unilateral flexion/extension, sacral torsions).  Sacral torsions (eg, left on left or right on left) are named by the direction of sacral rotation on a specific oblique axis, with L5 position often serving as a diagnostic shortcut.

Osteopathic manipulative treatment, particularly the direct muscle energy and high velocity–low amplitude techniques, is the main management modality for sacral somatic dysfunctions.

articles.markdown:
# Osteopathic Manipulative Treatment: Scoliosis # Introduction Scoliosis is an abnormal lateral curvature of the spine, commonly associated with back pain, stiffness, and related somatic dysfunctions.  Osteopathic manipulative treatment (OMT) is beneficial in managing scoliosis by addressing musculoskeletal imbalances, reducing pain, and enhancing functional mobility.  This article discusses anatomic and biomechanical characteristics, monitoring and management strategies, and the role of OMT. # Incidence and etiology Scoliosis affects approximately 2%-3% of the population, predominantly adolescents during periods of rapid skeletal growth.  Female patients are more commonly affected, particularly with spinal curves that progress and require intervention.  Most scoliosis cases (~80%) are idiopathic, meaning they have no identifiable cause.  However, scoliosis can also result from neuromuscular conditions (eg, cerebral palsy, muscular dystrophy), congenital vertebral anomalies, trauma, and leg-length discrepancies. # Anatomy and biomechanics ## Dextroscoliosis and levoscoliosis Scoliosis involves lateral spinal curvature with vertebral rotation and associated sidebending, typically classified as either dextroscoliosis or levoscoliosis ((Figure 1)): - **Dextroscoliosis** is characterized by a spinal curvature **convex** to the **right** side, involving left sidebending of vertebral segments. - **Levoscoliosis** involves a curvature **convex** to the **left**, with right sidebending of spinal segments. ## Functional versus structural scoliosis Scoliosis curves can be either functional or structural: - **Functional** curves are temporary and typically result from muscular imbalances, postural habits, or leg-length discrepancies.  These curves resolve or significantly improve with positional changes or correction of underlying factors. - **Structural** curves are fixed deformities involving permanent vertebral rotation and sidebending, which persist regardless of position or posture. ## Thoracic versus lumbar scoliosis Curves are also categorized by spinal regions involved: - **Thoracic** scoliosis, involving the upper to midback, is commonly associated with **rib prominence** due to vertebral rotation. - **Lumbar** scoliosis, affecting the lower spine, frequently results in **pelvic asymmetry** and **leg-length discrepancies**. # Diagnosis and classification Diagnosis involves clinical evaluation, palpation, and x-rays.  The standard method for quantifying spinal curvature is the **Cobb angle**, measured on an upright spinal radiograph ((Figure 2)): - Identify the vertebrae at the superior and inferior ends of the spinal curve (most displaced vertebrae). - Draw parallel lines along the superior endplate of the upper vertebra and the inferior endplate of the lower vertebra. - The intersection of perpendicular lines drawn from these lines defines the Cobb angle. Scoliosis severity classification is based on the Cobb angle, as follows: - **Mild**:  5-19 degrees. - **Moderate**:  20-49 degrees. - **Severe**:  ≥50 degrees. # Management ## Principles of management Management depends on scoliosis severity, rate of progression, and skeletal maturity (assessed via Tanner staging and radiographic markers): - **Mild** scoliosis:  Managed conservatively with **strengthening exercises** and OMT.  Follow-up imaging is usually unnecessary after reaching skeletal maturity due to low progression risk. - **Moderate** scoliosis:  Monitored every 6 months, primarily managed with **spinal bracing** (>18 hr daily) ((Figure 3)).  **Rapid curve progression** (>5 degrees per year) despite adequate bracing warrants **surgical evaluation**. - **Severe** scoliosis:  Typically managed **surgically** due to an increased risk of **cardiopulmonary compromise** (eg, restrictive lung disease, reduced preload impairing cardiac output) and further deformity progression. ## Osteopathic manipulative treatment OMT complements scoliosis management by addressing associated somatic dysfunctions, decreasing pain, and improving musculoskeletal function.  Common techniques include: - Muscle energy:  Facilitates improved vertebral alignment and reduces muscular tension. - Myofascial release:  Alleviates fascial restrictions and muscle imbalances. - Facilitated positional release:  Gently normalizes hypertonic muscles and vertebral dysfunction. In addition, OMT addressing pelvic and lower extremity dysfunctions reduces compensatory mechanisms and enhances overall alignment and mobility.  Associated innominate asymmetry and leg-length discrepancies are discussed in a separate article. # Summary Scoliosis is an abnormal lateral curvature of the spine, often accompanied by vertebral rotation and sidebending, classified as either dextroscoliosis (convex curve to the right with left sidebending) or levoscoliosis (convex curve to the left with right sidebending).  Management involves understanding the incidence, etiologies, and differences between functional (temporary, reversible) and structural (fixed, permanent) curves.  Diagnosis and severity are assessed using the Cobb angle, which guides treatment and monitoring strategies.  Mild scoliosis is typically managed conservatively, moderate cases usually require regular monitoring and bracing, and severe cases may necessitate surgical intervention due to significant cardiopulmonary risks ((Table 1)).  Osteopathic manipulative treatment provides supportive care to alleviate pain, correct somatic dysfunctions, and enhance musculoskeletal function and is particularly beneficial for mild to moderate scoliosis. ​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​​‌​​‌​​‌​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​

articles.title: Osteopathic Manipulative Treatment: Short-Leg Syndrome (Leg-Length Discrepancy)
articles.markdown: # Osteopathic Manipulative Treatment: Short-Leg Syndrome (Leg-Length Discrepancy) # Introduction Short-leg syndrome, also known as leg-length discrepancy (LLD), is characterized by unequal lower limb lengths, leading to pelvic asymmetry, spinal curvature, and chronic pain.  Osteopathic manipulative treatment (OMT) is valuable in managing short-leg syndrome, particularly functional LLD, by addressing biomechanical imbalances and associated somatic dysfunctions and by promoting symptom relief and functional improvement.  This article discusses anatomic considerations, etiologies, clinical presentations, diagnostic methods, and therapeutic roles of OMT and heel lifts in managing short-leg syndrome. # Incidence and etiology Clinically significant LLDs **(>5 mm)** occur in roughly 10%-15% of individuals.  LLD can be classified into anatomic and functional causes. ## Anatomic Anatomic discrepancies involve **bone length differences** that are measurable radiographically.  These commonly result from **congenital** conditions (eg, growth plate disturbances, hip dysplasia), **trauma**, or surgical procedures.  A common example is **hip replacement surgery**, which often aims to restore the affected limb to its prearthritic length ((Figure 1)). ## Functional Functional discrepancies arise from **reversible** causes affecting pelvic alignment (eg, **scoliosis**, muscular imbalances) ((Figure 2)).  These typically improve with OMT or correction of underlying causes. # Anatomy and biomechanics LLDs alter biomechanics, causing compensatory pelvic and spinal adaptations: - **Pelvic tilt and rotation**:  A shorter leg typically induces a downward pelvic tilt and anterior innominate rotation on the affected side as the body attempts to functionally lengthen the limb, resulting in an inferior anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) on that side. - **Lumbar spine compensatio**n:  Functional scoliosis, characterized by vertebral rotation and lateral curvature with the convexity typically toward the short limb, is a common adaptation. - **Lower extremity compensation**:  Adaptations within the lower extremities, such as knee hyperextension on the short side or flexion on the long side, and changes in foot and ankle mechanics (eg, supination on the short side, pronation on the long side) can lead to altered gait, muscle imbalances, increased joint stress, and potential degenerative changes over time. ## Diagnosis and measurement Diagnosis involves clinical evaluation, palpation of pelvic landmarks (ASIS, posterosuperior iliac spine \[PSIS\]), standing flexion tests, gait assessment, and radiographic imaging to measure **femoral head heights and sacral base unleveling**.  Severity classification is generally as follows: - **Mild**:  <10 mm. - **Moderate**:  10-20 mm. - **Severe**:  >20 mm. # Management Management strategies are guided by severity, underlying cause, and patient age: - **Mild**:  Managed **conservatively** with footwear modifications, exercises, and OMT to address pelvic and spinal compensations. - **Moderate**:  Managed with **heel lifts**, regular monitoring, and targeted OMT.  Heel lift initiation for young, flexible patients includes 3.2 mm (1/8 inch) increments every 2 weeks and for elderly patients, 1.6 mm (1/16 inch) increments every 2 weeks. - **Severe**:  **Surgical** interventions or significant orthotic management combined with rehabilitative and osteopathic care. ## Heel lift recommendations Heel lifts are recommended when femoral head height discrepancies exceed 5 mm (3/16 inch) despite OMT.  The aim is typically to correct **half to three-fourths of the measured LLD** in **chronic** conditions; **full correction may be considered in acute cases** (eg, following recent hip replacement surgery).  Typically, the maximum heel lift is 1/2 inch total (1/4 inch inside shoe, 1/4 inch outside shoe).  Aggressiveness in the correction rate depends on patient tolerance; in general: - **Young**, flexible patients:  Begin with **1/8 inch** increments every **2 weeks.** - **Elderly** patients:  Begin with **1/16 inch** increments every **2 weeks**. ## Osteopathic manipulative treatment OMT effectively treats functional LLD and related somatic dysfunctions.  Commonly used techniques include: - Muscle energy techniques:  Improve pelvic alignment and reduce muscular hypertonicity. - Myofascial release:  Relieve fascial restrictions affecting compensatory patterns. - High velocity–low amplitude technique:  Particularly, leg-pull techniques for correcting posterior innominate rotations and partially lengthening the shorter leg. - Balanced ligamentous tension:  Normalize ligamentous tension, enhancing alignment and mobility. Specific somatic dysfunction presentations, such as superior ASIS and inferior PSIS indicating posterior innominate rotation, can guide precise diagnosis and targeted OMT. # Summary Short-leg syndrome, also known as leg-length discrepancy, encompasses both anatomic (true bone difference) and functional (apparent) differences in leg lengths.  These discrepancies can lead to pelvic asymmetry, compensatory spinal curvatures, and altered biomechanics throughout the body.  Diagnosis relies on thorough clinical evaluation and imaging studies.  Management strategies are tailored to the individual and may incorporate osteopathic manipulative treatment, heel lifts, and, in severe cases, surgical interventions.  Osteopathic manipulative treatment is particularly beneficial for addressing functional discrepancies and the musculoskeletal compensations associated with anatomic causes, aiming to improve alignment, reduce pain, and enhance overall musculoskeletal function. ​‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌​​​​​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​‌‌​​​​‌‌​​‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​​​​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​​‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​

articles.markdown:
# Osteopathic Manipulative Treatment: Techniques # Introduction Osteopathic manipulative therapy (OMT) is a form of manual medicine aimed at improving physiologic function and supporting the body's self-healing mechanisms.  OMT integrates precise anatomic knowledge with hands-on therapeutic interventions to address somatic dysfunction.  This article provides a general overview of key OMT techniques, including muscle energy; high-velocity low-amplitude; counterstrain; facilitated positional release; Still technique; balanced ligamentous tension; and lymphatic techniques. # Direct versus indirect techniques OMT is broadly classified into direct and indirect techniques, depending on how the physician engages the restrictive barrier (ie, where further movement is prematurely "stuck") of dysfunctional tissues: - **Direct** techniques:  Involve moving the restricted structure **toward the barrier of restriction**.  They often require more physical force and patient participation and are typically used when the tissues are not acutely inflamed or overly sensitive. - **Indirect** techniques:  Involve moving the dysfunctional tissue **away from the barrier of restriction** and into a position of ease.  These are typically gentler and often better suited for acute conditions or patients with heightened pain sensitivity. # Active versus passive OMT techniques are also classified based on the level of patient involvement required: - **Active** techniques:  Require patient participation and voluntary muscle contraction.  The patient actively engages in movements or muscle contractions as guided by the physician. - **Passive** techniques:  Require minimal to no patient effort, relying entirely on the physician's actions.  The patient remains relaxed while the physician applies specific forces or positions the patient passively. # Muscle energy Muscle energy techniques (METs) involve active muscle contraction by the patient against a counterforce applied by the physician.  The type of muscle contraction performed by the patient is called **isometric contraction**, in which a muscle contracts without changing length, producing tension without movement ((Figure 1)).  METs utilize **postisometric relaxation**, in which the muscle experiences a period of reduced tone after a sustained isometric contraction lasting 3-5 seconds.  These techniques restore mobility, reduce muscle tension, and reestablish joint alignment.  METs can be performed directly or indirectly. ## Direct muscle energy Direct MET engages the muscle contraction directly **against the restrictive barrier**.  The physician positions the patient at the restrictive barrier and instructs the patient to perform a specific isometric contraction against resistance, held for 3-5 seconds, followed by relaxation and passive repositioning into a new restrictive barrier ((Figure 2)).  This is repeated multiple times to achieve optimal range of motion using postisometric relaxation. For example, an innominate outflare somatic dysfunction can be corrected by resisting the patient's hip rotation in the direction opposite to the restricted movement. ## Indirect muscle energy Indirect MET moves **away from the restrictive barrier** into a position of ease, utilizing reciprocal inhibition (when an agonist muscle contracts, its antagonist automatically relaxes) or postisometric relaxation.  It is particularly beneficial in acute or highly sensitive conditions, where direct pressure might be too painful. For example, acute lumbar muscle spasm can be treated by positioning muscles in their direction of ease and engaging the antagonistic muscles gently to induce relaxation of the spasming muscle. # High-velocity low-amplitude High-velocity low-amplitude (HVLA) techniques involve the application of a brief, controlled, and rapid force to move a joint past its restrictive barrier (ie, **direct**), correcting misalignments and restoring functional mobility ((Figure 3)).  The hallmark of this technique is its speed rather than force. For example, treatment of a thoracic vertebra with restricted rotation can involve precise positioning followed by a quick, shallow thrust that realigns the vertebral segment, improving spinal mechanics immediately.  Contraindications for HVLA techniques are shown in the following table ((Table 1)). # Myofascial release Myofascial release is a versatile technique that can be applied either directly or indirectly to release restrictions within the fascial system.  Fascia is the connective tissue that envelops muscles, organs, and other structures, and restrictions in this tissue can contribute to pain, dysfunction, and decreased mobility.  Myofascial release involves palpating the affected area and applying a sustained, gentle pressure or stretch until a release is felt.  The physician may follow or gently oppose tissue motion, depending on the desired therapeutic effect. For example, congestion/edema found in sinusitis and otitis media (ear infection) can be treated using the Galbreath technique to facilitate patency of the Eustachian tube and increase lymphatic drainage through the preauricular and parotid lymph nodes.  To perform the Galbreath technique, the physician applies slow, repetitive anterior and medial traction to the mandible (increasing displacement at the temporomandibular joint) for several minutes. Myofascial release techniques can also effectively modulate autonomic function by targeting specific ganglia throughout the body.  The superior ganglia release technique (T10 through T11) and inferior ganglia release technique (T12 through L2) both reduce sympathetic tone, affecting the jejunum to midtransverse colon and lower gastrointestinal tract, respectively.  These applications make myofascial release particularly valuable for conditions such as postoperative ileus and constipation.  Visceral autonomic innervation and additional techniques are discussed in more detail in a separate article. # Articulatory techniques Articulatory techniques are direct, passive osteopathic manipulative methods involving rhythmic, repetitive movements that guide a joint through its full range of motion.  The primary goal is to gradually increase mobility, reduce restrictions, and restore normal joint function.  The physician employs controlled, low-velocity movements to repeatedly approach and disengage the restriction, enhancing local circulation and reducing muscle tension and joint stiffness. For example, rib raising involves applying rhythmic lifting motions to the rib cage, repeatedly engaging restrictive barriers around the costovertebral joints.  This repetitive mobilization gradually reduces restrictions, improving rib cage compliance, respiratory mechanics, and lymphatic drainage.  Another example is the Spencer technique, which is used for adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder) ((Figure 4)). # Counterstrain Counterstrain is a gentle, **indirect** technique designed to relieve musculoskeletal pain by passively placing the affected area into a position of maximum comfort.  This reduces inappropriate proprioceptive feedback, muscle spasm, and the sensitivity of **tender points**—palpable areas of localized tenderness associated with dysfunctional segments.  The therapeutic effect is believed to occur as a result of **resetting muscle spindle** activity, which regulates muscle tone and reflex contraction. For example, a tender point in the psoas muscle is treated by positioning the patient's hip into flexion until pain diminishes significantly ((Figure 5)).  The position is held comfortably for about 90 seconds to allow the muscle spindles to reset.  Tender points and counterstrain are discussed in more detail in a separate article. # Facilitated positional release Facilitated positional release quickly reduces muscle hypertonicity and restores mobility through **indirect** myofascial release.  The technique involves placing the body in a neutral position, followed by applying an activating force such as compression or torsion, facilitating immediate muscle relaxation. For example, cervical muscle spasm can be effectively addressed by performing the following steps: - First, move the affected cervical joint into the neutral position and apply a facilitative force (eg, axial compression), which relaxes the surrounding tissues and allows for easier manipulation. - Then, move the joint into a position of ease (ie, in the direction that it is "stuck") while maintaining the facilitative force to shorten and further relax the affected hypertonic muscles. - Last, hold the hypertonic muscles in this shortened position for several seconds, which causes release of muscle tension by decreasing input to the muscle spindles (the spindles normally activate muscle contraction in response to increases in muscle fiber length). # Still technique Still technique is a unique osteopathic method that **combines both indirect and direct** components in a fluid **sequence**.  The physician begins by positioning the affected area in a position of ease (indirect) and introducing a compressive or torsional force.  While maintaining this force, the physician slowly guides the tissue through the path of least resistance back toward the restrictive barrier (direct), facilitating release and improved motion.  The technique is subtle, efficient, and well tolerated, even in patients with acute pain. For example, a lumbar segment with rotational dysfunction is first placed in a position of comfort, after which compression is applied along the spinal axis, and the segment is gently moved through its range of motion toward the restriction. # Balanced ligamentous tension Balanced ligamentous tension (BLT) utilizes gentle and precise positioning to equalize ligamentous tension around joints.  It is an **indirect** technique that facilitates the body's intrinsic self-corrective mechanisms by holding tissues at their point of balance. For example, a sacroiliac joint dysfunction may be treated by carefully adjusting the joint until ligamentous tensions feel equally balanced.  The physician holds this position gently, allowing inherent physiologic mechanisms to realign tissues and reduce tension naturally. # Lymphatic techniques Lymphatic techniques involve the rhythmic pumping or release of fascial diaphragms to augment the body's intrinsic fluid movement.  They are especially useful in conditions such as congestion, edema, or infection, where clearing fluids and boosting immune cell transport are desired.  Commonly used lymphatic techniques include: - **Thoracic pump**:  The physician applies rhythmic pressure to the patient's sternum or lower rib cage, creating pressure changes that enhance lymphatic and venous return.  Benefits include improved lymph flow, mobilization of lymphocytes, clearance of pulmonary secretions, and reduction of upper body edema.  This technique stimulates deep breathing and improves chest wall compliance. - **Abdominal pump**:  Rhythmic compression over the abdomen enhances lymphatic drainage from abdominal organs and lower extremities.  This technique increases thoracic duct lymph flow and releases immune cells from mesenteric lymph nodes.  It supports immune function during infections and relieves organ congestion.  The motion can stimulate intestinal peristalsis to improve postsurgical bowel function. - **Pedal pump**:  The physician grasps the supine patient's feet and rhythmically dorsiflexes them, creating an oscillatory wave through the body that encourages lymphatic and venous return from the legs.  This gentle technique reduces peripheral edema, improves cardiac preload, and stimulates full-body lymphatic flow.  The approach is particularly useful for the prevention of stasis in patients who are postoperative or bedridden. Restrictions should be addressed in **sequence from central to peripheral**, as demonstrated by the following: - **Thoracic inlet release**:  All lymphatic drainage must pass through the thoracic inlet (ie, superior thoracic aperture; formed by T1, the first ribs, and the manubrium) before reentering the venous circulation.  Therefore, myofascial release to the thoracic inlet should be completed prior to other lymphatic treatments to decrease any restrictions and increase the overall lymphatic drainage from the entire body ((Figure 6)). - **Promote respiratory-assisted lymphatic flow**:  After thoracic inlet release, the next step is to maximize efficient movement of the diaphragm and ribs to facilitate respiratory-assisted lymphatic drainage.  Diaphragm motion can be enhanced by **doming the diaphragm** and mobilizing soft tissue at the inferior thoracic aperture (formed by T12, ribs 11 and 12, and the xiphoid process).  Techniques that improve thoracic spine motion and rib cage compliance (eg, rib raising, thoracic pump) also maximize respiratory-assisted lymphatic flow. - **Peripheral pump techniques**:  Once the thoracic inlet and diaphragm are free of restrictions, peripheral lymphatic pump techniques are performed to increase lymphatic return from different areas of the body. Contraindications to lymphatic techniques include severe localized **infection** (could potentially spread infection), **decompensated heart failure** (increased venous return), and **malignancy** (could facilitate metastasis). # Clinical applications OMT is clinically effective for a wide range of conditions (particularly those involving somatic dysfunction), including the following: - **Musculoskeletal pain**:  Low back pain, neck pain, and joint dysfunctions. - **Headaches**:  Tension-type and cervicogenic headaches. - **Respiratory disorders**:  Asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and pneumonia (improving rib mechanics and lymphatic drainage). - **Gastrointestinal issues**:  Postoperative ileus (restoration of visceral autonomic function). - **Lymphatic and circulatory conditions**:  Edema and immune system support. - **Chronic stress and autonomic imbalance**:  Techniques that influence parasympathetic/sympathetic tone. OMT is tailored to each patient's clinical presentation, level of discomfort, and sensitivity to manipulation, and techniques are often combined in a single session for maximum benefit. **Treatment sequencing** is a strategic aspect of OMT.  Sessions generally begin with gentle, indirect methods (eg, counterstrain, BLT) to reduce muscle tone and discomfort.  This prepares tissues for more direct interventions (eg, direct muscle energy, HVLA).  The session may conclude with lymphatic techniques to support lymphatic clearance and recovery. # Summary Osteopathic manipulative treatment (OMT) is a hands-on approach that restores structural and functional balance by engaging the body's self-healing mechanisms.  Techniques are classified as direct (moving toward the restriction) or indirect (moving away from the restriction), with clinical application tailored to tissue sensitivity and dysfunction.  Techniques are summarized in the following table ((Table 2)).  OMT is effective at treating musculoskeletal pain, headaches, respiratory and gastrointestinal dysfunctions, and somatic manifestations of stress.  Sequencing typically begins with indirect methods, progresses to direct techniques, and concludes with lymphatic drainage to maximize physiologic benefit. ​‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌

articles.title: Osteopathic Manipulative Treatment: Tender Points And Counterstrain
articles.markdown:
# Osteopathic Manipulative Treatment: Tender Points And Counterstrain # Introduction Tender points are discrete, highly sensitive areas associated with somatic dysfunctions and located in muscles, fascia, tendons, and ligaments.  Counterstrain, an osteopathic manipulative treatment (OMT) technique, utilizes these tender points diagnostically and therapeutically.  This article outlines the pathophysiologic basis, precise anatomic locations, and diagnostic implications of tender points, and the therapeutic approach of counterstrain. # Pathophysiology Tender points are tender nodules, generally 1-2 cm in diameter, that occur due to **inappropriate neuromuscular reflexes** following injury, strain, or chronic dysfunction.  Tender points represent altered proprioceptive reflexes, causing sustained muscle contraction and localized ischemia, thereby leading to **pain and tenderness**.  **Counterstrain** seeks to **interrupt** these **reflexive cycles** by positioning the patient to relax the affected tissues, diminishing neuromuscular strain and pain.  This is typically performed by positioning the patient to **shorten the involved muscle**.  An exception is for so-called "maverick tender points," which are uncommon and follow different rules for counterstrain: for these points (typically found in the cervical spine), counterstrain is performed by positioning the patient to lengthen the involved muscle. The following section outlines how to perform the counterstrain technique.  Specific tender points, which are systematically categorized by anatomic region, are discussed later in the article.  Tender points differ from trigger points in that tender points do not typically radiate pain when palpated, though they are notably sensitive and painful. # Counterstrain technique Counterstrain is a gentle, **indirect, and passive** treatment modality that positions the patient's body in a manner that reduces tenderness and allows neuromuscular reflexes to normalize.  The following provides a generalized approach to performing counterstrain: ## Identify the tender point The physician palpates anatomic areas for suspected tender points.  A positive point is one that produces a focal, sharp pain response with gentle pressure, usually rated **at least 7** out of 10 in tenderness. ## Establish a baseline Once a tender point is located, the physician asks the patient to quantify the tenderness level.  This allows for comparison after treatment. ## Position for comfort The patient is then passively positioned such that the tenderness at the point is **reduced by at least 70%**.  This usually involves shortening the muscle associated with the tender point (except for maverick tender points).  Positioning can include flexion, extension, rotation, sidebending, or limb adjustments. ## Fine-tune the position Small adjustments in positioning are made to find the most comfortable position. ## Hold the position The final position is **held for 90 seconds**.  During this time, the muscle spindle activity normalizes, and the proprioceptive reflex resets.  It is critical that the patient remains **passive and relaxed**. ## Slowly return to neutral After the 90-second hold, the patient is slowly and passively returned to a neutral position to avoid reactivating the dysfunction. ## Reassess The clinician palpates the original tender point to assess reduction of pain and tension.  A successful treatment will result in a significant reduction or resolution of the tenderness. For example, counterstrain for the psoas major muscle involves monitoring the tender point (located two-thirds of the distance between the anterior superior iliac spine \[ASIS\] and midline) while flexing the hip until pain is minimized ((Figure 1)).  This sequence is repeated for each tender point identified in a treatment session.  The following section discusses specific tender points and treatment positions. # Cervical tender points Anterior and posterior cervical tender points are discussed below and summarized in the following table ((Table 1)).  Counterstrain treatment positions, which involve moving the **neck**, are described. ## Anterior cervical (AC) - AC1: - Location:  Near the angle of the mandible and transverse process (TP) of C1. - Position:  Marked rotation away to lengthen (maverick point). - AC2-AC6: - Location:  Anterolateral aspect of corresponding TP. - Position:  Flex, sidebend away, rotate away (F, SA, RA). - AC7: - Location:  On clavicle, near clavicular attachment of sternocleidomastoid (SCM). - Position:  Flex, sidebend toward, rotate away (F, ST, RA) (maverick point). - AC8: - Location:  On clavicle, near sternal SCM attachment. - Position:  Flex, sidebend away, rotate away (F, SA, RA). ## Posterior cervical (PC) - PC1 (midline): - Location:  Just lateral to the inion. - Position:  *Flex* (maverick point) with fine-tuning with sidebending and rotation. - PC1 (lateral): - Location:  Between inion and mastoid process. - Position:  Extend, sidebend away, rotate away (E, SA, RA). - PC2 (midline): - Location:  Superior aspect of C2 spinous process (SP). - Position:  Extend, sidebend away, rotate away (E, SA, RA). - PC2 (lateral): - Location:  On inferior nuchal line. - Position:  Extend, sidebend away, rotate away (E, SA, RA). - PC3 (midline): - Location:  Inferior aspect of C2 SP. - Position:  Flex, sidebend away, rotate away (F, SA, RA). - PC3-PC7 (lateral): - Location:  Posterolatreal aspect of corresponding articular process. - Position:  Extend, sidebend away, rotate away (E, SA, RA). - PC4-PC8 (midline): - Location:  Inferior aspect of the SP of the above vertebrae (C3-C7). - Position:  Extend, sidebend away, rotate away (E, SA, RA). # Thoracic tender points Anterior and posterior thoracic tender points are discussed below and summarized in the following table ((Table 2)).  Counterstrain treatment positions, which involve moving the **torso**, are described. ## Anterior thoracic (AT) - AT1: - Location:  Midline at the sternal notch. - Position:  Flex. - AT2-AT6: - Location:  Midline at the sternocostal junctions. - Position:  Flex. - AT7-AT11: - Location:  Midline and lateral to the rectus abdominis (bilaterally). - Position:  Flex, sidebend toward, rotate away (F, ST, RA). - AT12: - Location:  Superior to the ASIS, near iliac crest. - Position:  Flex, sidebend toward, rotate away (F, ST, RA). ## Posterior thoracic (PT) - PT1-PT12: - Location:  Tender points can vary and may be found on the spinous or transverse processes. - Position:  Extend the torso and sidebend away (E, SA).  For tender points on the SP, rotate away (E, SA, RA).  For tender points on the TP, rotate toward (E, SA, RT). # Rib tender points Anterior and posterior rib tender points are discussed below and summarized in the following table ((Table 3)).  Counterstrain treatment positions, which involve moving the **torso**, are described. ## Anterior ribs (AR) - AR1: - Location:  Sternocostal junction of rib 1. - Position:  Flex, sidebend toward, rotate toward (F, ST, RT). - AR2: - Location:  Over rib 2 along midclavicular line. - Position:  Flex, sidebend toward, rotate toward (F, ST, RT). - AR3-AR10: - Location:  Over corresponding rib (3-10) along anterior axillary line. - Position:  Flex, sidebend toward, rotate toward (F, ST, RT). ## Posterior ribs (PR) - PR1: - Location:  1" lateral to the articulation of rib 1 and the T1 TP. - Position:  Extend, sidebend away, rotate toward (E, SA, RT). - PR2-PR10: - Location:  Angle of the corresponding rib (2-10). - Position:  Sidebend away, rotate away.  Fine-tuning with slight flexion or extension may be needed. # Lumbar tender points Anterior and posterior lumbar tender points are discussed below and summarized in the following table ((Table 4)).  Counterstrain treatment positions, which involve moving the **leg and hip**, are described. ## Anterior lumbar (AL) - AL1: - Location:  Near the ASIS. - Position:  Flex, sidebend toward, rotate away (F, ST, RA). - AL2-AL4: - Location:  Around the anterior inferior iliac spine. - Position:  Flex, sidebend away, rotate toward (F, SA, RT).  Slight variations exist. - AL5: - Location:  On the pubic symphysis. - Position:  Flex, sidebend away, rotate away (F, SA, RA). ## Posterior lumbar (PL) - PL1-PL5 - Location:  On the corresponding SP and TPs. - Position:  Extend, sidebend away, rotate away (E, SA, RA). # Pelvic tender points Anterior and posterior pelvic tender points are discussed below and summarized in the following table ((Table 5)). ## Anterior pelvic - Psoas major: - Location:  Two-thirds of the distance between the ASIS and midline. - Position:  Hip flexion. - Psoas minor (ie, low ileum): - Location:  Just lateral to the pubic symphysis. - Position:  Hip flexion. - Iliacus: - Location:  One-third of the distance between the ASIS and midline. - Position:  Flex the hip and knees, cross legs in a frog-leg position ((Figure 2)). - Pectineus (inguinal): - Location:  On the superior pubis. - Position:  Flex the hip and knee, cross opposite leg over the affected leg, and internally rotate. ## Posterior pelvic - Piriformis: - Location:  7 cm medial to and slightly above the greater trochanter. - Position:  With the patient prone, the hip and knee are flexed and abducted.  Then fine-tuning with internal rotation or external rotation is added. - Upper pole L5 (UPL5): - Location:  Just above the posterior superior iliac spine (PSIS). - Position:  With the patient prone, extend the hip, adduct and fine-tune with rotation of the thigh internally/externally. - Lower pole L5 (LPL5): - Location:  Just above the posterior superior iliac spine (PSIS). - Position:  With the patient prone, flex and adduct the hip.  Then internally rotate the thigh. # Extremity tender points ## Upper extremities - Levator scapula: - Location:  Superior angle of the scapula. - Position:  Extend the shoulder and retract the scapula. - Supraspinatus: - Location:  Within the supraspinatus muscle or greater tuberosity of the humerus. - Position:  Abduct the arm to 45 degrees. - Subscapularis: - Location:  Anterolateral scapula (near axillary region). - Position:  Extend, internally rotate, and slightly abduct the arm. - Acromioclavicular: - Location:  On the AC joint. - Position:  Flex and adduct the shoulder while applying slight traction downward. - Radial head: - Location:  Anterolateral or posterolateral head of radius. - Position:  Extend the elbow and supinate.  Fine-tune with ulnar abduction/adduction. - Wrist: - Location:  Distal forearm. - Position:  Flex the wrist (for flexor tender point) or extend the wrist (for extensor tender point). ## Lower extremities - Lateral trochanter: - Location:  On lateral thigh between greater trochanter and knee. - Position:  Abduct and slightly externally rotate the knee. - Patella: - Location:  On the patellar tendon. - Position:  Translate the distal femur posteriorly while supporting the ankle. - Menisci: - Location:  On the medial or lateral meniscus. - Position:  Flex the knee.  Then fine-tune with internal rotation and adduction (medial meniscus) or external rotation and abduction (lateral meniscus). - Anterior cruciate ligament: - Location:  On the distal hamstring. - Position:  Translate the proximal tibia posteriorly. - Posterior cruciate ligament: - Location:  Near the posterior tibial plateau (popliteus muscle). - Position:  Translate the distal femur posteriorly. - Ankles: - Location:  Anterior and inferior to the lateral malleolus (lateral ankle) or inferior to the medial malleolus (medial ankle). - Position:  Evert the foot (lateral) or invert the foot (medial). # Summary Tender points represent focal neuromuscular dysfunctions that are sensitive to palpation and indicative of underlying somatic dysfunctions.  They are treated with counterstrain, an osteopathic manipulative therapy technique based on passive positioning and neuromuscular reflex reset.  Understanding the anatomic distribution and diagnostic significance of tender points, as well as the therapeutic application of counterstrain, is important.  This article provided a comprehensive list of tender points with tables.  A summary of treatment position rules is shown in the following table ((Table 6)). ​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​​​‌​​​​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​​​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌​​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌
