articles.title: Osteopathic Manipulative Treatment: Thoracic Spine
articles.markdown: # Osteopathic Manipulative Treatment: Thoracic Spine # Introduction Osteopathic manipulative treatment (OMT) may effectively address thoracic spine dysfunction, relieving midback pain, improving respiratory mechanics, and enhancing overall thoracic mobility.  This article discusses thoracic spine anatomy, biomechanics, somatic dysfunctions, and OMT techniques.  The ribs and scoliosis are discussed in separate articles. # Thoracic vertebrae The thoracic spine consists of 12 vertebrae (T1 through T12) with facets oriented primarily in the coronal plane, facilitating **rotation**, with limited flexion, extension, and sidebending.  Stability is provided by robust ligamentous structures, including the anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments and intertransverse ligaments. Thoracic curvature naturally forms a **kyphotic** alignment, optimizing spinal stability and facilitating load distribution.  Excessive kyphosis (hyperkyphosis) or hypomobility can lead to biomechanical dysfunction, chronic pain syndromes, and impaired respiratory function.  The thoracic vertebrae articulate with the ribs via costovertebral and costotransverse joints, which are crucial for thoracic cage stability and respiratory mechanics. ## Anatomic landmarks **Scapular anatomic landmarks** are useful for quickly identifying specific thoracic vertebrae during the diagnosis of thoracic vertebral somatic dysfunctions ((Figure 1)): - The **spine** of the scapula is located at the level of the **T3** spinous process. - The **inferior angle** of the scapula is located at the level of the **T7** spinous process. The spinous process can then be used to locate the transverse processes, allowing for segmental motion testing (ie, rotation, sidebending).  The location of the spinous process relative to the transverse processes varies in the thoracic spine (referred to as the "rule of threes"): - **T1-T3** spinous process:  At the **same level** as the corresponding transverse processes. - **T4-T6** spinous process:  **Halfway between** the corresponding transverse processes and the transverse processes of the vertebra below. - **T7-T9** spinous process:  At the level of the transverse processes of the **vertebra below**. - T10-T12 spinous processes: - **T10** spinous process:  At the level of the transverse processes of the **vertebra below** (T11). - **T11** spinous process:  **Halfway between** the corresponding transverse processes (T11) and the transverse processes of the vertebra below (T12). - **T12** spinous process:  At the **same level** as the corresponding transverse processes (T12). Additional landmarks include the vena caval foramen (T8), esophageal hiatus (T10), and aortic hiatus (T12) ((Figure 2)). # Thoracic spine disorders ## Thoracic strain and sprain Thoracic strains (muscular injury) and sprains (ligamentous injury) occur from trauma, poor posture, or repetitive movements.  They present with localized pain, muscle spasms, and restricted motion.  Palpation demonstrates hypertonicity and tenderness in paraspinal muscles (eg, trapezius, rhomboids, erector spinae).  OMT techniques such as soft tissue manipulation, myofascial release, and muscle energy technique can restore mobility and relieve pain. ## Thoracic disc herniation Thoracic disc herniation is uncommon but, if severe, may cause localized thoracic pain, radicular symptoms, and neurologic deficits.  Conservative management includes OMT to reduce paraspinal hypertonicity, improve vertebral mobility, and alleviate compressive symptoms using gentle techniques such as facilitated positional release and indirect myofascial release. ## Thoracic vertebral somatic dysfunctions Somatic dysfunctions in the thoracic spine present as restricted vertebral segment motion, typically involving rotation, flexion, or extension dysfunctions.  OMT techniques such as high-velocity, low-amplitude (HVLA) thrust and muscle energy technique effectively restore normal segmental movement. HVLA thrust is a direct technique that moves the dysfunctional joint through its restrictive barrier to (ie, away from the direction that it is "stuck") by applying a rapid (high-velocity) and short (low-amplitude) thrust.  For thoracic dysfunctions, the "Kirksville crunch" is commonly used ((Figure 3)). # Summary Osteopathic manipulative treatment (OMT) effectively addresses thoracic spine dysfunction by alleviating mid-back pain, enhancing respiratory mechanics, and improving thoracic mobility.  Understanding the biomechanics, anatomy, and key landmarks of the thoracic spine, including the scapular positioning (spine at T3, inferior angle at T7) and the "rule of threes" governing spinous process relationships, is important for accurate diagnosis and treatment.  Thoracic disorders—including strains/sprains, disc herniation, and vertebral somatic dysfunctions—present with restricted vertebral movements, myofascial tension, and paraspinal hypertonicity.  OMT techniques (eg, high-velocity, low-amplitude thrust; muscle energy technique) provide targeted and individualized management to restore normal segmental movement, enhance thoracic function, and reduce symptoms. ​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​​​​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌​​​​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​​‌​​​​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌

articles.title: Osteopathic Manipulative Treatment: Upper Extremities
articles.markdown: # Osteopathic Manipulative Treatment: Upper Extremities # Introduction Osteopathic manipulative treatment (OMT) of the extremities can restore optimal function, alleviate pain, and enhance overall mobility.  An understanding of the mechanics of extremity movements, associated somatic dysfunctions, and relevant anatomic landmarks greatly enhances diagnostic accuracy and treatment effectiveness.  This article reviews these elements and discusses targeted osteopathic treatments for common upper extremity somatic dysfunctions. # Thoracic outlet syndrome The thoracic outlet is the area above the first rib (bordered by the clavicle, cervical vertebrae, and sternum) through which the primary upper extremity **neurovascular bundle** (ie, brachial plexus, subclavian vessels) passes to move from the neck to the shoulder ((Figure 1)). **Compression** of this neurovascular bundle in the thoracic outlet can be evaluated by assessing the radial pulse with specific provocative tests that accentuate compression.  An absent or diminished radial pulse indicates a positive test.  Compression can occur between distinct spaces: - **Anterior and middle scalene** (ie, scalene triangle):  Compression occurs due to muscle hypertrophy/hypertonia and is evaluated using the Adson test, which narrows this space by shoulder extension, external rotation, and slight abduction while the patient holds the breath and looks toward the side being tested. - **First rib and clavicle**:  Compression occurs due to somatic dysfunction of the clavicle and/or first rib and is evaluated using the military posture test, which narrows this space by shoulder extension and compression (ie, depression). - **Pectoralis minor and the upper ribs**:  Compression occurs due to hypertrophy/abnormal position of the pectoralis minor and is evaluated using the Wright (hyperabduction) test, which narrows this space by shoulder abduction and slight extension. The findings from these provocative tests help direct treatment with stretching, range of motion exercises, and OMT techniques (eg, muscle energy, myofascial release) to free the restrictions causing the neurovascular compression. # Adhesive capsulitis Adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder) is characterized by **glenohumeral joint capsule contracture** due to inflammation and fibrosis ((Figure 2)).  It usually develops spontaneously or secondary to immobilization after shoulder injury (eg, rotator cuff tear) or overuse.  The initial phase involves **inflammation** that causes severe shoulder pain.  This is followed by progressive fibrosis and glenohumeral capsule contracture that causes **reduced range** of motion (both active and passive) of the shoulder in all planes of motion. The primary goal of treating adhesive capsulitis is to reduce pain and increase shoulder mobility by releasing capsular contractions, thereby allowing patients to resume normal activities.  This can be achieved with the **Spencer technique** (passive range-of-motion treatment) and periodic corticosteroid injections.  The Spencer technique consists of **7 distinct stages of passive articulation** (eg, flexion, circumduction, internal rotation) at the glenohumeral joint that gently move the shoulder through the various restrictions caused by capsule contractures ((Figure 3)).  Patients in whom conservative management fails can be treated with arthroscopic capsular release or shoulder manipulation under general anesthesia. # Bicipital tendonitis Bicipital tendonitis results from inflammation and degeneration of the **long head of the biceps** tendon within the bicipital groove, often caused by overuse or chronic tendon subluxation ((Figure 4)).  The pain is often localized to the anterior shoulder over the bicipital groove but can also radiate down into the biceps.  Provocative tests that can assist in evaluation include: - **Speed test**:  Evaluates for pain during **shoulder flexion** beyond 90 degrees against resistance - Biceps squeeze test:  Assesses the integrity of the biceps tendon by evaluating for supination when the examiner firmly squeezes the patient's biceps. - Yergason test:  Evaluates for pain or instability of the biceps tendon while the examiner supinates and extends the patient's forearm (with the elbow flexed 90 degrees). Initial treatment consists of rest, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and physical therapy/OMT (eg, myofascial release, counterstrain).  If the pain is persistent or severe (ie, interferes with sleep or daily activities, as in this patient), ultrasonography-guided glucocorticoid injection into the sheath of the long head of the biceps tendon at the bicipital groove can improve function and decrease pain. # Radial head dysfunction The proximal radius (ie, radial head) and distal radius move in opposite directions (ie, **reciprocal motion**) during forearm supination and pronation ((Figure 5)): - During supination, the distal radius moves posterolaterally (ie, palm facing forward), resulting in an anterior glide of the radial head. - During pronation, the distal radius moves anteromedially (ie, palm facing backward), resulting in a posterior glide of the radial head. Disruption of this motion is seen in radial head dysfunction.  For example, **anterior radial head dysfunction** is characterized by restricted posterior glide of the radial head (ie, restricted forearm pronation).  This occurs because the radial head is "stuck" in an anterior position. Osteopathic manipulative therapy using either direct muscle energy or the high velocity–low amplitude (HVLA) technique aims to restore normal joint motion by moving the joint through the restrictive barrier to pronation/posterior glide.  Treating anterior radial head dysfunction with the HVLA technique involves engaging the restrictive barrier by moving the patient's forearm into pronation.  Next, the physician **moves the forearm into flexion** and further pronation while applying posterior pressure to the anterior aspect of the radial head (to move it posteriorly) ((Figure 6)). In posterior radial head dysfunction, the opposite applies regarding diagnostic findings and treatment; direct muscle energy is demonstrated in the following image ((Figure 7)). # Cubitus valgus and varus The **carrying angle** of the arm is normally 5-10 degrees in men and 10-15 degrees in women and allows for arm swing during ambulation ((Figure 8)).  Changes in the carrying angle due to somatic dysfunction result in alterations to both elbow and wrist mechanics because of the ligaments and fascia that span between the elbow and wrist.  Therefore, altered mechanics in one joint can affect the other ((Figure 9)): - Increased carrying angle (ie, **cubitus valgus**):  Medial displacement of the proximal ulna (ie, olecranon) and lateral displacement of the distal ulna (ie, ulnar abduction).  This causes the carpal bones to glide medially (ie, wrist adduction) and results in restriction of wrist abduction. - Decreased carrying angle (ie, **cubitus varus**):  Lateral displacement of the proximal ulna and medial displacement of the distal ulna (ie, ulnar adduction).  This causes the carpal bones to glide laterally (ie, wrist abduction) and results in restriction of wrist adduction. OMT uses balanced ligamentous tension and myofascial release techniques targeting ligamentous and fascial connections between the elbow and the wrist, restoring normal joint biomechanics. # Wrist dysfunctions Most wrist motion occurs primarily at the radiocarpal joint, which is a condylar (ie, modified ball and socket) joint between the distal radius and proximal carpal bones (scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum).  Normal wrist flexion/extension depends on dorsal/ventral glide of the carpal bones at this joint ((Figure 10)): - Wrist flexion causes the carpal bones to glide dorsally (toward the back of the hand). - Wrist extension causes the carpal bones to glide ventrally (toward the palm). For example, **flexion wrist dysfunction** is characterized by the wrist being restricted in extension (ie, "stuck" in flexion).  The carpal bones are restricted in ventral glide (ie, "stuck" dorsally), and there is hypertonicity of wrist flexor muscles.  Muscle energy treatment involves moving the hand toward the restrictive barrier by extending the wrist while the patient then attempts to flex the wrist while the physician provides an equal counterforce (ie, isometric contraction). # Carpal tunnel syndrome Carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) results from compression of the **median nerve** within the carpal tunnel, causing sensory loss, pain, and weakness primarily in the thumb and first 3 digits.  Diagnosis is facilitated by the Phalen maneuver and/or Tinel test ((Figure 11)).  CTS often coexists with **T2-T7 spine dysfunctions**.  This occurs because sympathetic nerve fibers that supply the upper extremity originate from these thoracic segments and share pathways with pain nerve fibers, potentially amplifying carpal tunnel pain through sympathetic activation. OMT involves **stretching the flexor retinaculum** and mobilizing the surrounding tissue ((Figure 12)).  Treating concurrent thoracic dysfunctions (eg, HVLA to T2-T7) can reduce upper extremity sympathetic tone and improve pain and function. # Summary Osteopathic manipulative treatment of the upper extremities applies anatomic and biomechanical understanding to restore motion, alleviate pain, and support systemic function.  In the upper extremities, conditions such as thoracic outlet syndrome are diagnosed with provocative tests and treated by releasing compressive restrictions.  Adhesive capsulitis is managed with the Spencer technique to improve shoulder mobility, whereas bicipital tendonitis benefits from myofascial release and counterstrain.  Radial head dysfunction disrupts normal supination-pronation mechanics and is corrected through the high velocity–low amplitude technique or through muscle energy.  Cubitus valgus/varus alters wrist mechanics via changes in the carrying angle, requiring ligamentous balancing.  Carpal tunnel syndrome is treated by stretching the flexor retinaculum and addressing thoracic dysfunctions to reduce sympathetic tone. ​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​​​‌​​​​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​​​​​​​‌​‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌​​​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌

articles.title: Somatic Dysfunctions
articles.markdown:
# Somatic Dysfunctions # Introduction Somatic dysfunction is an impairment in bone, joint, muscle, and fascia function, with subsequent effects on the neurovascular and lymphatic systems.  Identifying and treating somatic dysfunction is fundamental to osteopathic medicine treatment. # Definition and pathophysiology ## Definition Somatic dysfunction is defined by the mnemonic **TART**: - **T**issue texture changes:  These can vary widely depending on acuity (discussed below). - **A**symmetry:  The interconnectedness of tissues can create imbalances manifesting as asymmetry of anatomical landmarks. - **R**estriction of motion:  Normal physiologic motion is limited by anatomical barriers (eg, bone structure) and physiologic barriers (eg, ligamentous tension, muscle tone).  In somatic dysfunction, **restrictive (ie, pathologic) barriers** limit range of motion (well before anatomic/physiologic barriers are reached). - **T**enderness:  Pain that is disproportionate to the amount of pressure applied, most significantly during acute dysfunctions (although also present to a lesser degree with chronic dysfunctions). ## Pathophysiology Somatic dysfunction is believed to result from neuromuscular imbalance and abnormal sensory input, particularly from mechanoreceptors and nociceptors.  The dysfunction usually occurs due to an underlying **injury**, although it can also be due to visceral inflammation. A major contributing factor to somatic dysfunction is facilitation—a state of sustained subthreshold excitation of spinal interneurons that leads to exaggerated motor and autonomic responses.  This heightened responsiveness results in persistent muscle tone changes, restricted joint motion, and autonomic dysregulation.  Facilitation via the spinal reflex occurs as follows: - **Sensory (afferent) input**:  Injury to a somatic structure (eg, muscle, joint) activates mechanoreceptors and nociceptors.  For example, injury to the bicep muscle activates muscle spindle fibers that send increased afferent signals to the spinal cord at the C5-C6 level. - **Spinal pathway**:  Continued afferent input from the injured tissue sensitizes interneurons in the spinal cord.  These interneurons mediate communication between afferent and efferent pathways and become more easily activated over time. - **Motor (efferent) output**:  When interneurons are sensitized, a lower-than-normal threshold of sensory input is sufficient to trigger somatic motor neuron firing.  This results in sustained hypertonicity of the injured muscle (eg, bicep) and nearby muscles that share the same spinal level (eg, cervical paravertebral muscles). This process contributes to persistent muscle tone changes, joint restriction, and autonomic dysregulation. # Acute vs chronic somatic dysfunction Differentiating between acute and chronic somatic dysfunction is important for diagnosis and treatment planning ((Table 1)). ## Acute somatic dysfunction During the **acute** stage of somatic dysfunction (days to weeks following injury), pain occurs due to the initial damage and resulting release of **inflammatory mediators** (eg, histamine, prostaglandins) that produce local vasodilation.  Therefore, TART findings include **erythema**, **bogginess** (ie, edema), **hypertonic** muscles, and **significant tenderness** to palpation.  Movement at the restrictive barrier of affected joints causes pain, **limiting active range** of motion. ## Chronic somatic dysfunction In the **chronic** stage of somatic dysfunction (weeks to months following injury), **tissue remodeling** develops as the acute inflammatory response transitions to a chronic, fibrotic response due to the release of **profibrotic mediators** (eg, transforming growth factor beta).  Chronic pain also causes local **vasoconstriction** due to sustained, increased local sympathetic activity.  Therefore, TART findings include **cool skin** and pallor, **ropy and stringy tissue**, **decreased muscle tone**, and **limited active and passive range** of motion (due to fibrosis/contracture). # Laws of spinal motion (Fryette) The laws of spinal motion (Fryette) ((Figure 1)) describe patterns of vertebral **sidebending** (coronal displacement about an anteroposterior axis) **and rotation** (transverse displacement about a vertical axis) in the **thoracic** and **lumbar** spine, helping guide the diagnosis and treatment of somatic dysfunction.  These laws do not apply to the cervical spine, which has its own set of rules (discussed in a separate article). ## First law When the spine is in a **neutral** position (ie, no significant flexion or extension), sidebending and rotation occur in **opposite** directions.  This applies primarily to groups of vertebrae (eg, T10-T12).  For example, if a patient's lumbar spine sidebends to the left in the neutral position, it will rotate to the right. ## Second law When the spine is in a **nonneutral** position (**flexed** or **extended**), sidebending and rotation occur in the **same direction**.  This applies to a single vertebral segment.  For example, if L3 is flexed and sidebent left, it will also rotate left. # Nomenclature for somatic dysfunctions Somatic dysfunctions are named based on the position of the structure in relation to its **freedom of motion**, rather than its restriction.  Spinal dysfunctions are named by the **vertebral level** involved (eg, T3, T6-T8) and **position of ease** (ie, the direction in which the vertebra moves most freely).  For example: - T3-T5 NSLRR:  Vertebrae T3-T5 are in neutral, sidebent left, and rotated right (a group dysfunction following the first law \[ie, type I dysfunction\]).  On palpation, the transverse processes are more posterior on the right when the spine is in the neutral position, and the asymmetry becomes less pronounced with flexion or extension.  No improvement is seen with flexion or extension. - T3 FRSR:  T3 is flexed, rotated right, and sidebent right (a nonneutral dysfunction following the second law \[ie, type II dysfunction\]).  On palpation, the right transverse process is more posterior when the spine is in a flexed position, and the asymmetry worsens or does not improve when the spine is extended. Lumbar and thoracic vertebral diagnosis and nomenclature are summarized in the following flowchart ((Figure 2)).  Somatic dysfunctions for other structures are also named in relation to freedom of motion.  For example, in rib exhalation dysfunctions, the ribs are stuck in exhalation (ie, restricted in inhalation). ## Clinical relevance and treatment implications Somatic dysfunction is often implicated in a variety of systemic and regional conditions, including: - Musculoskeletal pain (eg, back and neck pain). - Headaches (eg, tension, cervicogenic). - Postural imbalances and gait abnormalities. - Visceral conditions (eg, appendicitis presenting with T12-L2 somatic dysfunction). - Gastrointestinal dysfunction (eg, constipation, postoperative ileus). - Respiratory disorders (eg, asthma, pneumonia). Acute somatic dysfunction typically responds with relative ease to techniques that are indirect (eg, counterstrain, indirect muscle energy).  In contrast, chronic dysfunction may require more persistent and deeper techniques (eg, direct muscle energy, high velocity low amplitude).  These techniques are discussed in a separate article. # Summary Somatic dysfunction is characterized by impaired function of the musculoskeletal system and associated neurovascular and lymphatic structures, clinically identified using the TART criteria (**T**issue texture changes, **A**symmetry, **R**estriction of motion, **T**enderness).  Its underlying mechanism involves neuromuscular imbalance, facilitation, and spinal reflexes that sustain muscle hypertonicity and joint restrictions.  Differentiating acute from chronic somatic dysfunction guides therapeutic decisions, influencing the choice of indirect versus direct osteopathic techniques. ​‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​​​​​​​‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​​​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​‌​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​

articles.title: Tender Points, Trigger Points, And Chapman Points
articles.markdown:
# Tender Points, Trigger Points, And Chapman Points # Introduction Tender points, trigger points, and Chapman points are distinct types of palpable regions, each with unique characteristics and clinical implications.  This article discusses their definitions, clinical significance, and therapeutic applications, including osteopathic manipulative treatment. # Tender points Tender points are small, discrete areas of **tenderness** that form in a **muscle** belly or corresponding **tendon**.  These points are a manifestation of sustained input from hyperactive muscle spindles caused by nearby somatic dysfunction.  They do not produce referred pain when palpated, differentiating them from trigger points (discussed next).  They also differ from the widespread painful points characteristic of fibromyalgia, a systemic condition with distinct diagnostic criteria and underlying mechanisms.  Over 200 tender points are mapped by anatomic region.  Naming conventions typically reflect location (eg, anterior vs posterior) and region (eg, cervical, thoracic, lumbar, rib, pelvic, extremity); for example, AC and PC refer to anterior and posterior cervical tender points. Tender points are typically treated with **counterstrain**, an indirect, passive technique that reduces tension and pain by holding the affected muscles in a shortened/relaxed position for 90 seconds (except for maverick tender points, which require the muscle to be lengthened).  Counterstrain resets the reflexive neuromuscular output from the muscle spindle that is facilitating the abnormally tense muscle/tendon. For example, a posterior lumbar tender point located on the left spinous or transverse process of the lumbar vertebrae is treated by extending, sidebending away, and rotating away from the tender point (ie, E, SA, RA) ((Table 1)).  This position—which, in this example, would be extending the thigh/hip in an adducted and externally rotated position—is held for approximately 90 seconds until muscle tension decreases and sensitivity diminishes ((Figure 1)). Tender points and counterstrain are discussed in further detail in a separate article. # Trigger points Trigger points are areas within a **taut band** of skeletal muscle that are tender to palpation and often **refer pain** to nearby structures.  Trigger points often develop from excessive muscle strain due to repetitive microtrauma, which facilitates a reflex from the muscle to the spinal cord and then back to other muscles in the area (ie, **somatosomatic reflex**).  The pattern of referred pain is specific to the affected muscle group (eg, upper trapezius referring pain to the occiput and shoulder). Trigger points are treated with a variety of methods, including stretching (which may be facilitated by application of a vapocoolant spray), injection of a local anesthetic (eg, lidocaine), and myofascial release/muscle energy. # Chapman points Chapman points are specific neurolymphatic reflex points located in predictable anatomic locations on the body's anterior and posterior surfaces.  They are thought to be due to impaired local lymphatic drainage leading to inflammation of the surrounding fascia, resulting in **neurolymphatic gangliform contractions**.  These 2-3 mm, tender nodules may aid in the diagnosis of certain visceral diseases.  In general, organs have associated **anterior** and **posterior** Chapman points ((Figure 2), (Figure 3)).  These points serve primarily diagnostic roles, guiding visceral-focused lymphatic treatments.  For example, the gallbladder Chapman point (located at the right seventh intercostal space) may aid in diagnosing cholecystitis.  A list of Chapman points is provided in a separate article. Chapman points are treated through gentle rotary pressure or circular massage, intended to normalize lymphatic flow and facilitate reflexive improvements in associated visceral organ function. # Summary Tender points, trigger points, and Chapman points are osteopathic physical examination tools with distinct pathophysiologic and clinical characteristics.  Tender points facilitate indirect muscle treatments, trigger points guide direct myofascial interventions for referred pain, and Chapman points inform visceral assessments and treatments ((Table 2)).  These points are distinct from the painful areas associated with fibromyalgia, which have separate diagnostic and treatment implications. ​‌​‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​​​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌

articles.title: Viscerosomatic Reflexes
articles.markdown:
# Viscerosomatic Reflexes # Introduction Viscerosomatic reflexes are physiologic interactions in which visceral dysfunction or irritation leads to somatic (ie, musculoskeletal) manifestations.  This form of somatic dysfunction is often perceived as pain, muscle tension, and/or tissue texture changes.  Viscerosomatic reflexes were particularly important before modern diagnostic techniques (eg, CT scans, ECGs) because physical examination findings could serve as key indicators pointing to underlying visceral pathology.  Although these reflexes are still clinically relevant in osteopathic medicine for understanding somatic contributions and demonstrating potential supportive signs, their role in diagnosing occult visceral disease is less critical today due to advanced diagnostics. # Pathophysiology ## Underlying mechanisms A viscerosomatic reflex occurs when afferent (sensory) signals from **visceral irritation** travel via autonomic pathways to the spinal cord and synapse on the dorsal horn.  These signals can influence **nearby somatic neurons**, particularly those innervating skin, muscle, and connective tissue.  A major contributing factor is facilitation, a state of sustained subthreshold excitation of spinal interneurons that leads to exaggerated motor and **sympathetic nervous system hyperactivity**.  Facilitation via the spinal reflex occurs as follows: - **Sensory (afferent) input**:  Injury to a visceral structure activates mechanoreceptors and nociceptors. - **Spinal pathway**:  Continued afferent input from the injured tissue sensitizes interneurons in the spinal cord.  These interneurons mediate communication between afferent and efferent pathways and become more easily activated over time. - **Motor (efferent) output**:  Once interneurons are sensitized, a lower-than-normal threshold of sensory input is sufficient to trigger somatic motor neuron firing. Increased sympathetic activity at a given spinal level contributes to the development of viscerosomatic reflexes that often manifest as paravertebral muscle hypertonicity and/or somatic dysfunction at corresponding vertebral levels. ## Sympathetic autonomic levels Sympathetic levels for various organs are shown in the list and summarized in this table ((Table 1)) (parasympathetic innervation is also shown but is not involved in viscerosomatic reflexes): - T1-T4:  Head and neck. - T1-T5:  Heart. - T2-T7:  Lungs. - T2-T8:  Esophagus. - T5-T9 (via the greater splanchnic nerve and celiac ganglion):  Upper gastrointestinal (GI) tract, including the stomach, proximal duodenum, spleen, liver, and gallbladder. - T10-T11 (via the lesser splanchnic nerve and superior mesenteric ganglion):  Middle GI tract, including the distal duodenum, jejunum, ileum, ascending colon, proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon, kidneys/adrenals, upper ureters, and gonads. - T11-L2 (via the least splanchnic nerve and inferior mesenteric ganglion):  Lower GI tract, including the distal third of the transverse colon, descending/sigmoid colon, rectum, uterus/cervix, prostate, lower ureters, and bladder. ## Chapman points Another manifestation of a viscerosomatic reflex is the formation of Chapman points (ie, 2- to 3-mm, tender neurolymphatic gangliform contractions) associated with an irritated organ; for example, Chapman points in cardiac ischemia may be palpable near the sternocostal junctions of the second and third ribs (anteriorly ((Figure 1)) and spinous and transverse processes of T2 (posteriorly ((Figure 2)).  Chapman points are discussed in more detail in a separate article. # Osteopathic manipulative treatment techniques Treatment always prioritizes appropriate medical or surgical management of the underlying visceral condition (eg, antibiotics for infection, surgery for acute cholecystitis).  Osteopathic manipulative treatment (OMT) may be considered as an adjunctive therapy to relieve associated musculoskeletal dysfunction.  The techniques of choice aim to **reduce sympathetic tone** and **enhance parasympathetic tone**.  These techniques are typically forms of soft tissue or myofascial treatment and include: - **Rib raising**:  To perform this technique, the physician gently lifts the posterior rib angles along the thoracic spine with the patient supine.  Stretching the costovertebral areas where the sympathetic chain ganglia lie, rib raising helps reduce sympathetic nervous system firing and improves rib cage mobility.  Common indications include **postoperative ileus** and **pneumonia**. - **Paraspinal inhibition**:  This technique is closely related to rib raising and is applied in areas without ribs (eg, lumbar region) or in patients who cannot be easily positioned for rib raising.  Steady pressure is applied to the paravertebral muscles, producing a similar downregulation of sympathetic tone.  This technique is frequently used for **postoperative pain** and muscular hypertonicity in hospitalized patients. - **Visceral ganglion release**:  Palpatory pressure can be applied to the prevertebral ganglia in the abdominal region to "release" or inhibit the ganglia, reducing sympathetic outflow to the corresponding digestive organs.  These organ regions include the foregut (celiac ganglion), midgut (superior mesenteric ganglion), and hindgut (inferior mesenteric ganglion).  Indications include **chronic abdominal pain** and **irritable bowel syndrome**. - **Sacral rocking**:  The sacrum is a key anatomic influence on the parasympathetic supply to the lower GI tract because the pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2 through S4) emerge from the sacral region to innervate the descending colon and pelvic organs.  To perform sacral rocking, the physician gently applies an oscillatory pressure to the sacrum in synchrony with breathing.  This rhythmic motion can stimulate or normalize parasympathetic activity from S2 through S4, thereby helping regulate bowel and bladder function.  Indications include **constipation** and **bladder dysfunction**. - **Sacral inhibition**:  Similar to sacral rocking, the physician applies steady, sustained pressure directly to the sacrum, typically with the patient prone.  This gentle pressure reduces excessive parasympathetic tone and relieves conditions associated with heightened pelvic autonomic activity, such as **dysmenorrhea** and lower pelvic dysfunctions (eg, prostatitis). # Clinical examples This section provides specific clinical examples of viscerosomatic reflexes. ## Acute coronary ischemia - Visceral dysfunction:  Ischemia/infarction of myocardial tissue. - Viscerosomatic reflex pathway:  Afferent signals travel via cardiac sympathetic nerves (T1-T5 spinal levels). - Somatic manifestations: - Hypertonicity and tenderness in paraspinal muscles between T1 and T5. - Referred pain in the left shoulder/arm, interscapular pain (T2-T5 dermatomes). - Palpable tissue texture changes (eg, warmth, edema) over the upper thoracic spine. - Chapman points:  Tender nodules palpable anteriorly near the second and third ribs at the sternocostal junction, and posteriorly near the T2 spinous/transverse processes. - OMT application:  Once acute cardiac care is initiated (eg, percutaneous intervention), rib raising (T1-T5 spinal levels) can be applied to reduce excessive sympathetic drive contributing to pain and muscle spasm. ## Cholecystitis - Visceral dysfunction:  Inflammation of the gallbladder (often due to gallstones). - Viscerosomatic reflex pathway:  Afferent signals travel via the greater splanchnic nerve (T5-T9 spinal levels, primarily T6-T9). - Somatic manifestations: - Hypertonicity and tenderness in right-sided paraspinal muscles T6 through T9. - Referred pain in the right subscapular region. - Palpable tissue texture changes over the right lower thoracic spine. - Chapman points:  Tender nodules palpable anteriorly in the intercostal space between ribs 5 and 7. - OMT application:  Alongside antibiotics/surgery, paraspinal inhibition (right T6 through T9) can help reduce sympathetic hyperactivity and associated muscle guarding/pain.  In addition, visceral ganglion release targeting the celiac ganglion can be considered. ## Appendicitis - Visceral dysfunction:  Inflammation of the appendix. - Viscerosomatic reflex pathway:  Afferent signals travel via the lesser splanchnic nerve (T10-T11 spinal levels). - Somatic manifestations: - Hypertonicity and tenderness in right-sided paraspinal muscles T10-T11/L1. - Cutaneous hyperesthesia (increased sensitivity) in the dermatomes around T10-T11 (umbilical region). - Tissue texture changes over the right thoracolumbar junction. - Chapman points:  Tender nodules palpable anteriorly on the tip of the right 12th rib. - OMT application:  Although surgery is the definitive treatment, paraspinal inhibition (right T10-L1) can be used before or after surgery to help modulate pain and reduce muscle guarding related to the reflex arc. # Summary Viscerosomatic reflexes represent connections between visceral pathology and somatic dysfunction, facilitating diagnosis and guiding therapeutic interventions in osteopathic medicine.  These reflexes arise due to the facilitation of spinal interneurons by persistent visceral afferent signals, manifesting clinically through characteristic somatic findings.  Chapman points are specific somatic indicators of visceral irritation, whereas targeted osteopathic manipulative treatment techniques aim to normalize autonomic balance, addressing both somatic symptoms and underlying visceral dysfunction.  Key techniques include rib raising/paraspinal inhibition, visceral ganglion release, and sacral rocking/inhibition. ​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​​​​​‌​​‌​‌​​​​‌​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌

articles.title: Visual Pathway
articles.markdown: # Visual Pathway # Introduction The visual pathway is the neural system responsible for transmitting visual information from the retina to the primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe.  It is essential for the perception of form, color, motion, and spatial orientation.  Visual processing begins with optical refraction by the cornea and lens, followed by the conversion of light into electrical signals by the retinal photoreceptors.  These signals are then relayed through a series of precisely organized neural structures, including the optic nerves, optic chiasm, optic tracts, lateral geniculate nuclei, optic radiations, and, finally, the visual cortex. # The eye ## Refraction of light Refraction is the bending of light as it passes through media of different optical densities.  It is essential for vision because it allows incoming light rays, which enter the eye from various angles, to be focused precisely onto the retina.  A sharp image is formed only when light converges accurately on the retinal photoreceptors, particularly in the fovea centralis.  Without proper refraction, light scatters and is improperly focused, resulting in a blurred image. The eye has several structures that bend and focus light onto the retina ((Figure 1)): - **Cornea**:  The eye's first and most powerful refractive surface, the cornea is the transparent, dome-shaped outer layer of the eye, which has a fixed curvature and contributes approximately 70% of the eye's total refractive power. - **Aqueous humor**:  This clear fluid within the anterior chamber contributes minimally to refraction but helps transmit light between the cornea and lens. - **Lens**:  The second major refractive structure of the eye, the lens has an adjustable curvature that allows for accommodation, the process by which the lens changes its shape to focus on objects at varying distances. - **Near vision**:  Ciliary muscle contracts → zonular fibers relax → lens thickens and becomes more convex → increases refractive power for focusing on near objects. - **Distance vision**:  Ciliary muscle relaxes → zonular fibers tighten → lens flattens → decreases refractive power for distant objects. After light passes through the lens and vitreous compartment, the image created on the retina is inverted and reversed ((Figure 2)).  This means that the temporal (lateral) retinas process images from the nasal (medial) visual field, and the nasal retinas process images from the temporal visual field. ## Refractive errors Visual impairments due to refractive errors include: - **Myopia (nearsightedness)** ((Figure 3)):  Light focuses in front of the retina, causing poor distance vision. - **Hyperopia (farsightedness)** ((Figure 4)):  Light focuses behind the retina, causing poor near vision. - **Astigmatism** ((Figure 5)):  Irregular curvature of the cornea or lens leads to a distorted, blurred image. - **Presbyopia:**  Age-related loss of lens elasticity results in impaired accommodation, especially for near focus (eg, reading). # The retina ## The neural sensor Located at the back of the eye, the retina converts light into electrical signals that are then sent to the brain via the optic nerve.  It contains layers of specialized cells that sequentially process visual information ((Figure 6)). - **Photoreceptors**:  Located in the outermost layer of the retina, photoreceptors hyperpolarize in response to light and modulate downstream neurons. - **Rods**:  Highly sensitive to light; provide night vision and low-resolution, monochromatic (no color) vision.  Rods are concentrated in the peripheral retina. - **Cones**:  Enable daytime and color vision (red, green, blue); responsible for high visual acuity.  Cones are concentrated in the fovea centralis. - **Bipolar cells**:  Transmit signals from photoreceptors to ganglion cells. - **Ganglion cells**:  Receive input from bipolar cells and generate action potentials.  Axons of ganglion cells form the optic nerve. - **Horizontal and amacrine cells**:  Modulate and integrate signals to enhance contrast, motion detection, and spatial resolution. ## Special regions of the retina - **Macula lutea**:  The central area of the retina with a high density of cones; specialized for high-acuity central vision. - **Fovea centralis**:  The center of the macula; a cone-only region with the sharpest visual resolution. - **Optic disc**:  Site where ganglion cell axons converge to form the optic nerve; no rods or cones are present, resulting in a physiologic "blind spot" ((Figure 7)). ## Retinal pathology - **Central retinal artery occlusion**:  Reduction or complete cessation of retinal perfusion leads to retinal ischemia and the sudden onset of painless monocular vision loss. - **Age-related macular degeneration**:  Progressive loss of central vision impairs reading and facial recognition; peripheral vision is preserved. - **Retinal detachment**:  Separation of the neurosensory retina (eg, photoreceptors) from the underlying retinal pigment epithelium (which provides oxygen and nutrients) impairs the function of retinal cells, often presenting with flashes of light and floaters.  It can lead to permanent photoreceptor degeneration and vision loss if not corrected. # Neural visual pathway Neural signals travel along the following visual pathway:  Retina → optic nerve → optic chiasm → optic tracts → lateral geniculate nucleus → optic radiations → primary visual cortex ((Figure 8)).  Lesions along this pathway produce various types of visual deficits based on the location and the nerve fibers that are affected. ## Optic nerve (CN II) - Formed by retinal ganglion cell axons.  Lesions in the optic nerve (eg, central retinal artery occlusion, optic neuritis) cause **monocular blindness (anopia)** ((Figure 9)). ## Optic chiasm - Fibers from the nasal half of the retina (which process the temporal visual field) cross at the optic chiasm, but the temporal retinal fibers (which process the nasal visual fields) remain ipsilateral.  The hemivisual fields of each eye are processed on the contralateral side of the brain (eg, left visual field of the left and right eye is processed in the right hemisphere) ((Figure 10)). - Lesions at the optic chiasm (eg, compression by a pituitary adenoma ((Figure 11))) cause a **bitemporal hemianopia** ((Figure 12)). ## Optic tracts - The optic tracts carry contralateral visual field information from the optic chiasm to the lateral geniculate nucleus. - Lesions in the optic tract (eg, occlusion of the anterior choroidal artery) cause a **contralateral homonymous hemianopia** (loss of the same visual field in both eyes) ((Figure 13)). ## Lateral geniculate nucleus - The lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) is a 6-layered visual relay center within the posterolateral thalamus that sends fibers to the visual cortex via optic radiations. - Lesions in this region (eg, stroke or tumor involving the LGN) cause a **contralateral homonymous visual field deficit**. ## Optic radiations - **Inferior optic radiations**:  Carry information from the superior visual field (inferior retina) through the temporal lobe (Meyer loop) to the visual cortex.  Lesions in this region (eg, stroke or mass involving the temporal lobe) cause a **contralateral homonymous superior quadrantanopia** ("pie in the sky") ((Figure 14)). - **Superior optic radiations**:  Carry information from the inferior visual field (superior retina) through the parietal lobe to the visual cortex.  Lesions in this region (eg, stroke or mass involving the parietal lobe) cause a **contralateral homonymous inferior quadrantanopia** ("pie on the floor") ((Figure 15)). Large infarctions involving the territory supplied by the middle cerebral artery can damage both the upper and lower limbs of the optic radiations, resulting in homonymous hemianopia. ## Primary visual cortex - Located in the occipital lobe and is retinotopically organized (eg, specific retinal areas map to specific areas of the visual cortex). - Macular vision is processed by the posterior cortex. - Peripheral vision is processed by the anterior cortex. - Lesions in this region (eg, occlusion of the posterior cerebral artery) cause a **contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing** (the cortical structures responsible for macular vision are dual-supplied from the middle and posterior cerebral arteries). After visual information is received in the occipital cortex, it is relayed along distinct pathways to association cortices for higher-order processing ((Figure 16)).  The ventral (P) pathways project to the occipitotemporal association cortex for the identification of letters, colors, shapes, and faces (ie, what is it?).  The dorsal (M) pathways project to the parietooccipital association cortex for processing of motion and spatial relationships (ie, where is it?). # Summary Vision begins when light is refracted by the cornea and lens and focused onto the retina, where rods and cones convert light into neural signals.  These signals travel via ganglion cells into the optic nerve, cross partially at the optic chiasm, and continue through the optic tracts, lateral geniculate nucleus, and optic radiations to reach the primary visual cortex.  Lesions along this pathway produce characteristic visual field defects ((Figure 17)). ​‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​

articles.title: Thyroid Physiology And Diagnostic Testing
articles.markdown: # Thyroid Physiology And Diagnostic Testing # Introduction The thyroid is a small endocrine gland that plays an important role in regulating the basal metabolic rate.  Thyroid disorders are very common globally and can include hyperthyroidism (overproduction of thyroid hormone), hypothyroidism (underproduction of hormone), and a variety of neoplastic and inflammatory conditions. # Embryology The thyroid is primarily an endodermal derivative.  In utero, the thyroid gland forms from an outpouching of pharyngeal epithelium at the base of the tongue ((Figure 1)).  It then descends to the base of the anterior neck via the thyroglossal duct, which extends from the foramen cecum at the base of the tongue to the superior midline border of the thyroid ((Figure 2)).  Normally, the duct then atrophies.  Occasionally, failure of normal migration can leave residual deposits of ectopic thyroid tissue along the route of descent, and residual patency of the duct can manifest as a thyroglossal duct cyst. As the cells migrate to the lower neck, they also fuse with parafollicular C cells from the ultimobranchial body of the 4th pharyngeal arch to form the mature thyroid glandular structure ((Figure 3)). # Anatomy The thyroid is a butterfly-shaped gland that sits on the midline in the lower neck, anterior to the trachea and inferior to the thyroid cartilage ((Figure 4)).  It is composed of 2 lobes with a central isthmus; most patients have a posterior extension from each lobe (tubercle of Zuckerkandl).  The gland is supported by the trachea via the lateral suspensory ligament and is typically mobile, rising with the thyroid cartilage during swallowing.  The parathyroids are a set (usually 4) of small glands that lie immediately posterior to the thyroid lobes. Blood supply to the thyroid is primarily via the paired superior and inferior thyroidal arteries ((Figure 5)).  Innervation to the thyroid is scant, primarily consisting of small sympathetic and parasympathetic fibers that regulate blood flow to the thyroid.  However, the recurrent laryngeal nerve passes through the thyroid, and the superior laryngeal nerve runs in close proximity; these nerves can be injured during thyroid dissection or thyroidectomy. The fundamental unit of thyroid microanatomy is the thyroid follicle ((figure 6)), spherical structures consisting of a core of glycoprotein colloid, which serves as substrate for synthesis of thyroid hormone, surrounded by cuboidal epithelium.  The reticular tissue between follicles is highly vascular with a dense network of capillaries.  The interfollicular space also contains the parafollicular C cells, which secrete calcitonin. # Thyroid hormone physiology Synthesis of thyroid hormone begins with thyroglobulin, a large glycoprotein produced in thyroid follicular cells and secreted into the follicular lumen ((Figure 7)).  The follicular cells also transport inorganic iodide from the bloodstream into the lumen.  There, thyroid peroxidase (TPO) oxidizes iodide to iodine, and covalently links it to tyrosine residues of thyroglobulin (ie, organification), forming mono- and diiodotyrosine.  TPO then couples the iodinated tyrosine residues to form triiodothyronine (T3) and tetraiodothyronine (T4, also referred to as thyroxine), which are collectively termed thyroid hormone. Thyroid hormone is stored in the thyroid follicles while still bound to thyroglobulin.  In preparation for release, it is taken up into follicular cells, liberated from thyroglobulin by proteolytic enzymes, and transported into the follicular capillaries.  Most thyroid hormone is released in the form of T4, with only a small amount of T3 released.  T3 (the more active form of thyroid hormone) is then produced by deiodination of T4 in peripheral tissues.  Most thyroid hormone in circulation is bound to plasma proteins, primarily thyroxine-binding globulin, transthyretin, and albumin.  A much smaller free thyroid hormone pool is metabolically active. Thyroid hormone acts on an intranuclear receptor that is ubiquitous in tissues throughout the body.  It acts to stimulate the basal metabolic rate, increasing energy consumption and thermogenesis.  It also increases expression of catecholamine receptors, amplifying adrenergic effects. # Regulation of thyroid endocrine function Thyroid hormone synthesis and release are regulated primarily by thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), which is secreted by thyrotroph cells of the anterior pituitary ((Figure 8)).  Release of TSH is stimulated in turn by thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) from the hypothalamus.  Production of both TRH and TSH is suppressed by negative feedback from thyroid hormone. In addition to T4 and T3, a small amount of thyroid hormone is released as reverse T3 (rT3), an inactive isomer.  Conversion of T4 to rT3 also occurs in peripheral tissues; increased rT3 conversion, as can occur in severe illness, leaves less T4 available for deiodination to active T3, which serves as a secondary check on thyroid hormone status. # Effect of pregnancy Pregnancy requires increased thyroid hormone production to meet metabolic demands.  Alterations to thyroid hormone levels occur through 2 primary mechanisms: - Estrogen stimulates the synthesis of thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG) and decreases TBG clearance, leading to higher circulating TBG levels and an increased pool of bound thyroid hormone.  T4 production subsequently increases to maintain free hormone levels ((Figure 9)). - hCG (which shares a common alpha subunit with TSH and a similar beta subunit) directly stimulates thyrotropin receptors on thyroid follicular cells, resulting in increased T4 production.  TSH levels typically fall due to negative feedback of thyroid hormone on pituitary TSH release. # Laboratory testing ## TSH Serum TSH is the primary laboratory test used in diagnosis and management of thyroid conditions.  Abnormalities include the following: - TSH is increased in primary hypothyroidism, central/secondary hyperthyroidism, and under-replacement in thyroid hormone therapy. - TSH is decreased/suppressed in primary hyperthyroidism, central hypothyroidism, and over-replacement in thyroid hormone therapy. Because the pituitary response to changes in thyroid physiologic status is rapid and vigorous, TSH is generally the most sensitive marker in thyroid disease, with levels rising or falling before thyroid hormone levels are outside their laboratory reference ranges.  The correlation between serum TSH and thyroid metabolic status is logarithmic, with changes at the lower end of the reference range representing a greater change in status than a proportional change at the upper end of the range. ## Thyroxine (T4), free and total The bulk of circulating thyroid hormone is in the form of T4.  Levels are elevated in primary and central hyperthyroidism, and decreased in primary and central hypothyroidism.  Because free T4 is the metabolically active fraction and is less affected by plasma binding protein levels, many experts prefer free T4 over total T4 measurement for clinical decision making. ## Triiodothyronine (T3) Serum T3 is often used in evaluation of hyperthyroidism; elevated levels serve to confirm an elevated T4 measurement.  However, TSH, which is elevated in primary hypothyroidism, increases the share of thyroid hormone released as T3, and serum T3 levels are often normal in mild to moderate hypothyroid states.  Therefore, T3 is not recommended in evaluation of hypothyroidism. ## Thyroglobulin A small amount of thyroglobulin is released with thyroid hormone from thyroid follicular cells.  Excessive thyroid hormone production in hyperthyroidism (eg, Graves disease) is typically associated with elevated serum levels of thyroglobulin.  Thyroglobulin levels can be strikingly elevated when hyperthyroidism is due to destruction of thyroid follicles with release of preformed thyroid hormone (eg, painless thyroiditis, subacute \[granulomatous\] thyroiditis).  Also, because thyroglobulin is made exclusively in the thyroid, patients who undergo total thyroidectomy (eg, for thyroid cancer) should have no detectable thyroglobulin in circulation; measurable levels suggest the presence of residual or recurrent neoplastic tissue. ## Thyroid peroxidase (TPO) antibodies (Anti-TPO) Anti-TPO is classically used as a marker for chronic autoimmune (Hashimoto) thyroiditis and related conditions (eg, painless and postpartum thyroiditis).  In these disorders, high anti-TPO levels are associated with increased risk for progression of subclinical hypothyroidism (ie, elevated TSH with normal free T4 levels) to overt hypothyroidism.  Anti-TPO is not specific to these disorders, however, and also can be seen in Graves disease and other autoimmune endocrinopathies. ## Thyrotropin (TSH) receptor antibodies (TRAb) Autoantibodies against the TSH receptor can activate the receptor independent of TSH (ie, thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin).  These antibodies are the hallmark of Graves disease and are a sensitive marker for diagnosis. # Imaging ## Ultrasound Because the thyroid occupies a relatively superficial position in the anterior neck, it is readily accessible to ultrasound imaging.  Ultrasound is the imaging modality of choice in evaluating thyroid nodules, and ultrasound characteristics (eg, size, echotexture, calcification) can be used to determine the risk for malignancy and need for tissue sampling.  Ultrasound is also commonly used to guide fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the thyroid. Ultrasound with Doppler can assess blood flow in the thyroid, which correlates roughly with metabolic activity and can clarify the differential diagnosis in hyperthyroidism.  Graves disease, which is characterized by increased thyroid hormone synthesis, typically shows increased blood flow; destructive thyroiditis, which causes release of preformed hormone with decreased new hormone synthesis, shows decreased flow.  Thyroid scintigraphy (see below) is usually preferred for this purpose but is contraindicated in pregnant women, in whom ultrasound is preferred. ## Nuclear medicine Radioactive iodine uptake scintigraphy is widely used in the evaluation of hyperthyroidism.  This imaging modality uses a radioiodine tracer to assess uptake and organification of iodine in the thyroid.  Typical patterns include the following: - Diffusely increased uptake ((Figure 10)) throughout the thyroid gland suggests Graves disease. - Focal uptake ((Figure 11)) with decreased uptake in the remainder of the gland suggests hypermetabolic thyroid nodules (toxic adenoma or toxic multinodular goiter). - Decreased uptake ((Figure 12)) throughout the gland suggests destructive thyroiditis or exogenous thyroid hormone intake. # Summary The thyroid gland synthesizes hormones that regulate the body's metabolic rate.  These hormones are produced through a multi-step process that utilizes iodine, and their release is controlled via a feedback loop involving the pituitary gland.  Thyroid-stimulating hormone, produced by the pituitary, is the primary screening tool for diagnosing thyroid conditions.  Imaging techniques such as ultrasound and radioactive iodine uptake scans can further pinpoint the cause of the thyroid dysfunction, such as Graves disease or thyroid nodules. ​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌​​​​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌​​​​‌‌​​‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​​​​‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌​​​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​​​​​​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​

articles.title: Thermoregulation
articles.markdown: # Thermoregulation # Introduction Thermoregulation maintains core body temperature within a narrow range (36.5-37.5 C \[97.7-99.5 F\]), despite environmental variation, through the integration of peripheral thermal sensing, central processing in the hypothalamus, and autonomic and behavioral responses that adjust heat production and dissipation.  The process reflects a negative feedback loop organized around a hypothalamic set point. # Thermal compartments and heat balance Body temperature varies across compartments due to differences in perfusion and exposure: - **Core compartment** (brain and visceral organs):  Core temperature is tightly regulated because enzymatic and cellular processes are temperature sensitive. - **Peripheral compartment** (skin and extremities):  Peripheral temperature may fluctuate, serving as a buffer between the core and the environment. Total body heat content is determined by the balance between heat production and heat loss: - **Heat production**:  Determined by several factors, including basal metabolic activity (major contributor at rest), skeletal muscle activity, shivering, and nonshivering thermogenesis (described later). - **Heat loss**:  Occurs through 4 major mechanisms: - Radiation:  Transfer of infrared heat to surrounding surfaces (dominant at rest). - Conduction:  Direct heat transfer to objects in contact. - Convection:  Heat transfer via moving air or fluid. - Evaporation:  Heat loss through vaporization of water (sweat, respiration). # Mechanisms: Feedback loop ## Peripheral and central thermal sensing Thermal inputs originate from peripheral and central receptors: - **Peripheral thermoreceptors**:  Located in skin, these receptors detect environmental temperature and allow anticipatory adjustments before core temperature changes. - **Central thermoreceptors**:  Located in the hypothalamus, spinal cord, and viscera, these receptors respond to core temperature changes. There are more cold-sensing than warm-sensing receptors, so responses are biased toward protection against heat loss. ## Central integration The hypothalamus integrates thermal signals and compares them to the hypothalamic set point, with the following locations playing important roles: - Preoptic/anterior hypothalamus:  Promotes heat dissipation. - **Posterior hypothalamus**:  Promotes heat conservation and production. Deviations from the hypothalamic set point trigger coordinated outputs through autonomic, endocrine, and somatic pathways to ensure a narrow physiologic temperature range ((Figure 1)). ## Effector mechanisms **Heat dissipation** Increases in body temperature stimulate: - **Diaphoresis** (sweating):  Evaporation of water from the skin is the most effective mechanism for releasing excess heat.  (Sweating, with production of the hypotonic fluid from eccrine glands, is mediated by sympathetic cholinergic fibers, an exception to the usual adrenergic sympathetic signaling.) - **Peripheral vasodilation** and shunting of blood and heat from internal organs to the skin (eg, through splanchnic vasoconstriction):  Heat dissipation from the skin occurs via conduction, convection, and radiation. - **Behavioral changes**:  Examples include voluntary decisions to seek shade or cooler environments. **Heat conservation and production** Decreases in body temperature stimulate: - **Shivering**:  Oscillatory skeletal muscle contraction generates rapid heat production. - **Nonshivering thermogenesis**:  Heat is generated from brown adipose tissue (eg, mainly adjacent to the heart and great vessels).  Upregulation of the mitochondrial uncoupling protein dissipates the proton gradient as heat (ie, instead of ATP) ((Figure 2)). - **Peripheral vasoconstriction**:  Blood shunting toward internal organs conserves heat. - **Behavioral thermoregulation**:  Examples include voluntary decisions to keep moving or to seek shelter. **Endocrine contributions** Beyond these relatively rapid responses, hormonal systems provide sustained regulation.  In particular, **thyroid hormone** increases basal metabolic rate and heat production via enhanced mitochondrial activity.  Cold exposure stimulates the hypothalamic release of thyroid-releasing hormone, increasing thyroid hormone production over time.  Conversely, heat-loss mechanisms include decreased thyroid hormone formation. Other hormones involved in thermoregulation include: - **Catecholamines (epinephrine, norepinephrine)**:  Stimulate glycogenolysis, lipolysis, and thermogenesis. - **Cortisol**:  Has permissive effects on metabolism during prolonged stress. # Adaptations ## Fever and set point regulation Fever reflects a regulated increase in the hypothalamic set point, typically in response to exogenous or endogenous pyrogens that stimulate production of prostaglandin E2 in the hypothalamus.  The elevated set point activates heat-conserving mechanisms (vasoconstriction, shivering), initially producing a sensation of cold and chills during the febrile episode.  Once the set point returns to normal (eg, after antipyretics), heat-dissipating mechanisms (sweating, vasodilation) are activated, producing a sensation of warmth during defervescence. ## Acclimatization Repeated heat exposure induces adaptive changes that improve thermoregulation, including: - Earlier onset and increased rate of sweating. - Reduced sweat sodium concentration due to aldosterone-mediated reabsorption. - Expansion of plasma volume, improving cardiovascular stability. These adaptations enhance heat dissipation and reduce the risk of heat-related illness. # Clinical correlations The following scenarios are described in more detail in separate articles. - **Hypothermia**:  Hypothermia occurs when heat loss exceeds production; it leads to impaired enzymatic function, decreased cardiac output, and risk of arrhythmias. - **Hyperthermia (heat stroke)**:  Heat-dissipating mechanisms fail without a change in hypothalamic set point; this can result in multiorgan dysfunction. # Summary Thermoregulation depends on the integration of peripheral and central temperature sensing with hypothalamic control of a defined set point.  Heat balance is achieved by modulating heat production (metabolism, shivering) and heat loss (radiation, evaporation, skin blood flow).  Rapid neural responses are complemented by slower endocrine adjustments that sustain temperature control.  Fever represents an upward resetting of the set point mediated by inflammatory signaling. ​‌​‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​​​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌​‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​​​​​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​​​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌
