articles.markdown: # Pulmonary Physiology: Pulmonary Circulation # Introduction The pulmonary circulation refers to blood flow from the right side of the heart, through the lungs, and to the left side of the heart.  Normal pulmonary circulation is a low-resistance, low-pressure system.  This article discusses the factors that influence pulmonary vascular resistance and the ways that the right ventricle (RV) responds to changes in its afterload. # Properties In anatomic order, the pulmonary circulation includes the RV, RV outflow tract, main pulmonary artery (PA), pulmonary arterial branches, pulmonary arterioles, pulmonary capillaries, pulmonary venules, pulmonary veins, and left atrium (LA). The pulmonary circulation handles the same cardiac output (CO) as the systemic circulation, in keeping with the continuity of flow principle (Qpulmonary = Qsystemic).  To accommodate this same flow within the lungs' smaller volume, the pulmonary circulation has **high compliance**.  Pulmonary arteries have thinner walls with less elastin and smooth muscle, allowing greater distensibility compared to systemic arteries.  Along with its high compliance, the pulmonary circulation is a **low-resistance, low-pressure** system: - Low resistance:  Pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) is approximately one-sixth of systemic vascular resistance (SVR):  PVR = 30-200 dynes·s/cm5, whereas SVR = 800-1200 dynes·s/cm5. - Low pressure:  Mean PA pressure (mPAP) is approximately one-sixth of mean arterial pressure (MAP):  mPAP = 15 mm Hg, whereas MAP = 90 mm Hg. # Right heart catheterization ## Procedure Right heart catheterization (ie, Swan-Ganz) records pressures at key points in the pulmonary circulation ((Figure 1)).  A catheter is introduced via the internal jugular or femoral veins and advanced into the superior vena cava.  Waveform and pressure readings are captured at the following: - Right atrium:  The classic central venous waveform (a, c, v, x, y) is seen ((Figure 2)).  The average value of all wave heights is the mean right atrial pressure. - RV:  When the catheter enters the RV, a sine waveform appears, ranging from 0-5 mm Hg at the end of diastole to approximately 25 mm Hg during peak systole. - PA:  As the catheter advances from the RV into the main PA, a pressure step-up occurs immediately after the catheter crosses the pulmonic valve.  Unlike the RV, the PA retains pressure during diastole due to vascular resistance and pulmonic valve closure.  This establishes a PA diastolic pressure (dPAP), which is approximately 10 mm Hg.  The PA systolic pressure (sPAP) closely matches the RV systolic pressure, which is approximately 25 mm Hg. - Wedge:  The catheter has a small balloon at its tip that allows it to lodge in a distal pulmonary artery ((Figure 3)).  The pressure at this location is known as the pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP).  When wedged, the catheter tip is isolated from the proximal PA pressure (due to the balloon) and detects only pressure transmitted backward from the pulmonary veins and LA.  Therefore, PCWP is a surrogate for LA pressure (LAP) ((Figure 4)).  Normally, PCWP is 5-8 mm Hg. Pressures collected during right heart catheterization are used to calculate PVR. ## Calculation of PVR From the Ohm law, the pressure drop across a circuit is equal to the flow multiplied by the resistance of the circuit (ΔP = Q × R).  In the pulmonary circulation: - ΔP is the difference between the main PA and LA.  Therefore, ΔP = mPAP − LAP. - mPAP = ⅓ × sPAP + ⅔ × dPAP = ⅓ × 25 + ⅔ × 10 = 15 mm Hg in healthy adults (because more time is spent in diastole than in systole).  As discussed previously, PAP is measured during right-sided heart catheterization of the main pulmonary artery. - LAP ≈ PCWP = 8 mm Hg in healthy adults.  As discussed previously, PCWP is measured during right-sided heart catheterization by occluding the distal pulmonary artery. - Q is the CO, or the total flow through the lungs.  CO is measured during right-sided heart catheterization using thermodilution (temperature curve after cold bolus injection into the PA) or the Fick method (difference in oxygen saturation between arterial and mixed venous blood).  Under normal conditions, CO ≈ 5 L/min. Therefore, substituting these values into ΔP = Q × R, the equation becomes (mPAP − LAP) = CO × PVR.  Rearranging this equation yields PVR = (mPAP − LAP) / CO ≈ (15 − 8)/5 = 1.4 mm Hg / (L/min) = 1.4 Wood units (wU).  (To convert between wU and dynes·s/cm5, the units of the International System of Units, multiply by 80.) ## Interpretation of PVR Pulmonary hypertension (PH) is defined as elevated mean PAP >20 mm Hg.  PH can occur with elevated or normal PVR: - **PH with elevated PVR** (≥3 wU):  In this scenario, PH is due to remodeling of the PAs and arterioles (the resistance vessels).  Known as **precapillary PH**, this encompasses PA hypertension (PAH, Group 1), PH due to chronic lung disease or hypoxemia (Group 3), and PH due to chronic pulmonary thromboembolism (Group 4). - **PH with normal PVR** (<3 wU):  In this scenario, PH is due to the transmission of venous pressure backward from the left atrium.  Known as **postcapillary PH**, this encompasses PH due to left-sided heart disease (eg, heart failure) or mitral valve disease (Group 2).  This is the most common cause of PH in the United States.  PCWP is expected to be elevated (eg, >15 mm Hg). # Determinants of PVR PVR is determined by vascular tone, compression, recruitment, and remodeling. ## Vascular tone The balance between endogenous vasoconstrictors and vasodilators sets the vascular tone. - The major pulmonary **vasodilators** include nitric oxide and prostacyclin (or prostaglandin I2). - The major pulmonary **vasoconstrictors** include endothelin-1 and catecholamines (eg, epinephrine).  Pulmonary vasoconstriction is also stimulated by hypoxemia, hypercapnia, and acidosis, as well as by other vascular mediators such as angiotensin II, serotonin, and leukotrienes. ## Vascular compression Pulmonary capillaries are divided into extraalveolar (interstitial) and intraalveolar vessels. - At low lung volumes (near residual volume), extraalveolar vessels are compressed, but intraalveolar vessels remain open. - Conversely, at high lung volumes (near total lung capacity), extraalveolar vessels are open, whereas intraalveolar vessels are compressed. Both vessel types are maximally open at intermediate lung volumes (near functional residual capacity) ((Figure 5)). Like alveolar volume, alveolar pressure has a direct effect on vascular compression.  High positive airway pressure (eg, mechanical ventilation) can compress all capillaries, raising PVR. ## Vascular recruitment At rest, only around 66% of the pulmonary vessels are open.  The remaining 33%, particularly at the lung apices, are unperfused.  During exertion, increased CO recruits these underperfused vessels while the other vessels distend to accommodate the higher blood volume.  This combination of **recruitment and distension** helps keep PVR stable despite increased blood flow. ## Vascular remodeling Normal PA have a relatively thin wall.  In PH, the arteries can undergo structural changes, including neointimal hyperplasia, smooth muscle thickening, and adventitial fibrosis ((Figure 6)).  The vascular bed can be obliterated by emphysema or obstructed by chronic thromboemboli. Remodeled vessels progressively lose their ability to respond to vasodilators and vasoconstrictors.  In advanced stages, they may become completely unresponsive.  These structural changes are typically irreversible and contribute to elevated PVR. # RV function ## RV versus LV The RV has several key functional differences from the LV: - **Preload tolerance**:  The RV adapts well to sudden increases in preload due to its high compliance; in contrast, the LV adapts poorly due to its low compliance (eg, volume overload can quickly lead to pulmonary congestion and edema). - **Afterload tolerance**:  The LV adapts well to sudden increases in afterload, whereas the RV adapts poorly (eg, a sudden increase in PA pressure, such as acute pulmonary embolism, can quickly lead to RV dilation and failure). - **Contraction**:  RV myocytes are arrayed linearly, so the ventricle contracts lengthwise, and RV ejection fraction is best assessed by **longitudinal shortening**.  In contrast, LV myocytes are arrayed helically, so the ventricle contracts torsionally, and LV ejection fraction is best assessed by circumferential contraction. - **Ventricular interdependence**:  The LV "owns" the septum, whereas the RV "borrows" the septum for contractile efficiency.  RV pressure overload (eg, severe PH) or pericardial constriction (eg, tuberculosis) leads to septal bowing into the LV, compromising its filling and subsequent output (eg, pulsus paradoxus).  Conversely, LV pressure overload does not move the septum to the right and has minimal impact on RV filling. - **Coronary perfusion**:  The LV is perfused only during diastole when intraventricular pressure drops below coronary artery pressure.  In contrast, the RV, with its lower pressure, is perfused throughout the cardiac cycle ((Figure 7)).  Therefore, the RV is more vulnerable to hypotension and ischemia due to its reliance on continuous perfusion. ## RV-PA coupling As discussed, the RV is much more **afterload sensitive** than the LV.  If too sudden, even a small increase in PAP (eg, 20 mm Hg) can cause acute RV dysfunction.  This explains why signs of RV dysfunction (eg, peripheral edema, jugular venous distension) typically appear earlier than signs of low CO (eg, hypotension, cool extremities). Over long periods, the RV hypertrophies to adapt to high afterload.  This maintains **ventriculoarterial (RV-PA) coupling** despite the high PAP.  Patients with chronic PH can often have PAP approaching or even exceeding systemic pressures but appear remarkably well compensated due to RV adaptation.  However, some conditions can induce concurrent myocardial fibrosis (eg, scleroderma, sarcoidosis), impairing RV coupling and leading to earlier failure and more significant symptoms at comparatively lower PAP.  RV coupling is also impaired by factors that depress myocardial contractility (eg, cytokines, ischemia, acidosis, beta blockers).  Coupling can be conceptualized as the ratio of RV contractility to RV afterload. # Summary The pulmonary circulation is a low-resistance, low-pressure, and high-compliance system that transports blood from the right side of the heart, through the lungs, and to the left side of the heart.  Pulmonary vascular resistance is influenced by vascular tone (eg, nitric oxide, endothelin-1), physical compression (eg, high lung volume), vessel recruitment (eg, exercise), and structural remodeling (eg, medial thickening).  The right ventricle is highly sensitive to afterload and can acutely fail, with sudden increases in pulmonary artery pressure. ​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​​​​​​​​​‌​‌‌​​​​​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​​

articles.title: Pulmonary Physiology: Oxygen-Hemoglobin Dissociation Curve
articles.markdown:
# Pulmonary Physiology: Oxygen-Hemoglobin Dissociation Curve # Introduction Oxygen (O2) and carbon dioxide (CO2) must be transported efficiently between the lungs and tissues through the bloodstream.  Most O2 is transported via the carrier protein hemoglobin, whereas most CO2 is transported in the form of bicarbonate (HCO3−).  Hemoglobin has unique properties that create varying affinity for O2 and help optimize O2 loading in the lungs and unloading in the tissues.  These are reflected in the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve.  Several factors influence the overall affinity of hemoglobin for O2, allowing the body to adjust O2 loading and unloading as needed. # Gas transport and the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve ## Hemoglobin structure and cooperative binding Hemoglobin is a tetrameric hemeprotein contained within red blood cells (RBCs).  It is usually composed of 2 alpha and 2 beta globin chains, each containing a heme group capable of binding a single O2 molecule; therefore, each hemoglobin molecule can bind up to 4 O2 molecules ((Figure 1)).  Most O2 in the blood (~98%) is carried by hemoglobin, whereas a small percentage is transported dissolved in the plasma. The **oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve** illustrates the relationship between the degree of O2 saturation of hemoglobin and the partial pressure of O2 (PO2) dissolved in the blood.  The curve reflects hemoglobin's varying binding affinity for O2 and its ability to load O2 in the lungs and release O2 in the tissues. O2 binding to hemoglobin is cooperative, meaning that after a single O2 molecule binds, the conformation of hemoglobin changes and the remaining heme groups bind O2 more readily.  This **cooperative binding** interaction between hemoglobin subunits creates a characteristic sigmoidal (S-shaped) hemoglobin dissociation curve ((Figure 2)): - At very low PO2, hemoglobin is largely deoxygenated and its O2 affinity is relatively low, so the first O2 molecule binds poorly, and the curve is flat. - Once the first O2 molecule binds to 1 hemoglobin binding site, increased affinity of the remaining sites creates the steep middle portion of the curve. - With increasing PO2, more binding sites become occupied and hemoglobin approaches full saturation, creating the plateau portion of the curve. ## O2 loading in the lungs and unloading in the tissues The cooperative nature of O2 binding allows hemoglobin to transport O2 efficiently between the lungs and the tissues. In the lungs, alveolar PO2 is typically around 100 mm Hg.  At this high O2 tension, hemoglobin operates on the plateau portion of the dissociation curve and becomes nearly fully saturated.  Because the plateau is relatively flat, moderate reductions in alveolar PO2 lead to only small reductions in hemoglobin saturation.  This acts as a safety mechanism because it helps maintain adequate O2 loading even when some degree of lung hypoxia is present. In the peripheral tissues, PO2 is typically around 40 mm Hg, which corresponds to the steep portion of the curve.  In this region, small reductions in PO2 create relatively large decreases in hemoglobin saturation.  This facilitates O2 release into the tissues. ## CO2 transport and the Bohr and Haldane effects The majority of CO2 is carried in the blood as HCO3− (~70%), whereas some is bound to hemoglobin and an additional small portion is transported dissolved in the plasma ((Figure 3)).  Molecular interactions, namely the Bohr and Haldane effects, contribute to the efficient transfer of O2 and CO2 in the lungs and tissues ((Figure 4)): - In the capillaries of the **peripheral tissues**, high levels of CO2 increase local (ambient) acidity, which decreases overall hemoglobin affinity for O2 (ie, shifts the entire oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve to the right) and facilitates the unloading of O2 (factors that shift the entire dissociation curve are discussed later).  This is known as the **Bohr effect**.  CO2 combines with water (H2O), resulting in a hydrogen (H+) ion and HCO3−.  The H+ ions are carried by hemoglobin, whereas the HCO3− is transferred to the plasma for transport to the lungs. - In the capillaries of the **lungs**, binding of O2 molecules to hemoglobin decreases the affinity of hemoglobin for CO2, which facilitates the unloading of CO2 from hemoglobin.  The binding of O2 also increases the acidity of the hemoglobin molecule and facilitates the release of H+ ions from hemoglobin binding sites.  This is known as the **Haldane effect**.  The H+ ions combine with HCO3− to produce H2O and CO2.  The CO2 then crosses the alveolar capillary-membrane into the lungs and is expired. ## Role of bisphosphoglycerate RBCs do not have mitochondria and therefore use glycolysis, rather than oxidative phosphorylation, as the major pathway to generate energy.  During normal glycolysis, ATP is generated when 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate (1,3-BPG) is converted to 3-phosphoglycerate by the enzyme phosphoglycerate kinase ((Figure 5)).  However, RBCs can bypass this part of the pathway using an enzyme called BPG mutase to convert 1,3-BPG to 2,3-BPG.  2,3-BPG binds to deoxyhemoglobin in a pocket between the 2 beta globin chains.  Positively charged amino acids within this pocket interact with the negatively charged phosphate groups of 2,3-BPG, allosterically reducing hemoglobin's affinity for O2.  The conversion of 1,3-BPG to 2,3-BPG is increased with hypoxemia or other conditions of low blood O2 content (eg, anemia):  Higher 2,3-BPG levels within RBCs facilitate easier delivery of O2 to the peripheral tissues. # Physiologic factors that shift the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve A commonly used parameter from the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve is the P50, which is the PO2 at which 50% of hemoglobin binding sites are occupied by O2 molecules.  The average P50 of hemoglobin under normal conditions is 26 mm Hg, such that >50% of hemoglobin sites are occupied even in venous blood, where PO2 is generally approximately 40 mm Hg. Changes in the P50 reflect changes in the overall O2 affinity of hemoglobin: - **Lower P****50** indicates **higher O****2** **affinity** and manifests as a **left shift** of the entire curve. - **Higher P****50** indicates **lower O****2** **affinity** and manifests as a **right shift** of the entire curve. Several physiologic variables alter the O2 affinity of hemoglobin and shift the position of the dissociation curve ((Figure 6)): ## Rightward shift - A **rightward shift** indicates **decreased O****2** **affinity** and **encourages O****2** **release into the tissues**.  It also somewhat discourages O2 uptake in the lungs, but this effect is minimal because it involves the plateau portion of the dissociation curve.  A rightward shift is driven by conditions that increase O2 need in the tissues (eg, exercising muscle, elevated metabolic rate) and occurs with: - Decreased pH. - Increased temperature. - Increased 2,3-BPG. ## Leftward shift A **leftward shift** indicates **increased O****2** **affinity** and **discourages O****2** **release to the tissues**.  It also somewhat encourages O2 uptake in the lungs, but again, this effect is minimal at the plateau portion of the dissociation curve.  A leftward shift occurs with: - Increased pH. - Decreased temperature. - Decreased 2,3-BPG. # Hemoglobin A and other types of hemoglobin (different chain compositions) Hemoglobin, composed of 2 alpha chains and 2 beta chains, is the normal and most common type of adult hemoglobin.  It is referred to as **hemoglobin A**. ## Abnormal variants of hemoglobin A Genetic mutations (usually point mutations affecting a single amino acid) can create abnormal variants of hemoglobin A that have altered conformation and different O2 affinity than normal hemoglobin A. Increased O2 affinity variants include hemoglobin Chesapeake and hemoglobin Kempsey.  The increased affinity reduces O2 unloading in the tissues, creating tissue hypoxia that stimulates erythropoietin production and erythrocytosis (high RBC count). Decreased O2 affinity variants include hemoglobin C and hemoglobin sickle cell (hemoglobin S): - Hemoglobin C results in a decreased RBC lifespan and usually mild anemia.  Increased O2 unloading in the tissues allows most affected patients to generally remain asymptomatic. - Hemoglobin S allows increased O2 unloading in the tissues, but it creates other substantial disruptions.  Low PO2 encourages polymerization of hemoglobin S, which disrupts RBC shape and can impair blood flow.  RBC lifespan is markedly shortened, which can result in severe anemia. ## Other types of hemoglobin Other types of hemoglobin result from combinations of different types of globin chains ((Table 1)).  Relevant for O2 transport are the following: - **Fetal hemoglobin**:  Fetal hemoglobin (hemoglobin F) is synthesized primarily during fetal development (~8 weeks gestation until term) and consists of 2 alpha chains but with 2 gamma chains instead of beta chains.  The gamma chains do not bind effectively to 2,3-BPG due to the replacement of a histidine residue with serine ((Figure 7)); therefore, fetal hemoglobin has significantly higher O2 affinity than adult hemoglobin ((Figure 8)).  This allows fetal hemoglobin to extract more O2 from the adult hemoglobin in the placenta, providing the developing fetus with an adequate supply of O2. - **Hemoglobin H**:  Hemoglobin H is an abnormal hemoglobin composed of 4 beta chains.  It is dysfunctional and cannot effectively transport O2.  It is seen in adults with alpha thalassemia intermedia (substantially impaired production of alpha chains) ((Table 2)). - **Hemoglobin Bart**:  Hemoglobin Bart is an abnormal hemoglobin composed of 4 gamma chains.  It is dysfunctional and cannot effectively transport O2.  It is seen in fetuses with alpha thalassemia major (absent production of alpha chains), which is incompatible with life and usually results in intrauterine demise. # Other clinically important structural relatives of hemoglobin ## Carboxyhemoglobin Carbon monoxide (CO) has extremely high binding affinity for hemoglobin and is highly toxic (and potentially fatal) in anything other than small quantities.  CO outcompetes O2 for hemoglobin binding sites, and, once bound, creates carboxyhemoglobin, which has a dissociation curve shifted far to the left with an asymptotic (rather than sigmoid) shape ((Figure 9)).  Toxicity results from fewer O2 molecules being able to bind to hemoglobin, and those that do bind cannot be released into the tissues.  Carboxyhemoglobin is normally present in small amounts (eg, <1%-2% of all hemoglobin) but is present in higher quantities in smokers (eg, ~10%).  Higher blood levels, typically due to exposure to high levels of ambient CO (eg, house fire, faulty indoor heating equipment), are considered toxic. ## Myoglobin In contrast to hemoglobin, myoglobin is a monomeric heme protein and is the primary O2\-storage protein in skeletal and cardiac muscle.  Myoglobin has only 1 heme group and does not exhibit cooperative binding interactions; therefore, its O2\-dissociation curve has a hyperbolic shape ((Figure 10)).  The affinity of myoglobin for O2 is far higher than that of hemoglobin, with myoglobin having a P50 of only 1 mm Hg (compared to ~26 mm Hg for hemoglobin), such that myoglobin is highly saturated with O2 even in a low-O2 environment. # Summary Most oxygen is transported in the bloodstream via the carrier protein hemoglobin, whereas most carbon dioxide is transported in the form of bicarbonate (but some is carried by hemoglobin).  The most common type of normal adult hemoglobin (hemoglobin A) is composed of 2 alpha and 2 beta globin chains, and the unique structure allows for cooperative binding properties that help optimize oxygen loading in the lungs and unloading in the tissues.  Factors that decrease the overall affinity of hemoglobin for oxygen (ie, shift the dissociation curve to the right) and facilitate oxygen delivery to the tissues include decreased pH, increased temperature, and increased 2,3- bisphosphoglycerate levels. ​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​​​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌​​​​​​‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​​‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​​‌

articles.title: Pulmonary Physiology: Hypoxemia
articles.markdown:
# Pulmonary Physiology: Hypoxemia

# Introduction

Hypoxemia, hypoxia, anemia, and ischemia are related, yet distinct processes:

-   **Hypoxemia**:  Low dissolved oxygen (O<sub>2</sub>) content of arterial blood, commonly defined as an arterial partial pressure of O<sub>2</sub> (PaO<sub>2</sub>) <60 mm Hg.  Example:  parenchymal lung disease.
-   **Hypoxia**:  Low O<sub>2</sub> content at the end-organ and tissue level.  It can be caused by hypoxemia, anemia, or ischemia.  Prolonged hypoxia typically results in tissue necrosis.  Example:  myocardial infarction.
-   **Anemia**:  Low number of circulating red blood cells (and therefore, hemoglobin content) in arterial blood.  Example:  iron deficiency.
-   **Ischemia**:  Low perfusion of end-organs and tissues, resulting in decreased O<sub>2</sub> and other nutrients (eg, glucose).  Example:  arterial thrombosis.

This article discusses the mechanisms, pathophysiology, and evaluation of hypoxemia.

# Normal oxygenation

Normal oxygenation requires 3 elements:

-   Normal inspired O<sub>2</sub> (ie, normal PiO<sub>2</sub>).
-   Normal alveolar ventilation (ie, normal PaCO<sub>2</sub>).
-   Normal alveolar-capillary exchange (ie, normal A-a gradient).

## Normal inspired oxygen (PiO<sub>2</sub>)

**PiO**<sub>**2**</sub> (partial pressure of inspired O<sub>2</sub>) is the O<sub>2</sub> available in the atmosphere for breathing.  It is determined by the fraction of inspired O<sub>2</sub> (FiO<sub>2</sub>), the atmospheric pressure (P<sub>atm</sub>), and the water vapor pressure (P<sub>H2O</sub>).

Under standard conditions:  PiO<sub>2</sub> = FiO<sub>2</sub> × (P<sub>atm</sub> − P<sub>H2O</sub>) = 0.21 × (760 − 47) ≈ **150 mm Hg**:

-   **FiO**<sub>**2**</sub> = fraction of inspired O<sub>2</sub>.  It is the percentage of air molecules that are O<sub>2</sub>.  Normal FiO<sub>2</sub> is 21% everywhere on Earth.
-   **P**<sub>**atm**</sub> = atmospheric pressure.  Normal P<sub>atm</sub> is 760 mm Hg at sea level and decreases with altitude.
-   **P**<sub>**H2O**</sub> = vapor pressure of water in the atmosphere.  Normal P<sub>H2O</sub> is 47 mm Hg.

## Normal alveolar ventilation (PaCO<sub>2</sub>)

**PaCO**<sub>**2**</sub> (partial pressure of arterial carbon dioxide) reflects the effectiveness of ventilation, which removes ("blows off") carbon dioxide (CO<sub>2</sub>).  It is determined by minute ventilation, the product of respiratory rate (RR) and tidal volume (V<sub>T</sub>).  Normal minute ventilation is 6-8 L/min because normal RR is 12-16/min and normal V<sub>T</sub> is 500 mL (= 0.5 L).

PaCO<sub>2</sub> is measured directly by arterial blood gas (ABG) analysis.  PaCO<sub>2</sub> is in equilibrium with PACO<sub>2</sub> (partial pressure of alveolar carbon dioxide) because CO<sub>2</sub> diffuses instantly between the pulmonary capillary blood and the alveolar airspace.  Therefore, under normal conditions, P<sub>A</sub>CO<sub>2</sub> = PaCO<sub>2</sub> = **40 mm Hg**.

In the alveolus, each molecule of CO<sub>2</sub> displaces 0.8 molecule of O<sub>2</sub>.  **PAO**<sub>**2**</sub> (partial pressure of alveolar oxygen) is the O<sub>2</sub> content present in the alveolar airspace after dilution by CO<sub>2</sub>.  Normally, P<sub>A</sub>O<sub>2</sub> = PiO<sub>2</sub> − P<sub>A</sub>CO<sub>2</sub> / 0.8 = 150 – 40 / 0.8 = **100 mm Hg**.

## Normal alveolar-capillary exchange (A-a gradient)

**A-a gradient** (alveolar-arterial gradient) is the difference between P<sub>A</sub>O<sub>2</sub> and PaO<sub>2</sub>.

-   P<sub>A</sub>O<sub>2</sub> is normally 100 mm Hg as previously described.
-   **PaO**<sub>**2**</sub> is normally **75-100 mm Hg** and is measured directly by ABG analysis.

A small A-a gradient is normally present due to physiologic right-to-left shunting (eg, thebesian veins, bronchial circulation).  This expected A-a gradient can be predicted from age:  normal A-a gradient ≈ age / 3 ≈ (age / 4) + 4.  The A-a gradient is widened by conditions that disrupt the uptake of oxygen, such as V/Q mismatch, diffusion limitation, and abnormal right-to-left shunting.

# Five mechanisms of hypoxemia

There are 5 mechanisms of hypoxemia:

-   1\. Low PiO<sub>2</sub>.
-   2\. Alveolar hypoventilation (↑ PaCO<sub>2</sub>).
-   Abnormal (↑) A-a gradient.
    -   3\. V/Q mismatch.
    -   4\. Diffusion limitation.
    -   5\. Right-to-left shunt.

## Low inspired oxygen (↓P<sub>i</sub>O<sub>2</sub>)

Low PiO<sub>2</sub> refers to hypoxemia due to insufficient atmospheric O<sub>2</sub> available for breathing.  It occurs in 2 situations:

-   **Decreased FiO**<sub>**2**</sub> (ie, **normobaric hypoxemia**):  Normal FiO<sub>2</sub> is 21% everywhere on Earth.  It drops if another gas displaces O<sub>2</sub> in the inspired air.  For example, a massive nitrogen spill can severely depress FiO<sub>2</sub>, even though P<sub>atm</sub> remains the same.  In practice, this is a very rare scenario.
-   **Decreased P**<sub>**atm**</sub> (ie, **hypobaric hypoxemia**):  Normal P<sub>atm</sub> is 760 mm Hg at sea level.  Atmospheric pressure is decreased at **high altitudes**.  For example, P<sub>atm</sub> is only 250 mm Hg at the top of Mount Everest, even though FiO<sub>2</sub> is still 21%.  PaO<sub>2</sub> declines with rising elevation ((Figure 1)), with hypoxemia generally becoming problematic at >2,500 m (8,000 ft), corresponding to the development of high-altitude illness.

With low PiO<sub>2</sub>, hypoxemia occurs because the initial O<sub>2</sub> content reaching the alveoli is decreased.  However, the **A-a gradient is norma**l because O<sub>2</sub> transport across the alveolar membrane is unaffected.

## Alveolar hypoventilation (↑ PaCO<sub>2</sub>)

Alveolar hypoventilation ((Figure 2)) refers to hypoxemia due to the retention of carbon dioxide.  An increase in PaCO<sub>2</sub> **(hypercapnia)** occurs in 3 situations:

-   **Central hypoventilation** ("won't breathe"):  Central hypoventilation occurs when neural respiratory drive is diminished.  Etiologies include opioids, alcohol, benzodiazepines, and damage to brainstem respiratory centers (eg, tumor, stroke).  Patients have **slow and shallow** breathing (↓ RR × ↓ V<sub>T</sub>), indicating a lack of drive.
-   **Peripheral hypoventilation** ("can't breathe"):  Peripheral hypoventilation occurs when respiratory mechanics are impaired, even though neural respiratory drive is intact.  Etiologies include neuromuscular disease (eg, myasthenia gravis), chest wall deformities (eg, severe kyphosis), advanced obstructive lung disease (eg, emphysema), and advanced restrictive lung disease (eg, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis).  Patients have **rapid and shallow** breathing (↑ RR × ↓↓ V<sub>T</sub>), and minute ventilation decreases when tachypnea cannot compensate for low V<sub>T</sub>.
-   **High dead space** (wasted ventilation):  Dead space refers to the portion of the V<sub>T</sub> that does not participate in gas exchange.
    -   **Anatomic** dead space is formed where no gas exchange occurs in the conducting airways (eg, trachea, bronchi).  It remains constant but can be increased if additional tubing is added to the respiratory circuit (eg, mechanical ventilation).
    -   **Alveolar** dead space is formed by alveoli that are ventilated but not perfused.  It is normally negligible but can be increased by conditions that block alveolar perfusion (eg, pulmonary embolism).  Minute ventilation is decreased **despite** rapid and deep breathing (↑ RR × ↑ V<sub>T</sub>) because most of the V<sub>T</sub> does not participate in gas exchange.

With alveolar hypoventilation, hypoxemia occurs because O<sub>2</sub> is displaced by CO<sub>2</sub> retained in the alveoli.  However, **A-a gradient is normal** because O<sub>2</sub> transport across the alveolar membrane is intact.

## V/Q mismatch

V/Q mismatch ((Figure 3)) refers to hypoxemia due to a regional imbalance of air flow (V) and blood flow (Q) reaching the alveoli.  Normally, both V and Q are highest at lung bases and lowest at the lung apices.  Across the entire lung, this averages to a global V/Q ratio = 1 ((Figure 4)).  Defects in either V or Q can cause deviations from this ratio:

-   **Low V/Q** ((Figure 5)):  Alveoli are poorly ventilated but continue to be perfused.  Etiologies include **airway and airspace disorders** such as lobar pneumonia, asthmatic bronchoconstriction, mucus plugging, and atelectasis.
-   **High V/Q** ((Figure 6)):  Alveoli are poorly perfused but continue to be ventilated.  Etiologies include **pulmonary vascular disorders** such as segmental pulmonary embolus and pulmonary arterial hypertension.  (These high V/Q areas also contribute to increased alveolar dead space, as previously described.)

With V/Q mismatch, hypoxemia occurs because Q and V are not efficiently localized together, producing an **elevated A-a gradient**.

## Diffusion limitation

Diffusion limitation ((Figure 7)) refers to hypoxemia due to factors that impair O<sub>2</sub> transfer across the alveolar membrane.  Normally, O<sub>2</sub> diffuses quickly and is fully extracted by the time blood has traveled only a third of the pulmonary capillary length.  This explains why exercise, which can increase pulmonary Q, does not result in hypoxemia.  However, 2 major processes can limit diffusion:

-   **Destruction** of the alveolar membrane (eg, emphysema) decreases the surface area available for O<sub>2</sub> uptake.
-   **Thickening** of the alveolar membrane (eg, interstitial lung disease) increases the diffusion distance for O<sub>2</sub>.

Unlike V/Q mismatch, which involves regional or focal abnormalities (eg, segmental pulmonary embolus), diffusion limitation involves diffuse abnormalities of the lung parenchyma.

With diffusion limitation, hypoxemia occurs because O<sub>2</sub> transit across the alveolar membrane is impaired (ie, **elevated A-a gradient**).  In many cases, patients can be normoxic at rest but develop hypoxemia with exertion.

## Right-to-left shunting

Right-to-left shunting refers to hypoxemia due to the direct mixture of deoxygenated blood with oxygenated blood.  It occurs in 3 scenarios:

-   **Intracardiac anatomic shunt**:  An intracardiac communication is seen with atrial or ventricular septal defects.  Normally, oxygenated blood flows from the left chambers (higher pressure) to the deoxygenated right chambers (lower pressure).  However, the flow can reverse if the right-sided pressures increase, such as with the development of pulmonary hypertension, known as Eisenmenger syndrome ((Figure 8)).
-   **Intrapulmonary anatomic shunt**:  An intrapulmonary anatomic shunt is seen with pulmonary arteriovenous malformations, which are anomalous connections between the deoxygenated pulmonary arteries and oxygenated pulmonary veins (bypassing the alveolar capillaries).
-   **Intrapulmonary shunt effect**:  In patients with extensive alveolar edema (eg, severe acute respiratory distress syndrome), the V/Q ratio can be close to 0, such that blood passing through the lungs barely receives oxygen.  This produces a functional right-to-left shunt, even though no direct anatomic connection is present.

With right-to-left shunting, hypoxemia occurs because deoxygenated blood mixes directly with oxygenated blood.  The **A-a gradient is elevated**.  Hypoxemia is often severe and **does not correct** with supplemental O<sub>2</sub> because a portion of the blood flow never reaches the lungs to be oxygenated.

# Evaluation of hypoxemia

ABG analysis can be approached in 2 ways.  A physiologic method, emphasizing stepwise interpretation without clinical context, is presented here.  In contrast, a clinical method, in which ABG is reserved for complex cases of hypoxemia in which clinical data alone are insufficient, is discussed in a separate article.  When reviewing an ABG, it is a good habit to apply a systematic framework even when the condition seems clinically obvious.

Formal stepwise ABG analysis of hypoxia ((Figure 9)) involves the 3 steps illustrated below.

## Step 1:  Compare PaO<sub>2</sub> and SaO<sub>2</sub>

PaO<sub>2</sub> is measured on ABG, and SaO<sub>2</sub> (O<sub>2</sub> saturation) is measured by pulse oximetry.  They are related by the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve ((Figure 10)); a left shift of the curve indicates increased hemoglobin O2 affinity and can be caused by increased pH, decreased 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate, and decreased temperature.  The PaO<sub>2</sub> at which hemoglobin is 50% saturated (P50) is a value used as a conventional measure of hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen.

Dyshemoglobinemias can lead to discrepancies between PaO<sub>2</sub> and SaO<sub>2</sub>.

-   **Methemoglobinemia**:  Methemoglobin is hemoglobin in which iron is oxidized to the ferric (Fe<sup>3+</sup>) state, which cannot bind oxygen.  Therefore, the amount of functional hemoglobin available is reduced, leading to decreased SaO₂.  However, the amount of O<sub>2</sub> dissolved in plasma is normal (ie, arterial blood is normoxic), meaning that PaO<sub>2</sub> is normal.
-   **Carboxyhemoglobinemia**:  Carboxyhemoglobin forms when carbon monoxide (rather than oxygen) binds to hemoglobin.  Carboxyhemoglobin absorbs light at a similar wavelength to oxyhemoglobin, causing pulse oximeters to misclassify it.  Therefore, SaO<sub>2</sub> (measured by pulse oximetry) reads as normal (or even artificially high), and blood may appear deceptively pink, even though functional oxygen-carrying capacity is reduced and true hypoxemia (eg, PaO<sub>2</sub> <60 mm Hg) may be present.

Additional testing for abnormal hemoglobin species (eg, multiwavelength CO-oximetry) may be indicated to explain the PaO<sub>2</sub>\-SaO<sub>2</sub> gap.

Severe acidosis or alkalosis can shift the oxygen-hemoglobin curve to the right or left, respectively.  For example, acidosis leads to the SaO<sub>2</sub> reading higher than expected for PaO<sub>2</sub> because it favors unloading into tissues.

## Step 2:  Calculate A-a gradient

The A-a gradient is a 4-step process that follows inspired gas as it moves from the atmosphere into the alveolar capillaries.

-   First, **calculate PiO**<sub>**2**</sub>:
    -   When breathing room air at sea level, PiO<sub>2</sub> = FiO<sub>2</sub> × (P<sub>atm</sub> − P<sub>H2O</sub>) = 0.21 × (760 − 47) ≈ 150 mm Hg.  This value changes at different altitudes or with the use of supplemental oxygen.
-   Second, **calculate P**<sub>**A**</sub>**O**<sub>**2**</sub>:
    -   As discussed previously, P<sub>A</sub>O<sub>2</sub> is the alveolar O<sub>2</sub> content after dilution by CO<sub>2</sub>.  Each molecule of CO<sub>2</sub> displaces 0.8 molecules of O<sub>2</sub>.  PaCO<sub>2</sub> is taken from the ABG and is normally 40 mm Hg.  Therefore, normal PAO<sub>2</sub> = PiO<sub>2</sub> × PaCO<sub>2</sub> / 0.8 = 150 – 40 / 0.8 = 100 mm Hg.
-   Third, **calculate A-a gradient**:
    -   A-a gradient is the difference between P<sub>A</sub>O<sub>2</sub> (calculated above) and PaO<sub>2</sub> (measured from ABG).  For example, a normal PaO<sub>2</sub> = 90 mm Hg.  Therefore, normal A-a gradient = 100 − 90 = 10 mm Hg.
-   Finally, **determine expected A-a gradient for age**:
    -   The physiologic A-a gradient increases with age.  Expected A-a gradient = (age / 4) + 4 ≈ age / 3.  The calculated A-a gradient in the previous step should be compared to this expected value.  A normal A-a gradient is due to low PiO<sub>2</sub> or alveolar hypoventilation.  An elevated A-a gradient is due to V/Q mismatch, diffusion limitation, or right-to-left shunt.

An example using real patient data is provided in the table ((Table 1)).

## Step 3a:  If A-a gradient is normal

Hypoxemia with normal A-a gradient is due to alveolar hypoventilation (most common) or low PiO<sub>2</sub> (usually clinically obvious).

-   **Alveolar hypoventilation** is indicated by elevated PaCO<sub>2</sub> (ie, >45 mm Hg).
-   **Low PiO**<sub>**2**</sub>, such as high altitude, is usually accompanied by low PaCO<sub>2</sub> due to hyperventilation.

## Step 3b:  If A-a gradient is elevated

Hypoxemia with elevated A-a gradient is due to V/Q mismatch, diffusion limitation, or right-to-left shunting.  These can be differentiated by the response to supplemental oxygen.

-   **V/Q mismatch** or **diffusion limitation**:  The hypoxemia responds quickly to supplemental oxygen.  The A-a gradient is wide but remains relatively constant at all levels of supplemental oxygen.  For example:
    -   On room air:  P<sub>A</sub>O<sub>2</sub> = 100 and PaO<sub>2</sub> = 50, so A-a gradient = 50 mm Hg.
    -   On 40% FiO<sub>2</sub>:  P<sub>A</sub>O<sub>2</sub> = 240 and PaO<sub>2</sub> = 190, so A-a gradient = 50 mm Hg still.  (The higher starting PiO<sub>2</sub> can "overcome" the A-a gradient to normalize the PaO<sub>2</sub>.)
-   **Right-to-left shunting**:  Hypoxemia does not respond to any level of supplemental oxygen.  The A-a gradient is wide and continues to increase at higher levels of supplemental oxygen.  For example:
    -   On room air:  P<sub>A</sub>O<sub>2</sub> = 100 and PaO<sub>2</sub> = 50, so A-a gradient = 50 mm Hg.
    -   On 100% FiO<sub>2</sub>:  P<sub>A</sub>O<sub>2</sub> = 660 but PaO<sub>2</sub> = 50 still.  (Even pure O<sub>2</sub> is ineffective because shunted blood bypasses the alveoli entirely.)

# Effects of hypoxemia

## Tissue responses

Tissue hypoxia is sensed by hypoxia-inducible factor-1 alpha (HIF1ɑ) (Figure 11)).  HIF1ɑ is a transcription factor that is constitutively expressed by most cells.  In normoxic cytosol, HIF1ɑ is constantly degraded; in contrast, in hypoxic cytosol, it is posttranslationally stabilized.  HIF1ɑ can have adaptive or potentially maladaptive effects, depending on the severity and duration of hypoxia:

-   **Erythropoiesis**:  HIF1ɑ induces the upregulation of erythropoietin in kidney juxtaglomerular cells and stimulates iron uptake in gut epithelium ((Figure 12)).
    -   Adaptively, this allows for compensatory polycythemia (generally, hematocrit >50% and hemoglobin >16.5 mg/dL) to boost oxygen-carrying capacity.
    -   Maladaptively, extreme polycythemia (eg, generally, hematocrit >60%) can cause a type of hyperviscosity syndrome in which vascular sludging produces neurologic symptoms (eg, headache, confusion), thrombosis, retinal edema, mucosal bleeding (eg, epistaxis), and heart failure.
-   **Angiogenesis**:  HIF1ɑ induces the upregulation of vascular endothelial growth factor, mainly in the heart and skeletal muscle.
    -   Adaptively, this promotes the formation of collateral circulation (eg, to bypass chronic coronary artery stenosis).
    -   Maladaptively, disorganized neovascularization (eg, diabetic proliferative retinopathy) results in fragile, hemorrhage-prone vessels.
-   **Anaerobic (glycolytic) shift**:  HIF1ɑ induces upregulation of glycolytic enzymes (eg, hexokinase), mainly in the heart and brain.
    -   Adaptively, this preserves ATP production despite low O<sub>2</sub> (eg, hibernating myocardium).
    -   Maladaptively, this results in several downstream changes, such as cellular proliferation (eg, Warburg effect in cancer cells, in which glucose is converted to lactate via aerobic glycolysis in the cytosol rather than being fully metabolized in the mitochondria, fueling rapid cell growth).  This shift also results in inflammation (eg, leukocyte activation due to glycolytic products).

## Vascular responses

Effects of hypoxia on vascular resistance are not dependent on HIF1ɑ.  Instead, vessels respond directly to O<sub>2</sub> itself, reactive oxygen species, or related metabolites.

-   **Systemic vasodilation**:  Hypoxia (eg, exercising skeletal muscle) stimulates the production of anaerobic metabolites such as adenosine, lactate, and nitric oxide that promote vasodilation.  Low O<sub>2</sub> tension directly relaxes vascular smooth muscle (eg, O<sub>2</sub>\-sensitive potassium and calcium channels).  These processes increase arterial perfusion to hypoxic tissue.
-   **Pulmonary vasoconstriction** ((Figure 13)):  Hypoxia is sensed by pulmonary arterioles, likely through mitochondrial redox potential, stimulating vasoconstriction.
    -   This is adaptive for short-term, regional hypoxia (eg, atelectatic lobe), because the selective vasoconstriction limits perfusion to poorly ventilated alveoli, maintaining V/Q matching.
    -   However, it is maladaptive for chronic, global hypoxia (eg, untreated obstructive sleep apnea) because whole-lung vasoconstriction can lead to pulmonary hypertension (eg, cor pulmonale, Group 3)

## Ventilatory response

Hypoxemia stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors in the aortic arch and carotid bodies.  These chemoreceptors signal the medullary respiratory center to increase ventilation through deeper breaths and increased RR.  Hyperventilation has a much larger impact on lowering PaCO<sub>2</sub> than on raising PaO<sub>2</sub> ((Figure 14)).

-   **Ventilation**:  Hyperventilation causes an immediate reduction in PaCO<sub>2</sub> (respiratory alkalosis) because CO<sub>2</sub> elimination is directly proportional to minute ventilation.
-   **Oxygenation**:  Hyperventilation increases PaO<sub>2</sub> by only a small amount because perfusion to well-ventilated alveoli is already maximized, so further increases in ventilation do not significantly enhance O<sub>2</sub> uptake (ie, ceiling effect).  The hemoglobin in these regions is already near full saturation.

In other words, high V/Q areas (ie, hyperventilation) cannot compensate ((Figure 15)) for low V/Q units (eg, mismatch).  Breathing faster and harder will blow down CO<sub>2</sub> but does not improve oxygenation.

## Cell death

Severe or sustained hypoxemia can result in cell death, especially when combined with ischemia (eg, hypotension).  The dual insult of hypoxemia and hypotension is much more likely to cause tissue necrosis than either alone.  Tissue tolerance varies widely:  Kidneys (eg, acute tubular necrosis) can fully recover even after 15 minutes of complete circulatory arrest, whereas hypoxic-ischemic brain injury may be irreversible after just 3-5 minutes.

# Summary

Hypoxemia (PaO<sub>2</sub> <60 mm Hg) can be caused by 5 mechanisms:  low inspired oxygen (eg, high altitude), alveolar hypoventilation (eg, opioid-induced respiratory depression), ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) mismatch (eg, lobar pneumonia), diffusion limitation (eg, interstitial lung disease), and right-to-left shunting (eg, atrial septal defect).  The alveolar-arterial (A-a) gradient assesses oxygen exchange across the alveolar capillary membrane and helps to identify the underlying mechanism.  Hypoxemia with a normal A-a gradient is due to low inspired oxygen or alveolar hypoventilation (ie, high PaCO<sub>2</sub>).  Hypoxemia with an elevated A-a gradient is due to V/Q mismatch, diffusion limitation, or right-to-left shunting.  A poor response to 100% supplemental oxygen suggests shunt physiology.
