›Introduction

Hypoxemia, hypoxia, anemia, and ischemia are related, yet distinct processes:

  • Hypoxemia:  Low dissolved oxygen (O2) content of arterial blood, commonly defined as an arterial partial pressure of O2 (PaO2) <60 mm Hg.  Example:  parenchymal lung disease.
  • Hypoxia:  Low O2 content at the end-organ and tissue level.  It can be caused by hypoxemia, anemia, or ischemia.  Prolonged hypoxia typically results in tissue necrosis.  Example:  myocardial infarction.
  • Anemia:  Low number of circulating red blood cells (and therefore, hemoglobin content) in arterial blood.  Example:  iron deficiency.
  • Ischemia:  Low perfusion of end-organs and tissues, resulting in decreased O2 and other nutrients (eg, glucose).  Example:  arterial thrombosis.

This article discusses the mechanisms, pathophysiology, and evaluation of hypoxemia.

›Normal oxygenation

Normal oxygenation requires 3 elements:

  • Normal inspired O2 (ie, normal PiO2).
  • Normal alveolar ventilation (ie, normal PaCO2).
  • Normal alveolar-capillary exchange (ie, normal A-a gradient).

Normal inspired oxygen (PiO2)

PiO2 (partial pressure of inspired O2) is the O2 available in the atmosphere for breathing.  It is determined by the fraction of inspired O2 (FiO2), the atmospheric pressure (Patm), and the water vapor pressure (PH2O).

Under standard conditions:  PiO2 = FiO2 × (Patm − PH2O) = 0.21 × (760 − 47) ≈ 150 mm Hg:

  • FiO2 = fraction of inspired O2.  It is the percentage of air molecules that are O2.  Normal FiO2 is 21% everywhere on Earth.
  • Patm = atmospheric pressure.  Normal Patm is 760 mm Hg at sea level and decreases with altitude.
  • PH2O = vapor pressure of water in the atmosphere.  Normal PH2O is 47 mm Hg.

Normal alveolar ventilation (PaCO2)

PaCO2 (partial pressure of arterial carbon dioxide) reflects the effectiveness of ventilation, which removes ("blows off") carbon dioxide (CO2).  It is determined by minute ventilation, the product of respiratory rate (RR) and tidal volume (VT).  Normal minute ventilation is 6-8 L/min because normal RR is 12-16/min and normal VT is 500 mL (= 0.5 L).

PaCO2 is measured directly by arterial blood gas (ABG) analysis.  PaCO2 is in equilibrium with PACO2 (partial pressure of alveolar carbon dioxide) because CO2 diffuses instantly between the pulmonary capillary blood and the alveolar airspace.  Therefore, under normal conditions, PACO2 = PaCO2 = 40 mm Hg.

In the alveolus, each molecule of CO2 displaces 0.8 molecule of O2.  PAO2 (partial pressure of alveolar oxygen) is the O2 content present in the alveolar airspace after dilution by CO2.  Normally, PAO2 = PiO2 − PACO2 / 0.8 = 150 – 40 / 0.8 = 100 mm Hg.

Normal alveolar-capillary exchange (A-a gradient)

A-a gradient (alveolar-arterial gradient) is the difference between PAO2 and PaO2.

  • PAO2 is normally 100 mm Hg as previously described.
  • PaO2 is normally 75-100 mm Hg and is measured directly by ABG analysis.

A small A-a gradient is normally present due to physiologic right-to-left shunting (eg, thebesian veins, bronchial circulation).  This expected A-a gradient can be predicted from age:  normal A-a gradient ≈ age / 3 ≈ (age / 4) + 4.  The A-a gradient is widened by conditions that disrupt the uptake of oxygen, such as V/Q mismatch, diffusion limitation, and abnormal right-to-left shunting.

›Five mechanisms of hypoxemia

There are 5 mechanisms of hypoxemia:

  • 1. Low PiO2.
  • 2. Alveolar hypoventilation (↑ PaCO2).
  • Abnormal (↑) A-a gradient.
    • 3. V/Q mismatch.
    • 4. Diffusion limitation.
    • 5. Right-to-left shunt.

Low inspired oxygen (↓PiO2)

Low PiO2 refers to hypoxemia due to insufficient atmospheric O2 available for breathing.  It occurs in 2 situations:

  • Decreased FiO2 (ie, normobaric hypoxemia):  Normal FiO2 is 21% everywhere on Earth.  It drops if another gas displaces O2 in the inspired air.  For example, a massive nitrogen spill can severely depress FiO2, even though Patm remains the same.  In practice, this is a very rare scenario.
  • Decreased Patm (ie, hypobaric hypoxemia):  Normal Patm is 760 mm Hg at sea level.  Atmospheric pressure is decreased at high altitudes.  For example, Patm is only 250 mm Hg at the top of Mount Everest, even though FiO2 is still 21%.  PaO2 declines with rising elevation , with hypoxemia generally becoming problematic at >2,500 m (8,000 ft), corresponding to the development of high-altitude illness.

With low PiO2, hypoxemia occurs because the initial O2 content reaching the alveoli is decreased.  However, the A-a gradient is normal because O2 transport across the alveolar membrane is unaffected.

Alveolar hypoventilation (↑ PaCO2)

Alveolar hypoventilation refers to hypoxemia due to the retention of carbon dioxide.  An increase in PaCO2 (hypercapnia) occurs in 3 situations:

  • Central hypoventilation ("won't breathe"):  Central hypoventilation occurs when neural respiratory drive is diminished.  Etiologies include opioids, alcohol, benzodiazepines, and damage to brainstem respiratory centers (eg, tumor, stroke).  Patients have slow and shallow breathing (↓ RR × ↓ VT), indicating a lack of drive.
  • Peripheral hypoventilation ("can't breathe"):  Peripheral hypoventilation occurs when respiratory mechanics are impaired, even though neural respiratory drive is intact.  Etiologies include neuromuscular disease (eg, myasthenia gravis), chest wall deformities (eg, severe kyphosis), advanced obstructive lung disease (eg, emphysema), and advanced restrictive lung disease (eg, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis).  Patients have rapid and shallow breathing (↑ RR × ↓↓ VT), and minute ventilation decreases when tachypnea cannot compensate for low VT.
  • High dead space (wasted ventilation):  Dead space refers to the portion of the VT that does not participate in gas exchange.
    • Anatomic dead space is formed where no gas exchange occurs in the conducting airways (eg, trachea, bronchi).  It remains constant but can be increased if additional tubing is added to the respiratory circuit (eg, mechanical ventilation).
    • Alveolar dead space is formed by alveoli that are ventilated but not perfused.  It is normally negligible but can be increased by conditions that block alveolar perfusion (eg, pulmonary embolism).  Minute ventilation is decreased despite rapid and deep breathing (↑ RR × ↑ VT) because most of the VT does not participate in gas exchange.

With alveolar hypoventilation, hypoxemia occurs because O2 is displaced by CO2 retained in the alveoli.  However, A-a gradient is normal because O2 transport across the alveolar membrane is intact.

V/Q mismatch

V/Q mismatch refers to hypoxemia due to a regional imbalance of air flow (V) and blood flow (Q) reaching the alveoli.  Normally, both V and Q are highest at lung bases and lowest at the lung apices.  Across the entire lung, this averages to a global V/Q ratio = 1 .  Defects in either V or Q can cause deviations from this ratio:

  • Low V/Q :  Alveoli are poorly ventilated but continue to be perfused.  Etiologies include airway and airspace disorders such as lobar pneumonia, asthmatic bronchoconstriction, mucus plugging, and atelectasis.
  • High V/Q :  Alveoli are poorly perfused but continue to be ventilated.  Etiologies include pulmonary vascular disorders such as segmental pulmonary embolus and pulmonary arterial hypertension.  (These high V/Q areas also contribute to increased alveolar dead space, as previously described.)

With V/Q mismatch, hypoxemia occurs because Q and V are not efficiently localized together, producing an elevated A-a gradient.

Diffusion limitation

Diffusion limitation refers to hypoxemia due to factors that impair O2 transfer across the alveolar membrane.  Normally, O2 diffuses quickly and is fully extracted by the time blood has traveled only a third of the pulmonary capillary length.  This explains why exercise, which can increase pulmonary Q, does not result in hypoxemia.  However, 2 major processes can limit diffusion:

  • Destruction of the alveolar membrane (eg, emphysema) decreases the surface area available for O2 uptake.
  • Thickening of the alveolar membrane (eg, interstitial lung disease) increases the diffusion distance for O2.

Unlike V/Q mismatch, which involves regional or focal abnormalities (eg, segmental pulmonary embolus), diffusion limitation involves diffuse abnormalities of the lung parenchyma.

With diffusion limitation, hypoxemia occurs because O2 transit across the alveolar membrane is impaired (ie, elevated A-a gradient).  In many cases, patients can be normoxic at rest but develop hypoxemia with exertion.

Right-to-left shunting

Right-to-left shunting refers to hypoxemia due to the direct mixture of deoxygenated blood with oxygenated blood.  It occurs in 3 scenarios:

  • Intracardiac anatomic shunt:  An intracardiac communication is seen with atrial or ventricular septal defects.  Normally, oxygenated blood flows from the left chambers (higher pressure) to the deoxygenated right chambers (lower pressure).  However, the flow can reverse if the right-sided pressures increase, such as with the development of pulmonary hypertension, known as Eisenmenger syndrome .
  • Intrapulmonary anatomic shunt:  An intrapulmonary anatomic shunt is seen with pulmonary arteriovenous malformations, which are anomalous connections between the deoxygenated pulmonary arteries and oxygenated pulmonary veins (bypassing the alveolar capillaries).
  • Intrapulmonary shunt effect:  In patients with extensive alveolar edema (eg, severe acute respiratory distress syndrome), the V/Q ratio can be close to 0, such that blood passing through the lungs barely receives oxygen.  This produces a functional right-to-left shunt, even though no direct anatomic connection is present.

With right-to-left shunting, hypoxemia occurs because deoxygenated blood mixes directly with oxygenated blood.  The A-a gradient is elevated.  Hypoxemia is often severe and does not correct with supplemental O2 because a portion of the blood flow never reaches the lungs to be oxygenated.

›Evaluation of hypoxemia

ABG analysis can be approached in 2 ways.  A physiologic method, emphasizing stepwise interpretation without clinical context, is presented here.  In contrast, a clinical method, in which ABG is reserved for complex cases of hypoxemia in which clinical data alone are insufficient, is discussed in a separate article.  When reviewing an ABG, it is a good habit to apply a systematic framework even when the condition seems clinically obvious.

Formal stepwise ABG analysis of hypoxia involves the 3 steps illustrated below.

Step 1:  Compare PaO2 and SaO2

PaO2 is measured on ABG, and SaO2 (O2 saturation) is measured by pulse oximetry.  They are related by the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve ; a left shift of the curve indicates increased hemoglobin O2 affinity and can be caused by increased pH, decreased 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate, and decreased temperature.  The PaO2 at which hemoglobin is 50% saturated (P50) is a value used as a conventional measure of hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen.

Dyshemoglobinemias can lead to discrepancies between PaO2 and SaO2.

  • Methemoglobinemia:  Methemoglobin is hemoglobin in which iron is oxidized to the ferric (Fe3+) state, which cannot bind oxygen.  Therefore, the amount of functional hemoglobin available is reduced, leading to decreased SaO₂.  However, the amount of O2 dissolved in plasma is normal (ie, arterial blood is normoxic), meaning that PaO2 is normal.
  • Carboxyhemoglobinemia:  Carboxyhemoglobin forms when carbon monoxide (rather than oxygen) binds to hemoglobin.  Carboxyhemoglobin absorbs light at a similar wavelength to oxyhemoglobin, causing pulse oximeters to misclassify it.  Therefore, SaO2 (measured by pulse oximetry) reads as normal (or even artificially high), and blood may appear deceptively pink, even though functional oxygen-carrying capacity is reduced and true hypoxemia (eg, PaO2 <60 mm Hg) may be present.

Additional testing for abnormal hemoglobin species (eg, multiwavelength CO-oximetry) may be indicated to explain the PaO2-SaO2 gap.

Severe acidosis or alkalosis can shift the oxygen-hemoglobin curve to the right or left, respectively.  For example, acidosis leads to the SaO2 reading higher than expected for PaO2 because it favors unloading into tissues.

Step 2:  Calculate A-a gradient

The A-a gradient is a 4-step process that follows inspired gas as it moves from the atmosphere into the alveolar capillaries.

  • First, calculate PiO2:
    • When breathing room air at sea level, PiO2 = FiO2 × (Patm − PH2O) = 0.21 × (760 − 47) ≈ 150 mm Hg.  This value changes at different altitudes or with the use of supplemental oxygen.
  • Second, calculate PAO2:
    • As discussed previously, PAO2 is the alveolar O2 content after dilution by CO2.  Each molecule of CO2 displaces 0.8 molecules of O2.  PaCO2 is taken from the ABG and is normally 40 mm Hg.  Therefore, normal PAO2 = PiO2 × PaCO2 / 0.8 = 150 – 40 / 0.8 = 100 mm Hg.
  • Third, calculate A-a gradient:
    • A-a gradient is the difference between PAO2 (calculated above) and PaO2 (measured from ABG).  For example, a normal PaO2 = 90 mm Hg.  Therefore, normal A-a gradient = 100 − 90 = 10 mm Hg.
  • Finally, determine expected A-a gradient for age:
    • The physiologic A-a gradient increases with age.  Expected A-a gradient = (age / 4) + 4 ≈ age / 3.  The calculated A-a gradient in the previous step should be compared to this expected value.  A normal A-a gradient is due to low PiO2 or alveolar hypoventilation.  An elevated A-a gradient is due to V/Q mismatch, diffusion limitation, or right-to-left shunt.

An example using real patient data is provided in the table .

Step 3a:  If A-a gradient is normal

Hypoxemia with normal A-a gradient is due to alveolar hypoventilation (most common) or low PiO2 (usually clinically obvious).

  • Alveolar hypoventilation is indicated by elevated PaCO2 (ie, >45 mm Hg).
  • Low PiO2, such as high altitude, is usually accompanied by low PaCO2 due to hyperventilation.

Step 3b:  If A-a gradient is elevated

Hypoxemia with elevated A-a gradient is due to V/Q mismatch, diffusion limitation, or right-to-left shunting.  These can be differentiated by the response to supplemental oxygen.

  • V/Q mismatch or diffusion limitation:  The hypoxemia responds quickly to supplemental oxygen.  The A-a gradient is wide but remains relatively constant at all levels of supplemental oxygen.  For example:
    • On room air:  PAO2 = 100 and PaO2 = 50, so A-a gradient = 50 mm Hg.
    • On 40% FiO2:  PAO2 = 240 and PaO2 = 190, so A-a gradient = 50 mm Hg still.  (The higher starting PiO2 can "overcome" the A-a gradient to normalize the PaO2.)
  • Right-to-left shunting:  Hypoxemia does not respond to any level of supplemental oxygen.  The A-a gradient is wide and continues to increase at higher levels of supplemental oxygen.  For example:
    • On room air:  PAO2 = 100 and PaO2 = 50, so A-a gradient = 50 mm Hg.
    • On 100% FiO2:  PAO2 = 660 but PaO2 = 50 still.  (Even pure O2 is ineffective because shunted blood bypasses the alveoli entirely.)

›Effects of hypoxemia

Tissue responses

Tissue hypoxia is sensed by hypoxia-inducible factor-1 alpha (HIF1ɑ) .  HIF1ɑ is a transcription factor that is constitutively expressed by most cells.  In normoxic cytosol, HIF1ɑ is constantly degraded; in contrast, in hypoxic cytosol, it is posttranslationally stabilized.  HIF1ɑ can have adaptive or potentially maladaptive effects, depending on the severity and duration of hypoxia:

  • Erythropoiesis:  HIF1ɑ induces the upregulation of erythropoietin in kidney juxtaglomerular cells and stimulates iron uptake in gut epithelium .
    • Adaptively, this allows for compensatory polycythemia (generally, hematocrit >50% and hemoglobin >16.5 mg/dL) to boost oxygen-carrying capacity.
    • Maladaptively, extreme polycythemia (eg, generally, hematocrit >60%) can cause a type of hyperviscosity syndrome in which vascular sludging produces neurologic symptoms (eg, headache, confusion), thrombosis, retinal edema, mucosal bleeding (eg, epistaxis), and heart failure.
  • Angiogenesis:  HIF1ɑ induces the upregulation of vascular endothelial growth factor, mainly in the heart and skeletal muscle.
    • Adaptively, this promotes the formation of collateral circulation (eg, to bypass chronic coronary artery stenosis).
    • Maladaptively, disorganized neovascularization (eg, diabetic proliferative retinopathy) results in fragile, hemorrhage-prone vessels.
  • Anaerobic (glycolytic) shift:  HIF1ɑ induces upregulation of glycolytic enzymes (eg, hexokinase), mainly in the heart and brain.
    • Adaptively, this preserves ATP production despite low O2 (eg, hibernating myocardium).
    • Maladaptively, this results in several downstream changes, such as cellular proliferation (eg, Warburg effect in cancer cells, in which glucose is converted to lactate via aerobic glycolysis in the cytosol rather than being fully metabolized in the mitochondria, fueling rapid cell growth).  This shift also results in inflammation (eg, leukocyte activation due to glycolytic products).

Vascular responses

Effects of hypoxia on vascular resistance are not dependent on HIF1ɑ.  Instead, vessels respond directly to O2 itself, reactive oxygen species, or related metabolites.

  • Systemic vasodilation:  Hypoxia (eg, exercising skeletal muscle) stimulates the production of anaerobic metabolites such as adenosine, lactate, and nitric oxide that promote vasodilation.  Low O2 tension directly relaxes vascular smooth muscle (eg, O2-sensitive potassium and calcium channels).  These processes increase arterial perfusion to hypoxic tissue.
  • Pulmonary vasoconstriction :  Hypoxia is sensed by pulmonary arterioles, likely through mitochondrial redox potential, stimulating vasoconstriction.
    • This is adaptive for short-term, regional hypoxia (eg, atelectatic lobe), because the selective vasoconstriction limits perfusion to poorly ventilated alveoli, maintaining V/Q matching.
    • However, it is maladaptive for chronic, global hypoxia (eg, untreated obstructive sleep apnea) because whole-lung vasoconstriction can lead to pulmonary hypertension (eg, cor pulmonale, Group 3)

Ventilatory response

Hypoxemia stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors in the aortic arch and carotid bodies.  These chemoreceptors signal the medullary respiratory center to increase ventilation through deeper breaths and increased RR.  Hyperventilation has a much larger impact on lowering PaCO2 than on raising PaO2 .

  • Ventilation:  Hyperventilation causes an immediate reduction in PaCO2 (respiratory alkalosis) because CO2 elimination is directly proportional to minute ventilation.
  • Oxygenation:  Hyperventilation increases PaO2 by only a small amount because perfusion to well-ventilated alveoli is already maximized, so further increases in ventilation do not significantly enhance O2 uptake (ie, ceiling effect).  The hemoglobin in these regions is already near full saturation.

In other words, high V/Q areas (ie, hyperventilation) cannot compensate for low V/Q units (eg, mismatch).  Breathing faster and harder will blow down CO2 but does not improve oxygenation.

Cell death

Severe or sustained hypoxemia can result in cell death, especially when combined with ischemia (eg, hypotension).  The dual insult of hypoxemia and hypotension is much more likely to cause tissue necrosis than either alone.  Tissue tolerance varies widely:  Kidneys (eg, acute tubular necrosis) can fully recover even after 15 minutes of complete circulatory arrest, whereas hypoxic-ischemic brain injury may be irreversible after just 3-5 minutes.

›Summary

Hypoxemia (PaO2 <60 mm Hg) can be caused by 5 mechanisms:  low inspired oxygen (eg, high altitude), alveolar hypoventilation (eg, opioid-induced respiratory depression), ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) mismatch (eg, lobar pneumonia), diffusion limitation (eg, interstitial lung disease), and right-to-left shunting (eg, atrial septal defect).  The alveolar-arterial (A-a) gradient assesses oxygen exchange across the alveolar capillary membrane and helps to identify the underlying mechanism.  Hypoxemia with a normal A-a gradient is due to low inspired oxygen or alveolar hypoventilation (ie, high PaCO2).  Hypoxemia with an elevated A-a gradient is due to V/Q mismatch, diffusion limitation, or right-to-left shunting.  A poor response to 100% supplemental oxygen suggests shunt physiology.

​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​​​​‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​​​​

Alveolar-arterial (A-a) gradient calculation: worked example

48-year-old woman with emphysema
ABGs: pH 7.34, PaCO2 60 mm Hg, PaO2 50 mm Hg

Step 1

Calculate PiO2

  • PiO2 is the inspired oxygen that reaches the alveoli
  • Determined by atmospheric pressure (Patm), water vapor (PH2O) & FiO2 (21% at room air)

►Patient's PiO2 = (Patm − PH2O) × (FiO2) = (760 − 47) × (0.21) = 150 mm Hg

Step 2

Calculate PAO2

  • PAO2 is the oxygen in the alveolar airspace after admixture with CO2
  • Each molecule of O2 occupies the same space as 0.8 molecules of CO2

►Patient's PAO2 = PiO2 − PaCO2 / 0.8 = 150 − 60 / 0.8 = 150 − 75 = 75 mm Hg

Step 3

Calculate A-a gradient

  • Difference between PAO2 (calculated above) & PaO2 (from ABG analysis)
  • Elevated by a damaged alveolar membrane (eg, emphysema) or by right-to-left shunt

►Patient's A-a gradient = PAO2 − PaO2 = 75 − 50 = 25 mm Hg

Step 4

Compare to normal

  • Small A-a gradient is normal due to physiologic right-to-left shunting (eg, bronchial arteries)
  • Expected A-a gradient ~ age / 3 = 48 / 3 = 16 mm Hg

►Patient's A-a gradient is elevated (25 > 16)

ABG = arterial blood gas.

articles.title: Pulmonary Physiology: Gas Exchange
articles.markdown: # Pulmonary Physiology: Gas Exchange # Introduction Respiratory gas exchange involves the following processes: - Oxygenation (oxygen extraction in the lungs). - Ventilation (carbon dioxide elimination by the lungs). - Oxygen and carbon dioxide transport in the blood. - Respiratory quotient (carbon dioxide produced per oxygen consumed). This article discusses these processes, how they are regulated at rest, and how they respond during exercise. # Oxygenation Oxygenation refers to the extraction of oxygen in the lungs.  Normal oxygenation requires: - Normal inspired oxygen (ie, PiO2). - Normal alveolar ventilation (ie, PaCO2), which requires normal minute ventilation and dead space. - Normal alveolar-capillary exchange (ie, A-a gradient), which requires: - Proper ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) matching. - Efficient diffusion. ## V/Q matching Ventilation (V) and perfusion (Q) matching can be conceptualized as the **opportunity** for oxygen uptake.  Wherever air (ventilation) is present, there should be corresponding blood flow (perfusion).  When ventilation is wasted on areas with insufficient blood flow (ie, dead space) or when perfusion is wasted on areas with insufficient ventilation (ie, shunt), V/Q mismatching occurs. Ventilation and perfusion both decrease from the lung bases to the lung apices ((Figure 1)): - Ventilation is slightly greater at the lung bases because basal alveoli, compressed by overlying lung weight, start smaller and can expand relatively more during inspiration; conversely, apical alveoli are already stretched open and expand less. - Perfusion is significantly greater at the lung bases due to the effect of gravity.  Gravity increases hydrostatic pressure in the pulmonary arteries (PAs), allowing blood to flow continuously (because the PA blood pressure exceeds the alveolar air pressure).  At the apices, PA pressure falls below alveolar pressure; as a result, capillaries are compressed and perfusion is reduced. ## V/Q ratios Based on the relative pressures of the PAs, alveoli, and pulmonary veins, the lung is traditionally divided into 3 zones of West (named after physiologist John West) ((Figure 2)): - **Zone 1 (apices and upper lobes)**:  Ventilation is low at the apices because the already distended alveoli have limited capacity to expand further during inspiration.  Perfusion is even lower because hydrostatic PA pressure is reduced at the apices, allowing alveoli to compress the capillaries and limit blood flow (alveolar pressure > PA pressure).  As a result, the **V/Q is >1** (often >2).  This zone has a **dead space tendency** (ie, wasted ventilation) due to relative underperfusion. - **Zone 2 (midlung)**:  Ventilation is intermediate because the alveoli are moderately compressed and capable of further expansion during inspiration.  Perfusion is also intermediate because the increasing hydrostatic PA pressure toward the lung bases helps keep the capillaries from being compressed by alveolar pressure (PA pressure > alveolar pressure).  As a result, the **V/Q ~1**.  This zone has **ideal V/Q matching**. - **Zone 3 (bases and lower lobes)**:  Ventilation is high at the bases because the basal alveoli expand the most during inspiration.  Perfusion is even higher because the gravitational hydrostatic pressure in the PAs keeps the vessels open.  As a result, the **V/Q is <1**.  This zone has **shunt tendency** due to relative overperfusion. At **rest**, V/Q ratios normally range from 3 at the apices to ~0.6 at the bases, with a global average ratio of ~1 for the entire lung.  The spread of the V/Q ratios is often represented as a histogram centered at 1 ((Figure 3)). ## V/Q with exercise At rest, the V/Q ratio is ~3 at the apices, as described previously.  During exercise, a rise in cardiac output recruits the capillaries in the apices and upper lobes, increasing perfusion in these regions.  As a result, apical perfusion increases, lowering the V/Q ratio toward 1.  This enables V/Q matching to improve **even further** with exercise compared to at rest, optimizing oxygen uptake efficiency.  Consequently, a slight **increase** in PaO2 is considered a normal oxygenation response during exercise.  Desaturation is never normal. ## Diffusion Perfect V/Q matching brings air and blood into close proximity, but oxygenation is not complete unless oxygen effectively crosses the alveolar-capillary membrane, a process known as diffusion.  Normal diffusion is governed by Fick law ((Figure 4)).  The 2 most important variables in Fick laws of diffusion are the following: - Alveolar membrane **surface area (A)** determines the total area available for diffusion, with increased area increasing diffusion.  Membrane surface area is normally 100 m2 in a healthy adult (approximately the size of a tennis court).  It is reduced by conditions such as lung resection (eg, lobectomy) and emphysema. - Alveolar membrane **thickness (T)** determines the distance that oxygen needs to cross, with increased thickness decreasing diffusion.  Membrane thickness is normally 0.5 μm in a healthy adult and comprises 3 layers (epithelium, basement membrane, endothelium).  Thickness is increased by conditions such as interstitial lung disease and pulmonary edema. The other variables include the **diffusion coefficient (D)** (a unique value for each gas representing its solubility \[eg, highest for carbon dioxide\]) and **partial pressure difference (ΔP)** across the membrane (increased by altering the pressure or purity of inhaled gas). ## Diffusion with exercise Oxygen diffuses quickly enough to fully equilibrate between the alveoli and the capillary blood within the first third of the pulmonary capillary.  This rapid diffusion prevents hypoxemia during exercise (eg, even when blood flow triples).  Because diffusion reaches an early ceiling, oxygen uptake can be increased further only by greater perfusion.  As a result, in healthy individuals, oxygen uptake is said to be **perfusion limited**.  However, in individuals with alveolar membrane damage (eg, due to severe emphysema or interstitial lung disease), oxygenation can become diffusion limited ((Figure 5)).  Oxygenation might be marginally normal at rest, but significant desaturation can often be revealed by exertion. # Ventilation Ventilation refers to the elimination of carbon dioxide by the lungs.  It requires normal alveolar ventilation (VA).  Therefore, alveolar hypoventilation and hypercapnia (ie, PaCO2 >45 mm Hg) are synonymous. ## Minute ventilation Minute ventilation (VE) is the total respired volume per minute.  It is calculated as the product of tidal volume (VT) and respiratory rate (RR) (VE = VT · RR).  Normal VT is approximately 500 mL, and normal RR is 12/min, yielding a typical VE of 6 L/min. ## Alveolar ventilation Alveolar ventilation (VA) is the total respired volume that participates in alveolar gas exchange.  It is equal to VE **minus the dead space ventilation (V****D****)**.  Dead space is the fraction of VT that is unavailable for exchange.  There are 2 components of VD ((Figure 6)): - **Anatomic V****D** is created by the conducting airways, such as the trachea and bronchi, where no gas exchange occurs.  In adults, this is a fixed value of roughly 150 mL, so only 350 mL of a normal 500-mL VT ever reaches the alveoli.  As VT decreases, the anatomic dead space fraction increases ((Figure 7)).  For example, with a 300-mL VT, only 150 mL reaches the alveoli. - **Alveolar V****D** is created by alveoli with very high V/Q ratios (eg, extreme lung apices), where perfusion is low compared to ventilation.  Under normal conditions, alveolar dead space is minimal (eg, 5-10 mL), but it can be greatly increased by conditions that reduce perfusion (eg, pulmonary embolism). VA is calculated as VA = (VT − VD) · RR.  Therefore, in normal conditions, VA = (500 − 150) · 12 = 4.2 L/min.  A slower, deeper breathing pattern (eg, VT = 600 mL, RR = 10/min) is preferable to a faster, shallower one (eg, VT = 300 mL, RR = 20/min), even if VE is the same (eg, 6 L/min for both).  The shallow pattern results in a lower VA because more VT is wasted in anatomic dead space. ## PaCO2 PaCO2 is directly proportional to the carbon dioxide production rate (VCO2) and inversely proportional to VA (ie, PaCO2 ∝ VCO2 / VA): - VCO2 (ie, ventilatory load) is determined by metabolic rate.  It increases with exercise, pathologic conditions (eg, fever, hyperthyroidism, sepsis, burns, trauma), and overfeeding (especially with a carbohydrate-rich diet). - VA is determined by VE and dead space, as discussed previously. Normally, a rise in VCO2 is accompanied by a proportional rise in VA.  Peripheral and central chemoreceptors rapidly adjust ventilation to maintain arterial carbon dioxide within a normal range.  If VA fails to keep pace with VCO2, acute hypercapnic respiratory failure results.  This is seen in severe exacerbations of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, when patients generate more carbon dioxide from their own work of breathing than they can expel through ventilation. ## Ventilation with exercise Exercise leads to increases in both VT and RR.  The respiratory response differs based on the presence of lung disease: - **Healthy**:  With exercise that is low-to-moderate intensity, **V****T** **increases first**.  With higher-intensity exercise, RR increases as VT approaches inspiratory capacity. - **Abnormal**:  In patients with lung disease or neuromuscular weakness, RR increases earlier and more sharply because VT cannot increase sufficiently. In other words, VT is the primary mechanism for increasing ventilation, whereas RR becomes more important as ventilatory load increases.  In clinical practice, persistent tachypnea at rest often signals a serious underlying illness. # Gas transport ## Oxygen transport Oxygen is transported in the blood in 2 forms: - Some 98.5% of oxygen is bound to hemoglobin **(HbO****2****)**.  Each gram of hemoglobin can carry **1.34** mL of oxygen when fully saturated (ie, SaO2 100%). - Some 1.5% of oxygen is carried as a dissolved gas in the plasma **(PaO****2****)**.  Only **0.003** mL of oxygen can dissolve in each deciliter of blood per every 1 mm Hg of increase in partial pressure. Total blood oxygen content (CaO2) is the sum of HbO2 and PaO2: CaO2 = HbO2 + PaO2\= (1.34 · SaO2 · Hb) + (0.003 · PaO2) In a healthy patient with normal hemoglobin (eg, Hb = 15 g/dL) and normal oxygenation (eg, SaO2 = 99%, PaO2 = 90 mm Hg), the oxygen carrying capacity is 20.1 mL O2/dL of blood. Carrying capacity is determined **almost entirely** by hemoglobin concentration.  For example, when a patient with severe anemia (eg, Hb = 5 mg/dL) is breathing pure oxygen (ie, SaO2 = 99%, PaO2 = 600 mm Hg), the oxygen-carrying capacity is only 8.43 mL O2/dL of blood (only 42% of normal).  Therefore, the total CaO2 remains very low despite maximizing the dissolved oxygen. ## Carbon dioxide transport Carbon dioxide is transported in the blood in 3 forms: - 70% of carbon dioxide is transported as bicarbonate anion **(HCO****3****−****)**. - 23% of carbon dioxide is transported as carbaminohemoglobin **(HbCO****2****)**. - 7% of carbon dioxide is carried as a dissolved gas in the plasma **(PaCO****2****)**. These 3 states are in an equilibrium mediated by **carbonic anhydrase** in red blood cells ((Figure 8)).  When PaCO2 increases, more HCO3− is formed and subsequently transported out of red blood cells in exchange for chloride anions to maintain electrical neutrality (ie, Hamburger phenomenon).  This phenomenon is one of the reasons that metabolic alkalosis (excess plasma HCO3−) is often accompanied by hypochloremia. Some of the carbon dioxide binds to the terminal amine group of hemoglobin as carbaminohemoglobin; when exposed to high levels of oxygen in the lungs, the hemoglobin releases carbon dioxide so that it can bind oxygen instead (ie, Haldane and Bohr effects) ((Figure 9)).  This phenomenon contributes to oxygen-induced hypercapnia in patients with marginal VA (sometimes called "chronic carbon dioxide retainers") who receive excessive supplemental oxygen ((Figure 10)). # Respiratory quotient The respiratory quotient (RQ), sometimes referred to as the respiratory exchange ratio, is the ratio between carbon dioxide production and oxygen consumption (RQ = VCO2 / VO2).  The RQ is mainly affected by dietary composition and exercise. ## Effect of dietary composition Carbohydrates, fats, and proteins have differing RQ levels: - The RQ of **carbohydrates** is ~1 because complete oxidation of glucose produces 6 molecules of carbon dioxide and consumes 6 molecules of oxygen (C6H12O6 + **6 O****2** → **6 CO****2** + 6 H2O + 32 ATP). - The RQ of **fats** is ~0.7 because complete oxidation of a long-chain fatty acid (eg, palmitic acid) produces ~16 molecules of carbon dioxide and consumes 23 molecules of oxygen (C16H32O2 + **23 O****2** → **16 CO****2** + 16 H2O + 106 ATP). - The RQ of **proteins** is ~0.85 because complete oxidation of amino acids through intermediate reactions (eg, gluconeogenesis) produces 5 molecules of carbon dioxide and consumes 6 molecules of oxygen (eg, alanine \[C3H7​NO2\] ​+ **6 O****2** → **5 CO****2** + 3 H2O + 15 ATP). For a normal Western diet, the **overall RQ is ~0.8**.  This value is used in the alveolar gas equation (PAO2 = PiO2 − PaCO2 / **RQ** = 150 − PaCO2 / **0.8**). Overfeeding with high-carbohydrate diets can increase RQ and contribute to worsening hypercapnia in patients with underlying respiratory failure.  Therefore, fat- and protein-rich diets are often preferred to help reduce RQ and assist with respiratory recovery (eg, ventilator weaning). ## Effect of exercise The RQ increases during exercise.  At rest or during routine activity, the RQ is approximately 0.8.  With more intense exercise, tissues preferentially use carbohydrates for fuel, causing the RQ to increase toward 1.  With very-high-intensity exercise, the RQ increases further and can exceed 1 as the anaerobic threshold is reached (ie, oxygen is no longer being consumed, but carbon dioxide is still being produced from glycolysis). # Summary Respiratory gas exchange encompasses the processes of oxygenation, ventilation, and gas transport in the blood. Effective oxygenation requires normal alveolar-capillary exchange.  It requires tight ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) matching (ie, opportunity for air to contact blood) and rapid diffusion across the alveolar membrane (ie, speed of oxygen uptake).  V/Q mismatch or diffusion limitation leads to impaired alveolar-capillary exchange and a subsequent fall in PaO2 (ie, hypoxemia).  Blood oxygen content is mainly carried by hemoglobin (98.5%). Effective ventilation requires normal minute ventilation (tidal volume · respiratory rate) and minimal dead space volume.  Insufficient minute ventilation or abnormally increased dead space leads to alveolar hypoventilation and a subsequent rise in PaCO2 (ie, hypercapnia), which can also cause secondary hypoxemia.  Blood carbon dioxide content is mainly carried as intracellular bicarbonate in red blood cells (70%). ​‌​‌‌​‌​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌​​​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​​‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​​​‌

articles.title: Physiology: Normal Digestion
articles.markdown: # Physiology: Normal Digestion # Introduction Digestion is the process by which ingested food—dietary carbohydrate, protein, and fat—is mechanically and chemically broken down into absorbable molecules for energy and nutrition.  It requires coordinated activity across multiple gastrointestinal organs and is regulated through neural pathways, hormonal signaling, and local chemical stimuli. # Overview The gastrointestinal tract progressively processes ingested food ((Figure 1)).  Digestion begins with food ingestion and mechanical breakdown in the mouth.  After transport via the esophagus, the food is mixed with gastric secretions in the stomach, producing a semiliquid mixture (chyme).  As chyme enters the duodenum, hormones released from the intestinal mucosa coordinate the secretion of pancreatic enzymes and bile, which enable further digestion of carbohydrates, proteins, and lipids.  Accessory organs include the pancreas, which provides digestive enzymes and bicarbonate; the liver, which produces bile; and the gallbladder, which stores and concentrates bile.  Nutrients are absorbed primarily in the small intestine, which has 3 physiologically distinct segments: duodenum, jejunum, and ileum.  Finally, water and electrolytes are recovered in the colon, leaving solid or semisolid stool.  Regulation of digestion occurs through neural (enteric nervous system, autonomic nervous system) and hormonal pathways. # Oral phase of digestion Food undergoes both mechanical and chemical processing in the oral cavity. Mechanical digestion through mastication breaks food into smaller particles, increasing the surface area available for enzymatic digestion. Saliva produced by the salivary glands contains water and electrolytes, mucus for lubrication, and digestive enzymes ((Figure 2)).  The primary salivary enzymes are as follows: - **Salivary amylase**:  Produced predominantly in the parotid glands, amylase initiates the breakdown of starch into smaller polysaccharides and maltose. - **Lingual lipase**:  Produced predominantly in the lingual serous glands (Ebner glands), lipase breaks down triglycerides into diglycerides and free fatty acids.  Lingual lipase is most active in acidic conditions and maintains activity in the stomach. After food is masticated and mixed with saliva, coordinated contraction of the tongue and pharyngeal muscles propels the food bolus into the esophagus, where peristaltic waves transport it to the stomach. # Gastric digestion The major digestive functions of the stomach include: - Temporary storage of ingested food after meals. - Mechanical mixing to produce chyme. - Chemical digestion of proteins. articles.html:
›Introduction

Digestion is the process by which ingested food—dietary carbohydrate, protein, and fat—is mechanically and chemically broken down into absorbable molecules for energy and nutrition.  It requires coordinated activity across multiple gastrointestinal organs and is regulated through neural pathways, hormonal signaling, and local chemical stimuli.

›Overview

The gastrointestinal tract progressively processes ingested food .  Digestion begins with food ingestion and mechanical breakdown in the mouth.  After transport via the esophagus, the food is mixed with gastric secretions in the stomach, producing a semiliquid mixture (chyme).  As chyme enters the duodenum, hormones released from the intestinal mucosa coordinate the secretion of pancreatic enzymes and bile, which enable further digestion of carbohydrates, proteins, and lipids.  Accessory organs include the pancreas, which provides digestive enzymes and bicarbonate; the liver, which produces bile; and the gallbladder, which stores and concentrates bile.  Nutrients are absorbed primarily in the small intestine, which has 3 physiologically distinct segments: duodenum, jejunum, and ileum.  Finally, water and electrolytes are recovered in the colon, leaving solid or semisolid stool.  Regulation of digestion occurs through neural (enteric nervous system, autonomic nervous system) and hormonal pathways.

›Oral phase of digestion

Food undergoes both mechanical and chemical processing in the oral cavity.

Mechanical digestion through mastication breaks food into smaller particles, increasing the surface area available for enzymatic digestion.

Saliva produced by the salivary glands contains water and electrolytes, mucus for lubrication, and digestive enzymes .  The primary salivary enzymes are as follows:

  • Salivary amylase:  Produced predominantly in the parotid glands, amylase initiates the breakdown of starch into smaller polysaccharides and maltose.
  • Lingual lipase:  Produced predominantly in the lingual serous glands (Ebner glands), lipase breaks down triglycerides into diglycerides and free fatty acids.  Lingual lipase is most active in acidic conditions and maintains activity in the stomach.

After food is masticated and mixed with saliva, coordinated contraction of the tongue and pharyngeal muscles propels the food bolus into the esophagus, where peristaltic waves transport it to the stomach.

›Gastric digestion

The major digestive functions of the stomach include:

  • Temporary storage of ingested food after meals.
  • Mechanical mixing to produce chyme.
  • Chemical digestion of proteins.

The gastric surface contains longitudinal wrinkles and folds (rugae), which provide greater surface area and allow expansion of the stomach to accommodate food.  The surface epithelium invaginates into the underlying connective tissue (lamina propria) to form shallow gastric pits and deep, tubular glands.

Most of the gastric epithelium is composed of tall columnar epithelial cells.  These cells, also known as foveolar cells, produce bicarbonate-rich mucus that forms a protective barrier over the gastric mucosa, preventing acid-mediated injury .

Gastric glands within the stomach mucosa contain several specialized cell types:

  • Parietal cells secrete hydrochloric acid, which denatures proteins and activates digestive enzymes; it also creates a hostile environment for many microorganisms.  Parietal cells also secrete intrinsic factor , which aids in the absorption of vitamin B12.
  • Chief cells produce pepsinogen, an inactive precursor that becomes pepsin when exposed to acidic gastric fluid.  Pepsin cleaves peptide bonds and initiates protein digestion .  These cells also produce gastric lipase, which aids in fat digestion.
  • Neuroendocrine cells produce signal molecules (eg, histamine, gastrin, somatostatin) that regulate parietal cell acid production and coordinate other digestive processes.

Partially digested food exits the stomach through the pylorus and enters the duodenum as acidic chyme.

›Duodenal processing

When acidic chyme enters the duodenum, intestinal mucosal cells release hormones that coordinate pancreatic and biliary secretions.  Two key intestinal hormones are secretin and cholecystokinin.

Secretin

Secretin is released by S cells in the duodenal mucosa in response to acidic chyme entering the small intestine.  Secretin stimulates pancreatic ductal cells to release bicarbonate-rich fluid, which is transported to the duodenum via the pancreatic duct and neutralizes gastric acid.

Cholecystokinin

Cholecystokinin (CCK) is released by I cells of the duodenum and jejunum in response to fatty acids and amino acids in the intestinal lumen.  Major physiologic actions of CCK include the following:

  • Stimulates gallbladder contraction.
  • Promotes pancreatic enzyme (primarily amylase, trypsin, and pancreatic lipase) secretion.
  • Relaxes the sphincter of Oddi , facilitating passage of bile and pancreatic juice into the duodenal lumen.

›Pancreatic digestive function

The exocrine pancreas serves as an accessory organ to digestion by secreting approximately 1 L of digestive fluid daily into the duodenum.  These secretions consist primarily of digestive enzymes (produced by pancreatic acinar cells) and bicarbonate-rich fluid (produced by pancreatic ductal cells), which neutralizes gastric acid and creates optimal conditions for enzyme activity.

Pancreatic enzymes digest all major macronutrients.  Examples include:

  • Pancreatic amylase for carbohydrate digestion.
  • Proteases such as trypsin and chymotrypsin for protein digestion.
  • Lipase for triglyceride digestion.

Pancreatic enzymes are secreted in inactive forms to prevent autodigestion.  Enteropeptidase (also called enterokinase), a duodenal brush border enzyme, activates trypsin from its inactive precursor, trypsinogen.  Once active, trypsin cleaves peptide bonds in dietary proteins and activates the other pancreatic enzymes .

›Bile and fat digestion

Efficient digestion of dietary lipids requires both pancreatic enzymes and bile.

Bile is synthesized by hepatocytes in the liver and stored in the gallbladder (other accessory organs for digestion).  In the gallbladder, bile is concentrated through the reabsorption of water and electrolytes.  When fats enter the duodenum, CCK stimulates gallbladder contraction and bile release into the intestinal lumen.

Bile contains bile salts, which are amphipathic molecules that function as detergents.  These molecules emulsify large fat droplets into smaller particles, greatly increasing the surface area available for pancreatic lipase activity.  Pancreatic lipase then hydrolyzes triglycerides into fatty acids and monoglycerides, which combine with bile salts to form micelles that facilitate lipid absorption by intestinal epithelial cells .

›Small intestinal digestion and absorption

The small intestine is the primary site of nutrient absorption.  The mucosal surface is optimized to provide maximal surface area for absorption.  The intestinal lining contains complex circular folds with villi (finger-like structures that project into the lumen).  The primary mucosal cell is the enterocyte, a specialized columnar epithelial cell with a brush border (microvilli) that further increases absorptive surface area .  Enzymes concentrated in the brush border of the enterocytes complete the digestion of carbohydrates and proteins into absorbable molecules .

The small intestine is composed of 3 physiologically distinct segments, each of which emphasizes absorption of specific nutrients :

  • Duodenum: In addition to receiving bile and pancreatic juice, the duodenum serves as a site for absorption of certain metals (eg, iron, magnesium, copper), some water-soluble vitamins (eg, thiamine, niacin, folate), and fat-soluble vitamins (vitamins A, D, E, and K).
  • Jejunum:  The jejunum serves as the primary site for macronutrient absorption (ie, monosaccharides, lipids, amino acids), as well as absorption of many micronutrients, including a wide variety of vitamins and minerals.
  • Ileum:  The ileum serves as the primary site for reabsorption of bile acids, as well as absorption of cobalamin (vitamin B12).  Additional absorption of certain micronutrients that were not completely absorbed in the jejunum may also occur in the ileum.

Major absorption mechanisms include:

  • Monosaccharides transported via sodium-dependent cotransporters.
  • Amino acids and peptides transported through specialized carriers.
  • Fatty acids and monoglycerides absorbed from micelles.

After absorption, nutrients follow different pathways.  Water-soluble nutrients enter the portal circulation and travel to the liver.  Lipids are packaged into chylomicrons and transported via the lymphatic system.

›Colonic digestive phase

The colon does not play an active role in chemical digestion of macronutrients, although colonic bacteria break down some nondigestible fiber into short-chain fatty acids (ie, via colonic fermentation).  Colonic bacteria also contribute to the absorbable pool of certain vitamins (eg, vitamin K, biotin).  However, the colon is responsible for absorption of the remaining water and electrolytes from chyme, desiccating the chyme to produce solid stool.

›Neural and hormonal regulation of digestion and gut motility

Neural

Neural control of digestion involves both extrinsic and intrinsic gut neurons:

  • Enteric nervous system (intrinsic innervation): Network of neurons in the walls of the gastrointestinal tract, primarily in the myenteric and submucosal plexuses.  Provides autonomous control of motility (eg, peristalsis, segmentation, churning), secretory activity, and blood flow .
  • Autonomic nervous system (extrinsic innervation): Both parasympathetic (via vagus and pelvic nerves) and sympathetic (via splanchnic nerves) nervous systems influence motility, secretory activity, and segmental blood flow.  Generally, parasympathetic activity increases motility and blood flow, whereas sympathetic activity does the opposite.

Neural regulation of digestion is often described in 3 overlapping phases:

  • Cephalic phase: The sight, smell, or thought of food activates vagal pathways that stimulate salivation and gastric activity in preparation for meals.
  • Gastric phase:  The presence of food in the stomach triggers local and long-distance reflexes to increase acid secretion and motility.
  • Intestinal phase:  The passage of food into the intestine triggers feedback slowing of gastric emptying and modulates pancreatic and gallbladder activity.

As food passes down the esophagus, vagally stimulated enteric neurons release nitric oxide, which induces relaxation of the fundus of the stomach to accommodate the incoming food bolus.  Specialized gastric pacemaker cells (interstitial cells of Cajal) initiate pacesetter potentials (slow waves), which generate circumferential contractions of the gastric smooth muscle (peristalsis).  Gastric peristalsis facilitates food mixing and propulsion toward the pylorus.

Hormonal: Incretin hormones

Among the digestive regulatory hormones, incretins (insulin-secreting hormones) are released by the gut mucosa after feeding to regulate postprandial glucose metabolism.  The two primary incretins are glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) and gastric inhibitory peptide (GIP) (also known as glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide).

  • GLP-1 is secreted primarily by L cells in the distal small bowel and colon in response to luminal sugars .  It increases glucose-dependent insulin secretion by pancreatic beta cells, potentiating the effects of glucose on insulin secretion.  It also slows gastric motility, thereby increasing satiety.
  • GIP is secreted primarily by K cells in the upper small bowel and also potentiates insulin secretion.

GLP-1 and GIP are rapidly degraded by dipeptidyl peptidase-4 and cleared by the kidneys.

›Summary

Digestion involves the mechanical and chemical breakdown of food into absorbable molecules.  It starts in the mouth with chewing, mixing of food with saliva, and breaking down of starch and triglycerides by salivary enzymes.  Food moves to the stomach, where gastric acid and pepsin begin protein digestion as contractions form chyme.  In the duodenum, intestinal hormones such as secretin (stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate) and cholecystokinin (stimulates gallbladder contraction and pancreatic enzymes) regulate secretions.  The pancreas supplies enzymes for carbohydrate, protein, and fat hydrolysis.  Liver-produced bile emulsifies lipids for effective pancreatic lipase action.  Most digestion and nutrient absorption occur in the small intestine via brush border enzymes and specialized transport.  Finally, the colon absorbs water and electrolytes, yielding solid stool.

​‌​‌​​​​​​‌​​​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​​

articles.title: Physiology: Core Principles
articles.markdown: # Physiology: Core Principles # Introduction Physiology examines how living systems behave across different levels of biologic organization, from cells to tissues to organs, with an emphasis on functional relationships and adjustments to disturbances.  This article describes core principles of physiology using day-to-day examples and applications. # Homeostasis and allostasis ## Homeostasis Homeostasis, a core physiologic process, is the maintenance of relatively stable internal conditions despite external variability.  Variables such as body temperature, plasma osmolality, blood glucose, and arterial pressure are regulated within ranges compatible with cellular function.  Regulatory systems continuously adjust physiologic processes to counteract imbalances ((Figure 1)).  For example, a rise in body temperature detected by the hypothalamus leads to vasodilation and perspiration, bringing body temperature down to a normal range ((Figure 2)). ## Allostasis **Allostasis** describes regulation through adaptive change that prepares the organism for expected challenges.  During exercise, sympathetic activation increases heart rate, ventilation, and glucose mobilization before large disturbances in oxygen delivery or metabolic substrates occur. Homeostasis corrects deviations after they arise, whereas allostasis aims to accommodate anticipated demands.  However, persistent or excessive allostatic responses may impose physiologic cost (allostatic load). # Feedback regulation Physiologic regulation relies heavily on **feedback control systems**, particularly negative feedback. ## Negative feedback In a **negative feedback** loop, a change in a variable activates responses that **oppose** the initial disturbance.  At the cellular level, a stimulus causes a cellular response that inhibits continuation of the initial stimulus ((Figure 3)).  For example, when blood pressure rises, stretch-sensitive baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch increase firing.  This signal reduces sympathetic output and enhances parasympathetic activity, lowering heart rate, contractility, and vascular resistance.  The resulting decrease in pressure diminishes baroreceptor activation, completing the feedback loop.  Negative feedback stabilizes physiologic variables and limits excessive responses. The efficiency of a homeostatic system in maintaining stability is expressed by the gain, calculated as the correction applied divided by the remaining error: **gain = correction / remaining error**, where correction = (initial disturbance – remaining error).  The gain measures how effectively a negative feedback mechanism brings a physiological parameter (eg, blood pressure, temperature) back to its set point.  If blood pressure initially drops by 20 mm Hg upon standing (ie, initial disturbance = 20 mm Hg), but the baroreceptor feedback mechanism corrects it to a drop of 10 mm Hg (ie, remaining error = 10 mm Hg), then the gain = (20 – 10) / 10 = 2.  A gain of 2 means the system corrected twice as much disturbance as was left uncorrected. Positive feedback In contrast, positive feedback amplifies an ongoing process.  Such loops are uncommon in steady-state regulation but play roles in rapid transitions (eg, escalating oxytocin release and uterine contractions during parturition ((Figure 4))). ## Feedforward control Physiologic systems also use **feedforward control**, in which regulatory responses are initiated before the controlled variable changes.  Anticipatory increases in heart rate and ventilation at the onset of exercise arise from central neural commands and sensory input from muscles and joints.  These mechanisms reduce the magnitude of disturbances that would otherwise require slower feedback correction. # Physiologic variation and genotype-phenotype relationships Genetic differences influence the structure and function of proteins, receptors, enzymes, and regulatory pathways, producing variability in physiologic traits.  For example, polymorphisms affecting hemoglobin structure influence oxygen affinity and erythrocyte behavior.  Differences in enzyme activity affect drug metabolism and metabolic pathways.  This is why reference intervals (eg, for laboratory tests or blood pressure) represent distributions derived from populations. # Physiology across the life cycle Physiologic function changes across developmental stages. In the **fetal environment**, gas exchange, nutrient delivery, and waste removal occur through the placenta.  The fetal circulation contains shunts (eg, ductus arteriosus, foramen ovale) that direct blood flow to optimize oxygen delivery from placental blood.  At birth, rapid cardiopulmonary transitions close these pathways and establish pulmonary respiration. In the **neonatal period**, thermoregulation, renal concentrating ability, and metabolic control remain immature.  High metabolic demand and limited energy reserves influence responses to stress and illness. During **childhood and adolescence**, endocrine regulation drives growth, skeletal maturation, and sexual development.  Pubertal activation of the hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal axis alters hormone profiles and body composition. In **adulthood**, mature physiologic systems respond to changes in lifestyle and environment to maintain homeostasis.  With **healthy aging**, gradual structural and functional changes occur across organ systems.  Examples include reduced maximal cardiac output due to decreased beta-adrenergic responsiveness, diminished renal filtration rate, reduced lung elastic recoil, and changes in immune function.  Although baseline function often remains adequate for everyday activities, physiologic reserve declines, reducing the ability to respond to stressors such as illness or extreme environmental conditions. # Adaptation to environmental challenges Adaptations to environmental challenges may occur acutely (minutes to hours) through regulatory responses or chronically (weeks to months) through structural and biochemical changes. At **high altitude**, reduced atmospheric oxygen pressure lowers arterial oxygen tension.  Immediate responses include hyperventilation and increased sympathetic activity.  Over time, erythropoietin-mediated increases in red blood cell production, enhanced capillary density, and alterations in oxygen transport improve tissue oxygenation. Exposure to **microgravity** (spaceflight) removes the hydrostatic gradients normally imposed by gravity.  Fluid shifts toward the thorax and head initially increase central blood volume.  Over time, cardiovascular deconditioning, reduced plasma volume, and skeletal muscle atrophy occur.  These changes resemble the physiologic effects of prolonged bed rest, which serves as a terrestrial model for microgravity. Acute **exercise** increases oxygen consumption, cardiac output, ventilation, and skeletal muscle blood flow to meet metabolic demands.  With training, repeated exposure induces long-term adaptations (eg, increased mitochondrial density in muscle, improved capillary supply, enhanced stroke volume) that support improved performance. # Physiology and pathophysiology Understanding normal physiology provides the framework for interpreting disease.  Pathophysiology examines how disturbances in normal regulatory mechanisms produce clinical disorders.  For example, knowledge of normal insulin signaling and glucose metabolism clarifies how impaired insulin secretion or resistance leads to hyperglycemia in diabetes mellitus.  Conversely, the study of disease often reveals underlying physiologic principles that are difficult to observe in healthy systems.  Hormone deficiencies and receptor abnormalities have clarified endocrine feedback regulation.  Therefore, physiology and pathophysiology provide complementary perspectives on the same biologic processes. # Summary Physiology examines how biologic systems maintain function by regulating internal variables within viable ranges while adapting to perturbations.  Homeostasis stabilizes parameters via negative feedback, whereas allostasis anticipates demands but can impose cumulative strain if persistent.  Regulation also includes limited positive feedback (eg, parturition) and feedforward control that reduces anticipated disturbances.  Adaptation to environmental stressors occurs through acute responses and longer-term structural changes (eg, altitude acclimatization, exercise training).  These principles form the basis for understanding disease pathophysiology, which reflects disruption of normal regulatory mechanisms. ​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​​​​‌​​​‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​​​​​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌

articles.title: Muscle Physiology
articles.markdown:
# Muscle Physiology # Introduction Skeletal muscle function depends on the coordinated interaction of electrical, chemical, and mechanical processes.  At the core of this physiology is the excitation-contraction coupling mechanism, through which an action potential triggers calcium release and ultimately leads to muscle contraction.  Neuromuscular transmission, sarcolemmal excitability, and intracellular calcium dynamics are tightly integrated to ensure precise regulation of force generation.  Cardiac and smooth muscle, which contract involuntarily (unlike skeletal muscle), share some similarities with skeletal muscle but exhibit differences in structure and regulation. # Skeletal muscle structure Skeletal muscle is composed of long, cylindrical multinucleated cells called **muscle fibers**, which are formed by the fusion of myoblasts during development.  Each muscle fiber is surrounded by a plasma membrane known as the **sarcolemma** and contains numerous **myofibrils**, which are the contractile elements of the cell.  Myofibrils are organized into repeating structural units called **sarcomeres**, giving skeletal muscle its characteristic striated appearance ((Figure 1)).  These sarcomeres are aligned end-to-end along the length of the myofibril and serve as the fundamental unit of muscle contraction. A sarcomere is composed of overlapping filaments of **actin** and **myosin** as well as structural and binding proteins (eg, titin, alpha-actinin).  A single sarcomere is defined as the distance between 2 Z lines.  Thin filaments (actin, tropomyosin, troponin) are bound to structural proteins at the Z line.  The unbound ends of the actin filaments project into the middle of the sarcomere, where they interact with thick filaments (myosin) during muscle contraction.  The organization of the filaments gives rise to distinct bands and lines that can be seen on electron microscopy ((Figure 2)): - The Z line (Z disc) defines the lateral boundaries of each sarcomere and is the anchoring point for thin filaments.  The Z line is typically darker than the remainder of the sarcomere. - The M line, where myosin filaments anchor to structural elements, lies in the center of the sarcomere. - The I band is the light region of the sarcomere in which actin does not overlap with myosin. - The A band corresponds to a dark region of myosin filaments in the sarcomere.  In this region, there are myosin filaments overlapped with actin filaments as well as nonoverlapped myosin filaments. - The H band is the region in which myosin does not overlap with actin. During muscle contraction, the thin filaments slide over the thick filaments toward the M line, reducing the length of the H and I bands.  The A band always remains the same length. # Muscle fiber types and metabolism Muscle fibers are arranged into a motor unit composed of the same fiber type, with each unit innervated by a single motor neuron.  Skeletal muscle fibers are categorized into 2 major types: type I (slow-twitch) and type II (fast-twitch) ((Table 1)). ## Type I (slow-twitch) fibers Type I (slow-twitch) fibers specialize in stamina by using **oxidative** phosphorylation in the mitochondria for steady and sustained ATP production.  Type I fibers perform actions requiring low-level **sustained** force (eg, postural maintenance) and function primarily via **aerobic** metabolism, meaning they have high concentrations of myoglobin (oxygen storage) and mitochondria (aerobic respiration).  The high myoglobin content gives these fibers a **red** color. ## Type II (fast-twitch) fibers Type II (fast-twitch) fibers are specialized for generating **rapid** forceful movements; however, they fatigue quickly.  These fibers derive energy in the form of ATP mainly via glycogenolysis and subsequent anaerobic **glycolysis**.  The lower quantities of mitochondria and myoglobin lead to a **pale** color. Histologically, these motor units form a characteristic mixed checkerboard pattern of type I and type II fibers (lost during denervation and revenrvation as adjacent fibers become innervated by the same neuron). # Muscle contraction ## Overview - Muscle contraction begins with a neural signal that initiates an action potential in the motor neuron. - The action potential leads to acetylcholine (ACh) release at the neuromuscular junction. - ACh binding to nicotinic receptors initiates an end-plate potential and muscle fiber depolarization. - Depolarization spreads along the sarcolemma and into transverse tubules, triggering calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR). - Intracellular calcium binds to troponin C, allowing for actin-myosin cross-bridge cycling. - ATP is required for both cross-bridge cycling and calcium reuptake into the SR during relaxation. ## Excitation and action potential generation Skeletal muscle is activated by lower motor neurons originating from the anterior horn of the spinal cord.  The motor neuron action potential leads to calcium influx at the axon terminal, promoting ACh vesicle fusion and release into the synaptic cleft.  ACh binds to postsynaptic nicotinic receptors (ionotropic or ligand-gated channels), causing sodium influx and potassium efflux.  The resultant end-plate potential, if suprathreshold, triggers a muscle action potential. Muscle action potentials differ from neuronal action potentials in several key ways: - **More negative resting membrane potential** (~–90 mV vs ~–70 mV in neurons). - **Slightly longer duration**, which helps coordinate contraction. - **Propagate into the fiber via transverse tubules (T-tubules)**, not just along the surface. Sodium, potassium, and chloride are the main ions that determine the membrane potential.  Under normal physiologic conditions, there is a low concentration of sodium and chloride ions in the cell and high concentration of potassium in the cytoplasm.  Conversely, the extracellular space has a high concentration of sodium and chloride ions and low concentration of potassium ions.  When a specific ion channel opens, the respective ions will flow across the membrane in a direction that brings the resting membrane potential closer to that ion's equilibrium potential. Like neurons, muscle action potentials are initiated by depolarization and rely on voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels for rapid upstroke and repolarization.  However, in skeletal muscle, the action potential propagates not only along the sarcolemma but also deep into the fiber via T-tubules, which are invaginations of the plasma membrane ((Figure 3)).  T-tubules are closely associated with the SR, a specialized smooth endoplasmic reticulum that stores and releases calcium ions.  The T-tubules contain voltage-gated L-type calcium channels (dihydropyridine receptors \[DHPRs\]) that play a key role in the next step of muscle contraction, called excitation-contraction coupling. ## Excitation-contraction coupling **Excitation-contraction coupling** (ECC) refers to the process by which the electrical signal (muscle action potential) is translated into a mechanical response (contraction).  In skeletal muscle, this process works as follows: - The action potential in the T-tubules activates DHPRs, which undergo a conformational change. - DHPRs are mechanically linked to ryanodine receptor 1 (RyR1) on the SR membrane, and the conformational change in the DHPR triggers them to open.  This causes calcium release into the cytosol from the SR without requiring extracellular calcium influx. - Intracellular calcium binds to troponin C, causing tropomyosin to shift and expose myosin-binding sites on actin. - Actin-myosin cross-bridge cycling begins, powered by ATP hydrolysis, and results in contraction. This tightly coordinated process ensures that every muscle fiber contracts uniformly in response to a single neural signal. ## Actin-myosin cross-bridge cycling Once calcium is released into the cytosol during ECC, it initiates a sequence of molecular interactions between actin and myosin filaments within the sarcomere.  This process, known as **cross-bridge cycling**, is driven by calcium binding and ATP hydrolysis and is responsible for the actual shortening of skeletal muscle fibers during contraction.  The actin-myosin interaction cycle consists of several ATP-dependent steps ((Figure 4)): - **Rest**:  At rest, the myosin head is charged by ADP and inorganic phosphate (Pi) from previously bound and hydrolyzed ATP.  However, calcium-modulated regulatory complexes of troponin-C and tropomyosin block the myosin binding sites on actin. - **Cross-bridge formation**:  When calcium binds to troponin-C, troponin-tropomyosin complexes shift to expose the myosin binding sites; the myosin head then binds actin perpendicularly, forming a cross-bridge ((Figure 5)). - **Power stroke**:  The bound head releases Pi and bends the cross-bridge at a 45-degree angle, increasing filament overlap and shortening the sarcomere length.  Once the process is completed, ADP is released. - **Cross-bridge dissociation**:  A new ATP molecule must bind the myosin head to dissolve the crossbridge, returning the head to its original position to restart the cycle. - **Cross-bridge cycling**:  Continues while calcium and ATP are readily available; cycling across multiple myosin heads leads to increased or sustained contraction. Muscle relaxation occurs when the stimulus for contraction ceases and calcium is actively removed from the cytosol.  Intracellular calcium is removed primarily via 2 pumps: - **Na+/Ca2+ exchange pump (NCX)**:  NCX uses the large extracellular Na+ concentration gradient to pump Ca2+ out of the cell and, in the process, removes one intracellular Ca2+ in exchange for 3 extracellular Na+ ions. - **Sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca2+\-ATPase pump (SERCA)**:  SERCA is a Ca2+\-ATPase pump that actively transfers Ca2+ from the cytosol to the lumen of SR at the expense of ATP hydrolysis. The decline in cytosolic calcium causes tropomyosin to recover actin's binding sites, halting cross-bridge cycling and allowing the muscle to relax. # Muscle proprioceptors Proprioceptors are specialized sensory receptors that provide the CNS with information about body position, movement, and muscle tension.  In skeletal muscle, the 2 primary proprioceptors are muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs (GTOs) ((Figure 6)). ## Muscle spindles Muscle spindles (intrafusal muscle fibers) are stretch-sensitive receptors embedded within the muscle belly, parallel to the extrafusal (force-generating) muscle fibers.  They are innervated by group Ia and group II sensory axons and are sensitive to changes in muscle length.  Muscle spindles mediate the stretch (myotatic) reflex, which is commonly tested during the neurologic examination (deep tendon reflexes).  When a muscle is stretched, monosynaptic reflex activation of the alpha motor neuron (of the same muscle) results in contraction that resists the stretch. ## Golgi tendon organs GTOs are located at the junction between muscle fibers and tendons, innervated by group Ib afferent sensory axons.  GTOs are connected in series with contracting extrafusal skeletal muscle fibers.  When a muscle actively contracts against resistance, the increase in tension is transmitted through the tendon, activating the GTOs.  The Ib sensory axons from the GTOs contact inhibitory interneurons in the spinal cord, which in turn synapse with the alpha motor neurons that innervate the same muscle.  Therefore, the Golgi tendon circuit is a negative feedback system that regulates and maintains muscle tension.  When a muscle exerts too much force, the GTOs inhibit contraction of the muscle, causing sudden muscle relaxation.  This prevents damage to the musculoskeletal system. Together, muscle spindles and GTOs continuously modulate reflexes and motor output, allowing for coordinated movement, posture maintenance, and injury prevention. # Skeletal muscle vs cardiac and smooth muscle Whereas skeletal muscle is under voluntary control and contracts in response to somatic motor neuron stimulation, cardiac and smooth muscle differ in both structure and regulation: ## Cardiac muscle Cardiac muscle is also striated but contracts **involuntarily**.  In contrast to skeletal muscle ECC, cardiac ECC requires **extracellular calcium**.  During the action potential, calcium enters the myocyte through L-type calcium channels (DHPRs) in the T-tubules.  This influx triggers **calcium-induced calcium release** from the SR via RyR2, making both extracellular and intracellular calcium essential for contraction ((Figure 7)). ## Smooth muscle Smooth muscle is **nonstriated** and contracts **involuntarily**.  It lacks organized sarcomeres and T-tubules.  Contraction is initiated by intracellular calcium increases, which can come from the SR or extracellular space.  Calcium binds **calmodulin** (calcium-modulated protein) because smooth muscle cells lack troponin.  Calmodulin activates myosin light-chain kinase to enable actin-myosin interaction. # Neuromuscular disorders Several clinical conditions arise from abnormalities in muscle excitation or contraction: ## Myasthenia gravis Autoantibodies target nicotinic ACh receptors, reducing the number of functional receptors available for synaptic transmission.  This leads to decreased end-plate potentials and impaired muscle activation, particularly with sustained or repeated use, resulting in fluctuating weakness that classically affects ocular, bulbar, and proximal limb muscles. ## Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome Antibodies inhibit voltage-gated calcium channels on the presynaptic terminal of motor neurons, impairing calcium influx and reducing ACh release into the synaptic cleft.  The decreased neurotransmitter availability weakens neuromuscular transmission, typically producing proximal muscle weakness and autonomic symptoms that may improve with repeated stimulation due to calcium buildup. ## Malignant hyperthermia Genetic mutations in RyR1 render the channel abnormally sensitive to certain anesthetic agents (eg, succinylcholine), resulting in uncontrolled calcium release from the SR.  The excess cytosolic calcium causes sustained muscle contraction and a hypermetabolic state with severe muscle rigidity, hyperthermia, acidosis, and potentially life-threatening complications if untreated. ## Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy This condition is caused by mutations in proteins involved in sarcolemmal stability and ECC (eg, caveolin, dysferlin).  Disruption of the T-tubule network and associated signaling leads to impaired propagation of depolarization across the muscle fiber.  As a result, calcium release becomes asynchronous, reducing coordinated contraction and causing progressive weakness in the shoulder and pelvic girdle muscles. # Summary Skeletal muscle contraction is a multistep process dependent on action potential generation, intracellular calcium dynamics, and ATP-driven mechanical events.  The integration of electrical signaling and molecular motor activity enables skeletal muscle to generate controlled force.  The main steps involve the triggering of the muscle action potential by acetylcholine in the neuromuscular junction, depolarization spreading through the sarcolemma into T-tubules, excitation-contraction coupling, and actin-myosin cross-bridge cycling.  Cardiac and smooth muscle differ in both structure and regulation. ​‌​‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​​​​​‌‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌​‌​​‌​​​​​​​​‌​​​​‌

articles.title: Hypothalamic-Pituitary Hormones
articles.markdown: # Hypothalamic-Pituitary Hormones # Introduction The hypothalamic-pituitary axis is a core component of the endocrine system, responsible for regulating various physiologic processes, including growth, metabolism, reproduction, and stress responses.  The hypothalamus, located at the base of the brain, controls the release of hormones from the pituitary gland, which is divided into anterior and posterior lobes.  The anterior pituitary releases several hormones that regulate peripheral endocrine glands, whereas the posterior pituitary stores and releases hormones synthesized in the hypothalamus.  The interplay between these 2 organs maintains homeostasis in the body.  This article examines the hormones produced by both the hypothalamus and the pituitary gland and their functions, regulatory mechanisms, and physiologic effects. # Hypothalamic hormones The hypothalamus produces releasing and inhibiting hormones that control the secretion of hormones from the anterior pituitary.  These hormones help regulate a variety of bodily functions, including reproduction, stress response, and metabolism. ## Gonadotropin-releasing hormone **Function** - Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) is part of the **hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis** in women ((Figure 1)) and men ((Figure 2)), influencing secretion of **gonadotropins**, including luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), from the anterior pituitary. - GnRH and gonadotropins regulate the function of the gonads (testes, ovaries) and reproductive processes, including production of **sex hormones** (testosterone, estrogen, and progesterone), spermatogenesis, and ovulation. -
