Prepubertal GnRH secretion is **low and constant**, which suppresses anterior pituitary gonadotropin secretion and gonadal sex hormone production.  Puberty is marked by a transition to **pulsatile** GnRH secretion, which stimulates increased gonadotropin secretion (resulting in increased LH, FSH, and sex hormones). **Regulation** - **Positive feedback**:  Leading up to ovulation, a sustained increase in estrogen levels leads to positive stimulation of GnRH secretion (ie, GnRH and LH surge). - **Negative feedback**:  Elevated sex hormone levels generally inhibit GnRH secretion; this effect occurs consistently with testosterone and progesterone, but the effects of estrogen in women depend on the current phase of the menstrual cycle (see below). **Clinical applications** - **Central hypogonadism**:  Suppression of GnRH can occur in states of stress or undernutrition (eg, via suppressive effects of elevated corticotropin-releasing hormone and cortisol, discussed in the next section), leading to low GnRH and hypogonadism (eg, decreased LH, estrogen, testosterone). - **Hyperprolactinemia**:  Elevated prolactin levels suppress GnRH secretion ((Figure 3)), leading to hypogonadism (low LH, FSH, estrogen). - **Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism**:  Primary ovarian insufficiency or testicular failure lowers sex hormone production, which leads to hypogonadism with elevated GnRH secretion (high LH and FSH with low estrogen or testosterone). - **Polycystic ovary syndrome**:  Polycystic ovary syndrome is characterized by excessively rapid pulsatile secretion of GnRH leads to a persistent imbalance in LH relative to FSH production, resulting in increased ovarian and peripheral androgen production. ## Corticotropin-releasing hormone **Function** - Corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) is part of the **hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis** ((Figure 4)), stimulating the anterior pituitary to release **adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)**, which subsequently stimulates the adrenal cortex to produce **corticosteroids** (eg, glucocorticoids, mineralocorticoids). - Corticosteroids (especially cortisol) are involved in the body's response to stress and immune function; mineralocorticoids contribute to salt and volume homeostasis.  Corticosteroids also play a crucial role in regulating circadian rhythms. **Regulation** - **Positive feedback**:  Secretion of CRH is triggered by inflammatory cytokines (eg, infection), circadian rhythms, and limbic system input in states of high physiologic or psychologic stress (eg, trauma, hypoglycemia) via input from the suprachiasmatic nucleus; CRH secretion is highest in the early morning and is lowest at night. - **Negative feedback**:  High cortisol levels lower CRH and ACTH secretion ((Figure 5)). **Clinical correlations** - **Adrenal insufficiency**:  Adrenal insufficiency is characterized by low cortisol due to either primary adrenal failure or secondary (ie, central) suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis.  In primary adrenal insufficiency, cortisol is low and ACTH/CRH are high due to loss of negative feedback.  Glucocorticoid use can lead to iatrogenic central suppression, with atrophy of hypothalamic CRH-releasing neurons causing low ACTH/CRH and cortisol. - **Cushing syndrome**:  Cushing syndrome refers to the clinical manifestations of prolonged, excessive cortisol exposure.  It can result from an adrenal source, such as an autonomously functioning adrenal adenoma, which leads to elevated cortisol and suppressed ACTH and CRH (due to negative feedback).  Alternately, it may arise from a central (ACTH-dependent) source, most commonly Cushing disease, which describes an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma that causes elevated ACTH and cortisol, with suppressed CRH (due to negative feedback). ## Thyrotropin-releasing hormone **Function** - Thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH), part of the **hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis** ((Figure 6)), stimulates the release of **thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)** from the anterior pituitary.  TSH in turn stimulates the thyroid gland to produce and release **thyroid hormones** (T3 and T4). - Thyroid hormones are critical for regulating metabolism, growth, and development, affecting nearly every tissue in the body. **Regulation** - **Negative feedback**:  TRH (and TSH) secretion is suppressed by increased levels of T3 and T4.  Other inhibitors of TRH include high dopamine levels, and starvation or critical illness (due to decreased leptin levels, high cortisol, and cytokine release), - **Positive feedback**:  Cold exposure, increased leptin, estrogen levels, and alpha-adrenergic stimulation (eg, norepinephrine) increase TRH levels. **Clinical applications** TRH is not routinely measured in clinical practice. - **Hyperthyroidism**:  Hyperthyroidism may result from central causes (eg, TSH-secreting tumors) with high TSH and T3/T4 or, more commonly, from primary hyperthyroidism with high T3/T4 and low TSH (feedback inhibition). - **Hypothyroidism**:  Hypothyroidism may be due to primary thyroid dysfunction (eg, Hashimoto disease) with low T3/T4 and high TSH (from negative feedback) or due to central inhibition (in which TSH and T3/T4 are both low). - **Euthyroid sick syndrome**:  In critical illness, caloric deprivation along with glucocorticoid and inflammatory cytokine release induce several changes in thyroid physiology (known as euthyroid sick syndrome \[ESS\]).  TRH suppression causes low-normal TSH levels, and decreased peripheral 5′-deiodination of T4 to T3 causes low T3; free T4 levels are initially normal.  If the underlying illness continues, T4 and TSH levels may eventually decrease, mimicking central hypothyroidism.  Because ESS typically improves with recovery, thyroid function testing in acutely ill, hospitalized patients is generally not recommended. ## Growth hormone–releasing hormone and somatostatin **Function** Growth hormone–releasing hormone (GHRH) and somatostatin are important regulators of the **growth hormone (GH) axis** ((Figure 7)) involving GH and insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), which mediate growth, cell repair, and metabolism.  GHRH stimulates somatotrophs of the anterior pituitary to **release GH**.  In contrast, somatostatin is the primary inhibitor of GH secretion, counteracting the effects of GHRH.  Somatostatin also inhibits the release of other hormones (eg, TSH, insulin). **Regulation** - **Negative feedback**:  Elevated levels of IGF-1 inhibits GHRH release from the hypothalamus (and GH secretion from the anterior pituitary). - Other regulators:  Somatostatin suppresses GH release, whereas factors such as sleep, exercise, stress, and hypoglycemia stimulate GHRH and GH secretion. **Clinical applications** - **Dwarfism**:  Dwarfism is characterized by GH deficiency. - **Acromegaly**:  Acromegaly is characterized by GH excess. ## Dopamine **Function** - Dopamine inhibits the release of **prolactin** from the anterior pituitary.  Prolactin is primarily involved in milk production in lactating women, and dopamine prevents excessive secretion of prolactin when not needed. **Regulation** - Dopamine secretion is modulated by feedback from prolactin levels.  Elevated prolactin can reduce dopamine release, allowing prolactin levels to rise further. - **Estrogen** can increase the secretion of prolactin, especially during pregnancy. **Clinical correlations** - **Prolactin-secreting tumors**:  Pituitary adenomas (prolactinomas) autonomously secrete prolactin, bypassing hypothalamic dopamine inhibition.  Elevated prolactin can cause galactorrhea, menstrual irregularities, and infertility. - **Dopamine antagonist medications**:  Antipsychotics and other dopamine D2 receptor blockers inhibit hypothalamic dopamine action, removing suppression of prolactin secretion.  This can lead to medication-induced hyperprolactinemia with symptoms similar to those seen in prolactinoma. # Pituitary hormones The anterior and posterior pituitary release several hormones that influence the function of other endocrine glands and target tissues throughout the body.  These hormones include ACTH, TSH, GH, LH, FSH, prolactin, and vasopressin. ## Adrenocorticotropic hormone **Function** - Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) stimulates the adrenal cortex to secrete **cortisol** and other corticosteroids.  Cortisol is vital for managing the body's response to stress, regulating metabolism, immune response, and inflammation. **Regulation** - **Negative feedback**:  Suppression of ACTH (and CRH) secretion can occur with high cortisol levels (or in the setting of long-term exogenous glucocorticoid therapy). ## Thyroid-stimulating hormone **Function** - Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) stimulates the thyroid gland to produce and release **thyroid hormones** (T3 and T4).  These hormones regulate metabolism, thermogenesis, and overall growth and development. **Regulation** - Like ACTH secretion, TSH secretion is regulated by **negative feedback** from thyroid hormones.  Elevated levels of T3 and T4 inhibit TRH release from the hypothalamus and TSH secretion from the pituitary. ## Growth hormone **Function** - Growth hormone (GH) stimulates growth, particularly in bones and muscles, and regulates metabolism.  It promotes protein synthesis, lipolysis, and the growth of long bones and cartilage, mainly through the action of IGF-1. **Regulation** GH secretion is regulated by **both** positive and negative feedback mechanisms: - **Positive feedback** occurs via GHRH, which stimulates GH release. - **Negative feedback** occurs through IGF-1, which inhibits both GHRH release and GH secretion. ## Prolactin **Function** - Prolactin is essential for **milk production** in the mammary glands during lactation.  It also plays a role in regulating reproductive function, immune modulation, and metabolism. **Regulation** - Prolactin release is primarily inhibited by dopamine.  During pregnancy, estrogen increases prolactin levels, preparing the mammary glands for lactation. ## Luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone **Function** - Luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) are **gonadotropins** responsible for regulating reproductive functions.  In women, LH triggers ovulation and the formation of the corpus luteum, whereas FSH stimulates the growth of ovarian follicles.  In men, LH stimulates testosterone production from Leydig cells and FSH supports spermatogenesis. **Regulation** - In women, **estrogen** and **progesterone** mediate negative feedback on LH and FSH release, but during the menstrual cycle, rising estrogen levels mediate **positive feedback** by triggering the **LH surge**, which leads to ovulation. ## Antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin) **Function** - Antidiuretic hormone (ADH), also called vasopressin, regulates water balance by promoting water reabsorption in the kidneys.  It also plays a role in constricting blood vessels to maintain blood pressure. **Regulation** - ADH release is primarily regulated by **osmotic pressure** and **blood volume**.  When plasma osmolarity increases (indicating dehydration), ADH release is stimulated to conserve water.  Conversely, low blood volume or blood pressure also triggers ADH secretion. ## Oxytocin **Function** - Oxytocin is involved in uterine contractions during labor and facilitates milk ejection during breastfeeding.  It also has a role in social bonding, emotional responses, and maternal behaviors. **Regulation** - Oxytocin operates through **positive feedback** during labor.  The stretching of the cervix during labor stimulates oxytocin release, which intensifies uterine contractions, leading to further cervical dilation and more oxytocin release. # Summary The hypothalamic-pituitary axis plays a central role in regulating numerous physiologic functions, including metabolism, growth, reproduction, and stress response.  The hypothalamus produces hormones that either stimulate or inhibit the release of pituitary hormones, which in turn regulate the activity of peripheral endocrine glands.  Feedback mechanisms, primarily negative feedback, maintain hormonal balance, although positive feedback plays a role in certain physiologic processes such as ovulation and labor.  Disruption of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis can lead to a variety of endocrine disorders. ​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​​​​​​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​​​​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​​​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​

articles.title: Endocrinology: Core Principles
articles.markdown: # Endocrinology: Core Principles # Introduction The endocrine system participates in cellular communication and regulation of responses in the body, typically over chronic periods.  It uses hormones, chemical messengers carried in the bloodstream for long-distance communication among the body's cells.  This article provides an overview of the endocrine system, with an emphasis on functional aspects.  The individual hormones and associated disorders are described in separate articles. # Hormones Hormones are signaling molecules secreted from endocrine tissues into the circulation.  They can be classified based on their structure (peptide hormones, steroid hormones, and amino acid–derived hormones, described later) or their influence on other hormones: - **Tropic** hormones target endocrine tissues to influence secretion of other hormones (eg, adrenocorticotropic hormone, produced by the anterior pituitary, stimulates the adrenal cortex to release cortisol). - In contrast, **direct** hormones act directly on target cells to produce nonendocrine responses (eg, prolactin, released by the anterior pituitary, promotes milk secretion). Some hormones (eg, growth hormone) act as both a tropic hormone (eg, stimulate the liver to release hormones) and a direct hormone (stimulates tissues to uptake glucose). # Endocrine glands Endocrine glands lack ducts and secrete hormones into the bloodstream.  The major endocrine glands are shown in the figure ((Figure 1)).  The **hypothalamic-pituitary axis** is a core component of the endocrine system; it is responsible for regulating various physiologic processes, including growth, metabolism, reproduction, and stress responses.  The hypothalamus, located at the base of the brain, controls the release of hormones from the pituitary gland, which is divided into anterior and posterior lobes.  The anterior pituitary releases several hormones that regulate peripheral endocrine glands (eg, thyroid, adrenal glands, gonads), whereas the posterior pituitary stores and releases hormones synthesized in the hypothalamus.  The interplay between these 2 organs maintains homeostasis in the body. # Hormone transport Hormones travel to target cells via the blood; therefore, a hormone's solubility affects how it is transported and how it exerts its physiologic effects. ## Peptide hormones Peptide hormones are produced in the rough endoplasmic reticulum and stored in vesicles until a signal causes them to be released.  They typically possess an overall charge at physiologic pH, making them water soluble **(hydrophilic)**.  Therefore, they can circulate largely in a free form (ie, unbound to proteins) in the bloodstream; however, they cannot cross the hydrophobic lipid layer of the target cell plasma membrane and rely on intracellular molecules to transmit a signal to the interior of a cell.  They are relatively fast acting with relatively short-lived results. ## Steroid hormones Steroid hormones are procured in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum.  Because they are derived from cholesterol, they are lipophilic **(hydrophobic)** and can diffuse through the secreting cell's membrane.  They are bound predominantly to protein carriers to increase their solubility.  Their hydrophobicity facilitates diffusion through target cell plasma membranes, after which the hormones bind receptors in the cytoplasm or nucleus to regulate gene expression ((Figure 2)).  They are slower acting with longer-lasting results. ## Amino acid–derived hormones Amino acid–derived hormones can function similarly to peptide and steroid hormones, depending on their structure and regulation.  For example, the catecholamine hormones epinephrine and norepinephrine behave like peptide hormones, whereas thyroid hormones behave like steroid hormones. # Endocrine signaling Endocrine signaling is 1 of the 3 broad ways (autocrine, paracrine, endocrine) in which cell signaling occurs ((Figure 3)).  The reception of a signal by a target cell is the first step in endocrine signaling. Receptors for peptide hormones are located in the plasma membrane because peptide hormones are charged and cannot readily cross the phospholipid bilayer; these receptors are often coupled with a G protein.  The peptide hormone serves as a first messenger, which binds its receptor and triggers a **second messenger** (eg, cyclic adenosine monophosphate), another molecule inside the target cells that transmits the signals (often through phosphorylation) ((Figure 4)).  Signal amplification can occur along this signaling cascade due to the production of hundreds of secondary messengers. Because steroid hormones are lipophilic, they diffuse directly across the plasma membrane and bind **intracellular receptors** in the cytosol or the nucleus, typically without using second messengers.  The steroid hormone–receptor complex usually acts as a **transcription factor** and binds DNA, resulting in increased or decreased transcription of target genes.  Often, 2 steroid hormone–receptor complexes bind together (ie, dimerize) prior to DNA binding. # Regulatory organization and feedback Endocrine function is organized primarily into regulatory axes that link the hypothalamus, pituitary gland, and peripheral endocrine organs (eg, hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid, hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal, hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal).  Hypothalamic hormones stimulate the anterior pituitary to release tropic hormones, which in turn regulate hormone secretion from peripheral glands. Hormone secretion within these axes is governed primarily by feedback mechanisms.  In **negative feedback**, the final hormone produced by a peripheral gland suppresses further secretion of hypothalamic and pituitary hormones, stabilizing circulating hormone levels ((Figure 5)).  For example, thyroid hormones inhibit the release of both thyrotropin-releasing hormone from the hypothalamus and TSH from the anterior pituitary. Less commonly, **positive feedback** amplifies hormone secretion under specific physiologic conditions ((Figure 6)).  For example, rising estradiol levels during the late follicular phase stimulate a surge in LH, which triggers ovulation. Hormone secretion also follows characteristic temporal patterns.  Some hormones are released in a pulsatile manner (eg, GnRH), whereas others exhibit circadian variation (eg, cortisol, which peaks in the early morning).  These patterns are integral to normal endocrine function and can be disrupted in disease states. # Patterns of endocrine disease Disorders of the endocrine system can be broadly categorized based on abnormalities in hormone production or action. Hormone excess and deficiency can result from dysfunction at different levels of an endocrine axis. - In **primary** disorders, pathology originates in the peripheral endocrine gland itself, leading to altered hormone production. - In **secondary** or tertiary (central) disorders, abnormalities in the pituitary or hypothalamus result in inappropriate regulation of peripheral glands. These distinctions tend to produce predictable patterns of hormone levels due to feedback mechanisms.  For example, primary gland failure leads to reduced end-hormone levels with compensatory elevation of tropic hormones, whereas central dysfunction results in low levels of both. In some conditions, circulating hormone levels are normal or elevated, but target tissues fail to respond appropriately.  This end-organ resistance may result from defects in hormone receptors or downstream signaling pathways (eg, insulin resistance). # Evaluation of endocrine disorders Evaluation of endocrine disorders follows from axis physiology and feedback relationships.  Initial testing measures both the peripheral (end) hormone and its corresponding pituitary tropic hormone to determine whether feedback is intact: - In primary gland dysfunction, reduced end-hormone production removes negative feedback, resulting in elevated tropic hormone levels (eg, primary hypothyroidism: low T4, high TSH). - Conversely, excess end hormone suppresses tropic hormone secretion (eg, primary hyperthyroidism: high T4, low TSH). - In central (pituitary or hypothalamic) disorders, both tropic and end-hormone levels are inappropriately low or inappropriately normal relative to each other (eg, secondary hypothyroidism: low T4 with low or inappropriately normal TSH). When baseline measurements do not clearly localize the defect, dynamic testing is used to assess how the system responds to perturbation. - **Stimulation tests** are used when hormone deficiency is suspected, evaluating whether a gland can increase hormone production when appropriately stimulated (eg, cosyntropin stimulation test: failure of cortisol to rise indicates adrenal insufficiency). - **Suppression tests** are used when hormone excess is suspected, evaluating whether normal feedback can reduce hormone secretion (eg, dexamethasone suppression test: failure to suppress cortisol suggests Cushing syndrome). # Summary The endocrine system coordinates long-range cellular communication through hormones released into the bloodstream, with effects determined by hormone structure, transport, and receptor signaling.  Peptide hormones are water soluble and act via cell-surface receptors and second messengers, whereas steroid and thyroid hormones are lipophilic, circulate protein-bound, and regulate gene transcription through intracellular receptors.  Endocrine function is organized into hypothalamic–pituitary–target gland axes governed primarily by negative feedback, with additional modulation by pulsatile and circadian secretion.  Disorders arise from hormone excess or deficiency or from end-organ resistance and can be localized within an axis by interpreting feedback relationships.  Evaluation relies on paired measurement of tropic and end hormones, with dynamic stimulation or suppression testing used to assess glandular reserve or autonomy when baseline findings are inconclusive. ​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​​​​​​​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​​​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌

articles.title: Cardiovascular Hemodynamics
articles.markdown:
# Cardiovascular Hemodynamics # Basics of cardiovascular blood flow The cardiovascular system consists of a continuous circuit of blood vessels that supply oxygen and nutrients to the organs and tissues of the body.  The system is powered by 2 pumps: - The right ventricle (RV) powers the relatively low-pressure pulmonary circulation. - The left ventricle (LV) powers the relatively high-pressure systemic circulation. The parameters that govern cardiovascular blood flow are defined as follows. ## Stroke volume and cardiac output

Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate

Cardiac index = cardiac output / total body surface area

- **Stroke volume** is the volume of blood ejected from the RV or the LV with each contraction.  It is typically measured in milliliters.  The normal stroke volume for an adult at rest is approximately 70 mL. - **Cardiac output** is the amount of blood ejected from the RV or the LV per unit of time.  It is the product of stroke volume and heart rate and is typically measured in liters per minute.  The normal cardiac output for an adult at rest is approximately 5-6 L/min. - **Cardiac index** is a representation of cardiac output adjusted per body size; it is equal to cardiac output divided by total body surface area.  The normal cardiac index for an adult at rest ranges from 2.5-4.0 L/min/m2. - Because the RV and LV are connected in series, all blood passing through one ventricle must pass through the other ventricle at the same rate (otherwise blood will back up).  Therefore, under normal conditions, the cardiac output of the RV is the same as the cardiac output of the LV. ## Modified Ohm law

Voltage = current × resistance →

Pressure = cardiac output × resistance

- Ohm law (V \[voltage\] = I \[current\] × R \[resistance\]) was developed to describe energy flow through an electrical circuit, but the concept applies to all types of energy flow.  According to Ohm law, a voltage difference between points A and B drives electrical flow (current) against resistance between the 2 points. - In the modified Ohm law that describes cardiovascular hemodynamics, voltage is analogous to pressure and current is analogous to blood flow, such that the law becomes **P (pressure) = CO (cardiac output) × R (resistance)**.  In the circulatory system, blood flows from an area of higher pressure to an area of lower pressure, with the magnitude of flow inversely related to resistance. - Pressure and resistance are relatively low in the pulmonary circulation and relatively high in the systemic circulation.  Cardiac output is the same in both circulations. ## Resistance - Resistance is required to maintain pressure in the cardiovascular system. - **Systemic vascular resistance (SVR)** is created primarily by the systemic arterioles, and **pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR)** is created primarily by the pulmonary arterioles.  These arterioles can vasodilate and vasoconstrict to adjust resistance. ## Ejection fraction

Stroke volume = LV end-diastolic volume − LV end-systolic volume

LV ejection fraction = stroke volume / LV end-diastolic volume

- LV **stroke volume** is often calculated by subtracting the volume of blood in the LV at the end of contraction (ie, LV end-systolic volume) from the volume of blood in the LV at the beginning of contraction (ie, LV end-diastolic volume). - **Ejection fraction** ((Figure 1)), the relative volume of blood ejected from the LV with each contraction, is calculated by dividing stroke volume by the LV end-diastolic volume.  For instance, in a patient with LV end-diastolic volume of 150 mL and stroke volume of 75 mL, the ejection fraction is 50%.  An LV ejection fraction of 50%-70% is considered normal. ## Stroke volume:  Preload, contractility, and afterload Stroke volume is determined by 3 parameters ((Figure 2)):  preload, contractility, and afterload. **Preload** is the volume of blood in the ventricle at the end of diastole; it depends on venous return from the systemic circulation and the effectiveness of diastolic filling.  In a normally functioning heart, LV preload is directly related to RV preload, and the term "preload" usually refers to LV preload, which is synonymous with LV end-diastolic volume.  Stroke volume is directly related to preload according to the Frank-Starling law (as preload increases, stroke volume increases), which is discussed below. Factors that increase preload include: - Increased total blood volume. - Systemic venous vasoconstriction to mobilize blood from the venous capacitance system. Factors that decrease preload include: - Decreased total blood volume. - Systemic venous vasodilation. **Contractility**, also referred to as inotropy, is the intrinsic force of myocardial contraction and is determined by intracellular calcium concentration.  Stroke volume is directly related to contractility. Factors that increase contractility are primarily those that increase intracellular calcium and include: - Increased sympathetic tone. - Positive inotropic pharmacologic interventions (eg, digoxin, beta-1 agonists). Factors that decrease contractility are primarily those that decrease intracellular calcium and include: - Decreased sympathetic tone. - Negative inotropic pharmacologic interventions (eg, beta blockers, nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers). - Dilated cardiomyopathy and other disorders that impair cardiac sarcomere function (independent of intracellular calcium). **Afterload** is the pressure that the LV must contract against.  In contrast with preload, afterload is represented as pressure rather than volume; systolic blood pressure is generally indicative of LV afterload.  Stroke volume is inversely related to afterload:  As afterload increases, stroke volume decreases. Factors that increase afterload include: - Peripheral arteriolar vasoconstriction (increased SVR). - Increased contractility. - Increased preload. Factors that decrease LV afterload include: - Peripheral arteriolar vasodilation (decreased SVR). - Decreased contractility. - Decreased preload. ## Frank-Starling law The Frank-Starling law ((Figure 3)) of the heart states that, as LV preload increases, stroke volume increases accordingly to maintain forward blood flow (ie, "**the heart gives what it gets**").  The underlying mechanism is that increased preload causes increased myocardial stretching (ie, increased tension), which allows for more forceful contraction to expel the additional preload.  The increased force of contraction is entirely due to increased myocardial stretching and does not involve an increase in myocardial contractility (ie, there is no change in intracellular calcium concentration). ## Determinants of arterial blood pressure

Systolic blood pressure = diastolic blood pressure + pulse pressure

**Diastolic blood pressure (DBP)** is the baseline hydrostatic pressure in the arterial system and is directly related to SVR and arterial blood volume.  **Pulse pressure** is the amount that arterial pressure increases above DBP during LV contraction; it is directly related to stroke volume and inversely related to aortic compliance, which is generally constant but gradually decreases with advancing age. **Systolic blood pressure** is the sum of DBP and pulse pressure ((Figure 4)).  For example: - An isolated increase in SVR increases DBP and secondarily increases systolic blood pressure, with pulse pressure remaining unchanged. - An isolated increase in stroke volume increases pulse pressure and systolic blood pressure, with DBP remaining unchanged. Increased heart rate slightly increases DBP by mobilizing a higher percentage of blood volume from the venous capacitance system to the arterial circulation (increased arterial blood volume). ## Vascular compartments - The systemic veins act as a capacitance system ((Figure 5)), storing up to 90% of intravascular blood volume.  Vasodilation of the capacitance venules increases venous storage, whereas vasoconstriction reduces storage and mobilizes blood to the right side of the heart (increases venous return). - The pressure in the **systemic venous system** is referred to as **central venous pressure** (CVP) and is roughly 6-8 cm H2O (~5-6 mm Hg). - Blood that is mobilized from the venous system to the right atrium fills the RV during diastole.  Right atrial pressure and RV end-diastolic pressure are roughly equivalent ((Figure 6)) to CVP. - During RV systole, blood is ejected into the pulmonary arteries and delivered to the lungs for oxygen and carbon dioxide exchange.  The pulmonary arterioles create PVR and maintain pressure in the pulmonary circulation.  **RV systolic pressure** and **pulmonary artery systolic pressure** are roughly equivalent (~25 mm Hg). - After traveling through the pulmonary capillaries, blood travels through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium and then fills the LV during diastole.  Left atrial pressure is often estimated during right heart catheterization ((Figure 7)) by the measurement of **pulmonary capillary wedge pressure** (PCWP).  Left atrial pressure and LV end-diastolic pressure are roughly equivalent to PCWP (~8 mm Hg). - During LV systole, blood is ejected into the aorta and delivered to the organs and tissues of the body.  Vasodilation and constriction of the systemic arterioles regulate SVR to maintain systemic blood pressure and modulate flow to specific organs and tissues (eg, skeletal muscle vs intestines).  LV systolic pressure and systemic arterial systolic pressure are roughly equivalent (~120 mm Hg). - After passing through the systemic capillaries, blood returns to the venous capacitance system, where it can be mobilized again as venous return to the right atrium. # Blood pressure regulation ## Blood volume regulation via the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system Blood volume is determined primarily by total body **sodium** because the osmotic activity of sodium keeps water in the intravascular space.  Blood volume is regulated by the **renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system** (RAAS), a hormonal cascade ((Figure 8)) and feedback loop that culminates in aldosterone-mediated sodium and water reabsorption by the kidneys.  The juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA) ((Figure 9)) of the kidneys controls the RAAS by stimulating renin release in response to the following stimuli: - Decreased pressure in the renal afferent arterioles. - Decreased total sodium delivery to the macula densa. - Increased sympathetic drive to the JGA. As the JGA senses reduced blood volume, aldosterone secretion from the adrenal cortex ((Figure 10)) increases and blood volume increases.  During periods of adequate blood volume and blood pressure, renin activity (and downstream aldosterone activity) is inhibited ((Figure 11)). In addition to stimulating aldosterone secretion, angiotensin II also induces systemic vasoconstriction to help increase blood pressure. ## Baroreceptor reflex The baroreceptor reflex regulates blood pressure by stimulating autonomic-mediated changes in heart rate, contractility, and peripheral vasoconstriction to compensate for changes in blood pressure.  The **carotid and aortic arch baroreceptors** ((Figure 12)) are stretch-sensitive mechanoreceptors that increase their firing rate in response to arterial distension.  They transmit impulses to the solitary nucleus of the medulla, which then modulates sympathetic and parasympathetic (vagal) output in response to the baroreceptor firing rate. - With an abrupt **decrease** ((Figure 13)) in cardiac output and blood pressure, reduced stretch of the arterial walls leads to reduced baroreceptor firing and decreased activation of the solitary nucleus.  This causes an increase in sympathetic outflow with a corresponding reduction in parasympathetic tone, leading to vasoconstriction (increased peripheral resistance) and increased heart rate and contractility (increased cardiac output), minimizing the drop in blood pressure. - Conversely, an abrupt **increase** ((Figure 14)) in blood pressure leads to increased stretch of the arterial walls and increased baroreceptor firing.  In response, increased activation of the solitary nucleus causes reduced sympathetic tone and a corresponding increase in parasympathetic outflow, leading to alleviated vasoconstriction (decreased peripheral resistance) and decreased heart rate and contractility (decreased cardiac output), minimizing the rise in blood pressure. ## Valsalva maneuver The Valsalva maneuver ((Figure 15)) relies on changes in intrathoracic pressure to modulate baroreceptor reflex activity and create a brief surge in blood pressure.  It has 2 phases. During the initial **strain phase** of the Valsalva maneuver, air is inspired and then an exhale is held against a closed glottis.  This increases intrathoracic pressure and facilitates the following: - Increased intrathoracic pressure is transmitted directly to the aortic wall, causing a slight initial increase in blood pressure. - The increased intrathoracic pressure restricts venous return to the right atrium, which in turn leads to reduced cardiac output. - The baroreceptor reflex senses the reduced cardiac output (via a reduction in blood pressure) and triggers a compensatory sympathetic increase in heart rate and SVR to raise cardiac output and blood pressure. Once the exhale strain is released, the **relaxation phase** begins and facilitates the following: - With intrathoracic pressure released, pressure on the aortic wall decreases, causing a brief drop in blood pressure.  In addition, venous return is no longer restricted, and it surges into the right atrium and pulmonary circulation. - The increased venous return is ejected by the LV into the previously increased SVR, causing a surge in systemic blood pressure (ie, blood pressure "overshoot"). - The baroreceptor reflex senses the surge in blood pressure and triggers a compensatory surge in vagal tone to reduce SVR and return hemodynamics to baseline. Examples of clinical applications of the Valsalva maneuver include: - Heart murmur identification:  The reduction in venous return (ie, preload) during the strain phase can be used to help identify certain heart murmurs that are affected by changes in preload (eg, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, mitral valve prolapse). - Supraventricular tachycardia termination:  The surge in vagal tone toward the end of the relaxation phase can slow conduction through the atrioventricular (AV) node and can sometimes terminate AV node–dependent paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardias. # Left ventricular pressure–volume loops The LV pressure–volume loop ((Figure 16)) follows the cardiac cycle and illustrates the interactions between preload, contractility, and afterload.  At point 1, the LV is full of blood and begins isovolumetric contraction until the aortic valve opens at point 2, causing blood to eject into the aorta and LV volume to decrease.  LV contraction ends at point 3, and LV pressure rapidly decreases to point 4, where the mitral valve opens and LV diastolic filling begins again. ## Main parameters on the pressure-volume loop On the LV flow–volume loop, the following parameters are represented as follows: - **Preload** (end-diastolic volume) is the volume at point 1.  Shifting of point 1 to the right indicates an increase in preload, and shifting of point 1 to the left indicates a decrease in preload. - **Afterload** is generally represented by the peak pressure generated during blood ejection.  An increase in the peak pressure represents an increase in afterload, and a decrease in peak pressure represents a decrease in afterload. - **Contractility**, the intrinsic force the myocardium contracts with, is represented by the line tangent to point 3.  A shift in the contractility line up and to the left indicates increased contractility, and a shift down and to the right indicates decreased contractility. - **Stroke volume** is the difference in volume from end-diastole (point 1) to end-systole (point 3).  Stroke volume can increase or decrease due to changes in the other parameters. - **Compliance** is the slope of the diastolic filling line from point 4 to point 1 (ie, increase in pressure per increase in volume).  An increase in the slope of the line represents decreased compliance, and a decrease in the slope of the line represents increased compliance.  Unlike the other parameters, compliance is typically constant in the short term and is not subject to change. A primary change in one parameter leads to an immediate secondary change in other parameters (not considering baroreceptor-mediated reflex effects).  The immediate effects of primary changes are as follows. ## Preload - An isolated increase in preload occurs with an increase in blood volume (eg, infusion of normal saline).  Increased preload ((Figure 17)) leads to an increase in stroke volume and a slight increase in afterload. - An isolated decrease in preload occurs with a decrease in blood volume (eg, blood loss, dehydration).  Decreased preload ((Figure 18)) leads to a decrease in stroke volume and a slight decrease in afterload. ## Afterload - An isolated increase in afterload occurs with clamping of the abdominal aorta.  Increased afterload ((Figure 19)) leads to decreased stroke volume. - An isolated decrease in afterload occurs with a primarily arterial vasodilator such as hydralazine.  Decreased afterload ((Figure 20)) leads to increased stroke volume. ## Contractility - An isolated increase in contractility occurs with a positive inotrope such as digoxin or a primarily beta-1 agonist (eg, dobutamine).  Increased contractility ((Figure 21)) leads to an increase in stroke volume and a slight increase in afterload. - An isolated decrease in contractility occurs with a negative inotrope such as a primarily beta-1 antagonist (eg, metoprolol) or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (eg, verapamil).  Decreased contractility ((Figure 22)) leads to a decrease in stroke volume and a slight decrease in afterload. # Cardiac function–vascular function curves (Guyton curves) The cardiovascular system is a closed circuit:  Blood ejected from the LV (cardiac output) returns to the right atrium (venous return) before passing through the lungs and being ejected once again.  Cardiac function–vascular function curves (Guyton curves) ((Figure 23)) illustrate the relationship between cardiac output and venous return. - **Cardiac function curve**:  As right atrial pressure (an indication of preload) increases, **cardiac output** increases due to myocardial fiber stretching and a corresponding increase in stroke volume.  This curve is essentially a Frank-Starling curve, representing constant LV contractility (inotropy) along the curve.  Changes in contractility shift the curve to the left or the right. - **Vascular function curve**:  As right atrial pressure increases, **venous return** to the right atrium decreases as a reduced pressure gradient drives blood return to the right atrium.  Changes in blood volume, venous capacitance, and SVR shift the curve to the left or the right. - The **intersection point** of the curves represents the **steady-state** equilibrium of right atrial pressure and cardiac output/venous return for a given set of cardiac and vascular parameters. ## Shifting of the curves Shifting ((Figure 24)) of the cardiac function curve is facilitated by a change in contractility.  Shifting of the venous return curve is facilitated by a change in blood volume, venous capacitance, or SVR. ## Cardiac function curve - **Increased contractility** ((Figure 25)), as occurs with a positive inotrope (eg, digoxin), shifts the cardiac function curve to the **left** and creates a new steady-state equilibrium point at an increased cardiac output and a reduced right atrial pressure. - **Decreased contractility** ((Figure 26)), as occurs with a negative inotrope (eg, verapamil), shifts the cardiac function curve to the **right** and creates a new equilibrium point at a reduced cardiac output and an increased right atrial pressure. ## Vascular function (venous return) curve - **Increased** venous return ((Figure 27)) shifts the venous return curve to the **right** and creates a new equilibrium point at an increased venous return and an increased right atrial pressure.  Factors that increase venous return include: - **Increased blood volume**, as occurs with an infusion of normal saline. - **Decreased venous capacitance**, as occurs with a venous vasoconstrictor.  This mobilizes blood from the venous capacitance system to the right atrium. - **Decreased SVR**, as occurs with an arteriolar vasodilator.  This allows blood to return to the right atrium more easily. - **Decreased** venous return ((Figure 28)) shifts the venous return curve to the **left** and creates a new equilibrium point at a decreased venous return and a decreased right atrial pressure.  Factors that decrease venous return include: - Decreased **blood volume**, as occurs with dehydration or blood loss. - Increased **venous capacitance**, as occurs with a venous vasodilator (eg, nitroglycerin). - Increased **SVR**, as occurs with an arteriolar vasoconstrictor. - Changes in blood volume and venous capacitance cause the entire venous return curve to shift left or right.  Changes in SVR (arteriolar vasoconstriction or vasodilation) cause the venous return curve to pivot left or right at the x-axis, meaning that the curve appears steeper or flatter but the right atrial pressure at the *x*\-axis (ie, where cardiac output/venous return are zero) does not change.  This is because blood volume is mostly (90%) held in the venous (vs arterial) system, so when the system is stagnant (ie, cardiac output/venous return = 0), blood volume delivered to the right atrium is not significantly affected by changes in SVR. # Catheter-based cardiovascular pressure charts Catheter-based pressure charts reflect measurements made by introducing a catheter into the blood and and obtaining hemodynamic measurements at various points (eg, heart chambers).  They illustrate normal cardiovascular pressures ((Figure 29)) throughout the cardiac cycle and show how valvular disruptions affect cardiovascular pressures: - Aortic stenosis ((Figure 30)) restricts blood flow from the LV to the aorta and creates an abnormal pressure gradient between LV systolic pressure and aortic systolic pressure. - Aortic regurgitation ((Figure 31)) creates a backflow of blood from the aorta to the LV during diastole, which leads to a progressive decrease in aortic pressure and an increase in LV pressure during diastole. - Mitral stenosis ((Figure 32)) restricts blood flow from the left atrium to the LV to increase left atrial pressure and create an abnormal pressure gradient between left atrial pressure and LV diastolic pressure. - Mitral regurgitation ((Figure 33)) creates a backflow of blood from the LV to the left atrium during systole, which creates a surge in left atrial pressure (prominent V wave). # Jugular venous pressure and waveform Jugular venous pressure is representative of CVP and allows CVP to be estimated on physical examination ((Figure 34)). The shape of the jugular venous pulse waveform reflects pressure changes in the right atrium throughout the cardiac cycle.  The normal jugular venous pulse waveform is composed of the following waves and descents ((Figure 35)): - A wave created by atrial contraction toward the end of ventricular diastole. - C wave created by tricuspid valve closure at the start of ventricular systole. - x descent created by atrial relaxation. - V wave created by atrial filling during ventricular systole. - y descent created by atrial emptying during early ventricular diastole. Certain types of cardiac pathology create characteristic changes in the jugular venous pulse waveform.  For example: - The loss of organized atrial contraction with atrial fibrillation ((Figure 36)) creates loss of the A wave. - Tricuspid valve regurgitation ((Figure 37)) creates a prominent V wave and an absent x descent due to the transmission of RV pressure to the right atrium during ventricular systole. ​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​​​​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​​‌​‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​​​‌​‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌

articles.title: Bone Formation And Remodeling
articles.markdown: # Bone Formation And Remodeling # Introduction Bone remodeling is a dynamic process that maintains skeletal strength and contributes to mineral homeostasis.  It involves the resorption of old or damaged bone and the deposition and mineralization of new bone matrix.  Approximately 10% of the human skeletal structure undergoes remodeling annually.  In children, adolescents, and young adults, bone formation generally exceeds resorption; bone mass gradually increases to reach a peak at approximately age 30.  Thereafter, bone resorption progressively exceeds new bone formation, favoring net loss of bone mass. # Overview The remodeling process is tightly orchestrated by the interactions of 3 main cell types—osteoclasts, osteoblasts, and osteocytes—and regulated by mechanical stress, intercellular signaling, and hormones.  This article discusses remodeling sequences, major cells involved, local signaling pathways that couple resorption to formation, and hormones that modulate these pathways, and it provides a brief overview of clinical correlates. ## Remodeling sequence Remodeling requires the coordinated function of osteoclasts (bone-resorbing cells) and osteoblasts (bone-forming cells), which together are often called the basic multicellular unit (BMU).  Bone remodeling by the BMU occurs in a tightly regulated cycle ((Figure 1)) in which resorption of old bone and formation of new bone are linked.  Major steps include the following: 1. **Activation**:  Osteocytes sense microdamage or altered loading and initiate the remodeling process by releasing signaling molecules that recruit and activate osteoclast precursors. 2. **Resorption**:  Osteoclasts dissolve mineralized bone matrix and degrade collagen, forming resorption pits. 3. **Reversal**:  Osteoclasts undergo apoptosis and are replaced by mononuclear cells that prepare the surface for new bone formation. 4. **Formation**:  Osteoblasts lay down new osteoid and mineralize it with hydroxyapatite. 5. **Quiescence**:  The bone surface is covered by lining cells, and some osteoblasts mature into osteocytes, which become embedded within the bone. In brief, osteoblasts drive mineralization ("osteo**b**lasts **b**uild"), osteoclasts perform resorption, and osteocytes coordinate the cycle by translating hormonal and mechanical cues into signals adjusting osteoclast and osteoblast activity. # Osteoblasts **Osteoblasts** arise from mesenchymal stem cells and are responsible for producing and mineralizing the osteoid matrix, which consists primarily of type I collagen and other bone matrix proteins.  These cells express alkaline phosphatase, which hydrolyzes pyrophosphate to release inorganic phosphate, promoting formation of hydroxyapatite (ie, mineral calcium phosphate).  After matrix secretion, osteoblasts become lining cells, undergo apoptosis, or differentiate into osteocytes. # Osteoclasts Osteoclasts are multinucleated cells derived from the monocyte/macrophage lineage ((Figure 2)).  They require 2 essential factors for differentiation: - **Macrophage colony-stimulating factor**:  Promotes proliferation and survival of osteoclast precursors. - **Receptor activator of nuclear factor-κB ligand (RANKL)**:  Drives osteoclast maturation and activation via RANK on osteoclast precursors.  RANKL is produced by osteoblasts and osteocytes, especially in response to stimuli that favor resorption, such as parathyroid hormone (PTH) or mechanical unloading. Activated osteoclasts dissolve mineral and degrade organic matrix using bone-resorbing enzymes. # Osteocytes Osteocytes, which are derived from osteoblasts, have long cytoplasmic processes that traverse canaliculi and form gap junctions with neighboring osteocytes and surface cells.  This network allows for the transmission of signaling molecules, facilitating the coordinated regulation of remodeling across bone regions.  Osteocytes function as mechanosensors and endocrine signaling hubs.  Mechanical deformation of bone alters cytoskeletal and integrin-based tension in osteocytes, triggering the release of molecules that regulate bone turnover. # Local signals coupling bone resorption and formation Two pathways are important for local signaling: the RANKL signaling pathway and the Wnt signaling pathway. ## RANKL and osteoprotegerin RANKL, produced by osteoblasts and osteocytes in response to stimuli that favor bone resorption, binds to its receptor, **RANK**, on osteoclast precursor cells.  The resulting signaling cascade leads to precursor fusion, cytoskeletal reorganization, and upregulation of bone-resorbing enzymes (eg, cathepsin K, tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase). A key regulator of osteoclast physiology is **osteoprotegerin**, a decoy receptor secreted by osteoblasts that binds RANKL and prevents it from engaging RANK ((Figure 3)).  The **RANKL:osteoprotegerin ratio** is the main local determinant of osteoclastogenesis and bone resorptive activity.  This ratio is modulated by several metabolic factors: - Signals that **increase** the RANKL:osteoprotegerin ratio (increased RANKL or lower osteoprotegerin expression) and promote bone **resorption** include PTH, glucocorticoids, vitamin D, and inflammatory cytokines (eg, TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6). - Signals that **decrease** the RANKL:osteoprotegerin ratio (suppressed RANK/RANKL or increased osteoprotegerin production) and decrease bone **resorption** include estrogen, TGF-β, and exercise or mechanical strain. Through the RANK–RANKL–osteoprotegerin axis, osteoblasts and osteocytes exert precise control over osteoclast differentiation, linking local bone remodeling to systemic metabolic demands and hormonal status. ## Wnt signaling and sclerostin Wnt/beta-catenin signaling promotes osteoblast differentiation and bone formation and indirectly restrains osteoclast generation.  Wnt signaling is inhibited by sclerostin, which is produced by osteocytes and lowers osteoblast activity.  Mechanical loading tends to reduce sclerostin output, promoting bone formation. # Systemic hormonal regulation In addition to local factors, systemic factors also regulate the remodeling process by affecting calcium and phosphate balance, which is coordinated through the actions of PTH, vitamin D, and fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23).  In addition, estrogen influences the balance of osteoclast and osteoblast function. ## Parathyroid hormone PTH is secreted in response to falling serum calcium levels.  It increases bone resorption to mobilize calcium by promoting the expression of RANKL in osteoblast-lineage cells.  Chronically elevated PTH favors osteoclastogenesis and bone loss.  However, intermittent exposure to PTH, such as with therapeutic analogs like teriparatide, enhances osteoblast survival and promotes bone formation.  PTH also increases renal calcium reabsorption and stimulates 1α-hydroxylase activity, which boosts active vitamin D synthesis ((Figure 4)). ## Vitamin D Vitamin D is derived from dietary sources (eg, dairy) and from conversion of 7-dehydrocholesterol in the skin by sunlight.  It is converted in the liver to 25-hydroxyvitamin D, which is the primary storage form.  In response to PTH, 25-hydroxyvitamin D is subsequently converted by 1α-hydroxylase in the kidneys to 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, which is the active form ((Figure 5)). Vitamin D enhances intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphate to support mineralization.  It also upregulates RANKL expression in osteoblasts, contributing to osteoclast activation when calcium supply is insufficient.  In this way, vitamin D helps match bone resorption to calcium need while also supporting bone formation when mineral availability is adequate. ## Fibroblast growth factor 23 Secreted mainly by osteocytes, FGF23 is a phosphate-regulating hormone.  It reduces phosphate reabsorption in the renal proximal tubule and decreases 1α-hydroxylase activity, thereby lowering active vitamin D levels.  This dual effect reduces circulating phosphate, limiting mineral availability and bone matrix calcification under certain pathologic conditions. ## Estrogen Estrogen plays a key role in maintaining bone density (in women and also in men via conversion from testosterone) by suppressing RANK expression on osteoclast precursors and by inducing osteoprotegerin production by osteoblasts.  This reduces osteoclast survival and activity while preserving osteoblast function. # Clinical correlations ## Osteoporosis Osteoporosis is characterized by loss of bone mass and strength, leading to increased susceptibility to fracture.  By convention, osteoporosis is diagnosed when bone mass is more than 2.5 standard deviations below the mean for a healthy 30-year-old at peak bone mass (ie, DXA T-score <−2.5) or when an individual sustains a fracture from an injury that would not be expected to cause a fracture (ie, fragility fracture), such as a fall from standing height. Osteoporosis is more common in women than in men due to lower peak bone mass in young adulthood and more rapid bone loss following menopause.  At menopause, the rapid decline in estrogen leads to: - Reduced osteoprotegerin. - Increased RANK-mediated osteoclastogenesis. - Higher bone turnover skewed toward resorption. Early postmenopausal osteoporosis primarily affects cancellous bone, making vertebral compression fractures common.  Later, cortical bone becomes involved, increasing the risk for hip fractures.  Other age-related contributors include reduced calcium absorption and declining osteoblast function. Osteoporosis can also be caused by excessive levels of cortisol (or glucocorticoid medications).  Cortisol inhibits osteoblast activity and decreases osteoblast proliferation and differentiation, reducing collagen synthesis and bone matrix production.  It also increases the expression of RANKL, which promotes osteoclast differentiation and activity, leading to greater bone resorption.  Additional contributing factors include impaired intestinal calcium absorption, increased catabolism of type I collagen, and increased apoptosis of osteocytes. ## Osteomalacia Osteomalacia involves defective mineralization of osteoid, most often due to vitamin D deficiency.  Although bone density is decreased in both, the pathophysiology of osteomalacia is distinct from that of osteoporosis.  Bone resorption is not excessive in osteomalacia; rather, mineralization is insufficient.  Clinically, osteomalacia causes: - Bone pain and tenderness. - Muscle weakness and gait disturbance. - Increased fracture risk. Laboratory findings often include low calcium, low phosphate, and elevated alkaline phosphatase, reflecting unmineralized osteoid and compensatory osteoblast activity.  These markers are generally normal in osteoporosis, distinguishing the two conditions. ## Paget disease of bone Paget disease of bone is characterized by abnormal osteoclast function ((Figure 6)) with localized regions of disordered bone remodeling.  Pathophysiologic features include: - Focal areas of excessive resorption followed by chaotic bone formation. - Thickening of both trabecular and cortical bone. - Structural weakness and deformities. Manifestations of Paget disease include focal bone pain, enlargement of the skull, and compression of cranial nerves (eg, hearing loss).  Laboratory studies show elevated serum alkaline phosphatase with normal calcium and phosphate.  X-ray imaging may show cortical thickening with mixed lytic and sclerotic bone lesions ((Figure 7)).  Bone scintigraphy shows a focal increase in uptake. # Summary Bone remodeling involves the resorption of old or damaged bone and the deposition and mineralization of new bone matrix.  Resorption of old bone and formation of new bone are linked and tightly orchestrated by the interactions of osteoblasts, osteoclasts, and osteocytes in response to mechanical stress, intercellular signaling, and hormones. Remodeling requires the coordinated function of osteoclasts and osteoblasts, which together are often termed the basic multicellular unit.  The remodeling sequence includes activation (osteocytes recruit and activate osteoclast precursors), resorption (osteoclasts dissolve mineralized bone matrix and degrade collagen, forming resorption pits), reversal (osteoclasts are replaced by mononuclear cells that prepare the surface for new bone formation), formation (osteoblasts lay down and mineralize new osteoid), and quiescence (the bone surface is covered by lining cells, and osteoblasts mature into osteocytes). Major regulatory factors in bone remodeling include: - Receptor activator of nuclear factor-κB ligand (RANKL):  Stimulates osteoclast maturation and activation. - Osteoprotegerin:  A decoy receptor secreted by osteoblasts that binds RANKL and prevents it from engaging RANK (receptor). - Parathyroid hormone:  Increases bone resorption to mobilize calcium by promoting the expression of RANKL in osteoblast-lineage cells. - Vitamin D:  Enhances intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphate.  Also upregulates RANKL expression in osteoblasts to enhance osteoclast activation. - Estrogen:  Suppresses RANK expression on osteoclast precursors and induces osteoprotegerin production by osteoblasts.  Maintains bone density in premenopausal women as well as in men (by conversion from testosterone). - Sclerostin:  Inhibits osteoblast activity by suppressing Wnt signaling. - Fibroblast growth factor 23:  Inhibits renal phosphate reabsorption and vitamin D activation. ​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌​​​​​​​​‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌

articles.title: Body Fluid Compartments
articles.markdown: # Body Fluid Compartments # Introduction The body maintains a delicate balance of fluids distributed across distinct compartments, which is critical for cellular function, nutrient transport, and systemic homeostasis.  These fluid compartments are fundamental to physiologic function, serving as the medium for cellular metabolism, electrolyte balance, and waste removal.  This article focuses on the structural organization, physiologic regulation, and clinical relevance of body fluid compartments, highlighting their composition and the mechanisms that govern fluid shifts between spaces. Total body water and compartments ## Distribution of total body water **Total body water** (TBW) constitutes approximately **60%** of body weight in the average male adult.  Women, on average, tend to have less TBW due to the presence of more adipose tissue, which contains minimal water.  Age also influences TBW distribution, with infants having a higher percentage (70%-75%) due to their lower adipose tissue content.  TBW is distributed among two compartments: - **Intracellular fluid** (ICF):  Comprises approximately **40%** of body weight and two-thirds of TBW. - **Extracellular fluid** (ECF):  Constitutes approximately **20%** of body weight and one-third of TBW.  This is composed of plasma and interstitial fluid (separated by capillary walls). ICF and ECF are separated by semipermeable cell membranes (discussed later).  The percentage of **body weight** distributed among TBW, ICF, and ECF can be remembered by the **60-40-20 rule** ((Figure 1)).  Accurate measurement of fluid compartments relies on dilution principles using tracers that distribute specifically within target components, such as inulin or mannitol (ECF volume) and radiolabeled albumin (plasma volume). Intracellular fluid The intracellular compartment (two-thirds of TBW) is the largest fluid reservoir and is rich in **potassium** (K⁺) (120 mEq/L), **magnesium** (Mg2⁺), organic **phosphates** (eg, ATP), and **proteins**.  The high concentration of K⁺ relative to sodium (Na⁺) is critical for maintaining resting membrane potentials and facilitating signal transduction.  Intracellular proteins not only contribute to the osmotic balance, but also play pivotal roles in cellular structure and enzymatic activity. Within the ICF, metabolic reactions, energy production, and protein synthesis occur under tightly regulated conditions.  The integrity of this compartment is maintained by the cell membrane, which selectively regulates the passage of solutes and water through channels and transporters. ## Extracellular fluid The extracellular compartment (one-third of TBW) encompasses all fluid outside the cells and contains large amounts of **Na+** (140 mEq/L), **chloride** (Cl−) (105 mEq/L), and **bicarbonate** (HCO3−).  NaCl content, often referred to as simply total body sodium, is responsible for maintaining volume status by holding onto water within the ECF (due to tonicity, discussed later).  ECF is divided into: - **Plasma** (one-fourth of ECF):  As the fluid compartment for blood, this intravascular component circulates through the heart and vessels, carrying hormones, nutrients, and immune cells.  Plasma makes up 55% of blood volume, with the remaining 45% containing blood cells (eg, erythrocytes).  The proportion of blood volume occupied by erythrocytes is called hematocrit, which can indicate certain abnormalities (eg, decreased in anemia, increased in dehydration or polycythemia). - **Interstitial fluid** (three-fourths of ECF):  This extravascular fluid is an ultrafiltrate of plasma, containing a similar composition, excluding plasma proteins and blood cells.  It surrounds cells, providing a medium for nutrient and waste exchange. Plasma and interstitial fluid are separated by capillary walls, allowing plasma ultrafiltration.  A minor fraction of ECF is composed of transcellular fluid (eg, cerebrospinal fluid, synovial fluid). Within the ECF, fluid exchange across capillary walls is governed by **Starling forces**, which balance the hydrostatic and osmotic pressures across capillary walls, thereby **regulating fluid movement** between the plasma and interstitial spaces ((Figure 2)).  The lymphatic system aids in returning excess interstitial fluid to the circulatory system, preventing tissue edema under normal conditions ((Figure 3)).  Disruption of lymphatic drainage leads to interstitial fluid accumulation and tissue swelling (ie, lymphedema). # Osmolarity versus tonicity ## Osmolarity **Osmolarity** represents the **overall solute concentration** in the body and is expressed in milliosmoles per liter (mOsm/L).  It is affected by changes in the total amount of both solutes and water.  In the body, normal osmolarity is approximately 290 mOsm/L.  (*Osmolality*, expressed in kilograms of water, is often used interchangeably because 1 L of water weighs 1 kg.) Because water readily moves across cell membranes, osmotic differences between body compartments equilibrate rapidly.  Therefore, under steady-state conditions, osmolarity is essentially uniform throughout the body fluids (ie, isosmotic). ## Tonicity **Tonicity** specifically describes the **effective osmotic pressure** exerted by nonpenetrating solutes across a semipermeable membrane.  Tonicity directly determines cellular volume changes because only nonpenetrating solutes (eg, Na+/Cl− in ECF, K+/organic anions in ICF) create sustained osmotic gradients.  Tonicity determines water movement across membranes, even when osmolarity alone does not predict this effect: - An isosmotic solution has the same osmolarity as the body but can have different effects on compartment volume depending on the membrane permeability of the solutes. - Permeable:  For example, a 290 mOsm/L solution made of urea (a penetrating solute that crosses membranes) effectively acts as a hypotonic solution because urea cannot create a sustained osmotic gradient.  The fluid initially stays in the extracellular compartment, but, as urea equilibrates, water moves with it, and the intracellular and extracellular compartments both increase proportionately in volume. - Nonpermeable:  For example, a 290 mOsm/L solution made of sodium chloride acts as an isotonic solution, increasing only the extracellular volume because salt remains trapped in the extracellular space. - A hypoosmotic solution has lower osmolarity than the body, so both the intracellular and extracellular compartments expand as they absorb additional water. - Permeable:  Penetrating solutes equilibrate between both compartments, so the intracellular and extracellular compartments both increase proportionately in volume. - Nonpermeable:  A greater proportion of nonpenetrating solutes keeps more of the fluid in the extracellular space. - A hyperosmotic solution has higher osmolarity than the body but can have different effects on compartment volume, depending on the membrane permeability of the solutes. - Permeable:  Penetrating solutes equilibrate between both compartments, so the fluid effectively acts isotonically, increasing the volume of the intracellular and extracellular compartments proportionately. - Nonpermeable:  If the extra solutes are nonpenetrating, the fluid is hypertonic and draws water out of the intracellular space into the extracellular compartment. Therefore, whereas osmolarity describes total solute concentration compared to the ICF, tonicity determines the water movement, factoring in membrane permeability; the term "osmotic gradient" is traditionally used because it describes the universal principle of osmosis, even though the effective osmotic gradient is determined by a solution's tonicity rather than osmolarity. Hormonal regulation Regulatory mechanisms stabilize fluid volumes and osmolarity across compartments in response to homeostatic insults (eg, volume depletion).  Important regulatory hormones include: - **Antidiuretic hormone** (ADH) (also known as arginine vasopressin \[AVP\]):  Increases renal water reabsorption, raising TBW and diluting osmolarity.  ADH is released in response to increased osmolarity (osmotic stimulus) and other nonosmotic stimuli (eg, hypotension). - **Aldosterone**:  Enhances sodium (and water) reabsorption, expanding fluid compartments without significantly altering osmolarity because sodium retention is balanced by proportional water retention. # Conditions disrupting homeostasis ## Gastrointestinal hemorrhage or diarrhea - Initial insult:  The fluid that is lost (eg, via blood or diarrhea) from the ECF has the same osmolarity as the rest of the ECF.  This decreases ECF volume without changing ECF osmolarity (ie, isosmotic volume contraction).  ICF volume and osmolarity are unaffected because there is no osmotic gradient to shift water between compartments ((Figure 4)). - Homeostatic response:  Renal hypoperfusion activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), leading to aldosterone-mediated Na+ (and water) reabsorption.  This partially increases ECF volume. - Medical intervention:  The administration of isotonic fluids (eg, normal saline, blood transfusion) fully restores ECF volume. ## Arginine vasopressin deficiency or resistance (formerly diabetes insipidus) - Initial insult:  Impaired action of AVP (ADH) leads to urinary wasting of electrolyte-free water.  Water is lost first from the ECF from plasma filtered through the glomerulus, reducing ECF volume and increasing its osmolarity.  High ECF osmolarity then pulls water from the ICF until osmolarities are equal, although higher than baseline.  The net result is increased osmolarity and decreased volumes of both compartments (ie, hyperosmotic volume contraction) ((Figure 5)). - Homeostatic response:  Elevated osmolarity rapidly triggers thirst, leading to increased water ingestion.  Sustained water ingestion quickly normalizes ECF/ICF volumes and restores osmolarity to a high-normal level (at the expense of causing polyuria).  Aldosterone does not play a significant role because the ECF/ICF compartments have not lost Na+ (ie, there is adequate Na+ to keep ingested water within the compartments). - Medical intervention:  In patients with AVP deficiency, a synthetic AVP analogue (eg, desmopressin) should be administered to stop water losses.  Management of AVP resistance focuses on addressing the underlying cause (eg, correction of hypercalcemia, lithium cessation).  In those with disrupted thirst drive, such as those with a hypothalamic stroke or unconscious, critically ill patients, exogenous free water administration (eg, intravenous dextrose with water) is given to replace free water losses. ## Syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion - Initial insult:  Excess ADH causes excess retention of electrolyte-free water.  Water is first retained in the ECF (into the plasma), increasing ECF volume and lowering its osmolarity.  Reduced ECF osmolarity drives water into the ICF until osmolarities are equal (but lower than baseline).  The net result is decreased osmolarity and increased volumes of both compartments (ie, hypoosmotic volume expansion) ((Figure 6)). - Homeostatic response:  Volume expansion suppresses the RAAS, reducing aldosterone and promoting sodium excretion (aided by natriuretic peptides); therefore, syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion (SIADH) is clinically associated with euvolemia.  Under normal conditions, low osmolarity inhibits ADH release to promote free water excretion, but, in SIADH, inappropriate ADH secretion persists despite inhibition; therefore, a hypoosmotic state persists (ie, euvolemic hyponatremia). - Medical intervention:  Fluid restriction reduces free water intake and allows gradual renal excretion of excess water.  Salt tablets can be added to increase osmolarity; in severe cases, intravenous hypertonic saline (3%) can be administered.  In persistent cases, AVP receptor antagonists (eg, tolvaptan) can be used to block ADH effects, allowing free water excretion.  In addition, the source of ADH release should be addressed if possible (eg, cessation of causative medications). ## Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease) - Initial insult:  Primary adrenal insufficiency involves aldosterone and cortisol deficiency (due to adrenal failure).  Aldosterone loss causes urinary Na+ excretion, reducing ECF volume and causing hypotension.  Concurrent cortisol deficiency exacerbates hypotension by impairing vascular tone.  Hypotension triggers ADH release (volume stimulus), promoting water retention with decreased ECF osmolarity.  Low ECF osmolarity shifts fluid into the ICF, expanding ICF volume, although combined volume is reduced; ICF osmolarity decreases until it matches ECF osmolarity.  The net result is hypoosmotic volume contraction (ECF loss exceeds ICF gain) ((Figure 7)). - Homeostatic response:  Hypovolemia stimulates renin release, but adrenal failure prevents aldosterone secretion, rendering RAAS ineffective at retaining Na+.  Loss of cortisol's negative feedback increases ACTH and corticotropin-releasing hormone, attempting unsuccessfully to stimulate adrenal hormone production.  Both of these responses are unable to restore normal aldosterone and cortisol action, leading to persistent hypotension (and hyponatremia and hyperkalemia) (ie, hypovolemic hyponatremia). - Medical intervention:  Intravenous isotonic fluids are given to restore ECF volume, improving hypotension.  Glucocorticoids (eg, hydrocortisone) and mineralocorticoids (eg, fludrocortisone) are given to restore cortisol and aldosterone activity, respectively. # Effects of fluid administration ## Normal saline infusion - Isotonic fluid infusion (eg, 0.9% normal saline) increases ECF volume without affecting osmolarity (ie, isosmotic volume expansion).  Because osmolarity is unchanged, ICF volume remains the same. - To maintain homeostasis, excess ECF volume inhibits RAAS, which, with increased natriuretic peptide release, promotes renal excretion of Na+ and water to normalize ECF volume. ## Hypertonic saline infusion - Hypertonic saline contains a higher sodium concentration than plasma, so ECF osmolarity increases following infusion.  The added fluid volume also expands the ECF.  High ECF osmolarity pulls water from the ICF, decreasing ICF volume and further increasing ECF volume.  The net result is increased osmolarity of both compartments, with expansion of the ECF volume and decreased ICF volume (ie, hyperosmotic volume expansion) ((Figure 8)). - Homeostasis is achieved via suppression of RAAS, which promotes Na+ and water excretion, thereby normalizing ECF volume.  In addition, increased osmolarity triggers thirst, leading to increased water ingestion with a reduction of osmolarity and restoration of ICF volume. # Summary The body's fluid balance, essential for cellular function and homeostasis, is maintained through distinct intracellular (ICF) and extracellular (ECF) compartments.  Total body water, constituting approximately 60% of body weight, is distributed as ICF (two-thirds of total body water, 40% of body weight) and ECF (one-third of TBW, 20% of body weight) (60-40-20 rule). ICF, rich in potassium, magnesium, and proteins, supports metabolic processes, whereas ECF, dominated by sodium and chloride, includes plasma (intravascular) and interstitial fluid (extravascular).  Fluid dynamics between compartments are regulated by osmotic gradients and hormones, namely arginine vasopressin (antidiuretic hormone) (modulates water retention) and aldosterone (regulates sodium balance).  ECF/ICF volumes and osmolarity can be disrupted by various homeostatic insults, including gastrointestinal hemorrhage or diarrhea, arginine vasopressin disorders, syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion, and primary adrenal insufficiency. Clinical scenarios illustrate compartment-specific disruptions.  For example, hypertonic saline infusion increases ECF osmolarity, drawing water from the ICF, whereas adrenal insufficiency causes sodium loss, depleting the ECF and expanding the ICF.  Conditions such as AVP deficiency/resistance and syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion alter osmolarity and volume. ​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​‌​‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​​​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​​​​‌‌​​​​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌

articles.title: Adrenal Gland Anatomy And Physiology
articles.markdown:
# Adrenal Gland Anatomy And Physiology # Introduction The adrenal glands are small, triangle-shaped endocrine organs that are located on top of each kidney that play a crucial role in metabolism, fluid and electrolyte balance, and stress response modulation.  This article focuses on normal adrenal function.  Pathologic adrenal conditions are discussed in detail in separate articles. # Anatomy The adrenal glands are bilateral structures each weighing about 4-6 g in adults.  They are composed of 2 distinct regions:  the adrenal cortex and the adrenal medulla. ## Adrenal cortex The outer portion of the gland comprises about 80%-90% of its mass.  It is further divided into 3 zones: - Zona glomerulosa:  The outermost layer, responsible for mineralocorticoid production (primarily aldosterone) - Zona fasciculata:  The middle and largest layer, responsible for glucocorticoid production (primarily cortisol) - Zona reticularis:  The innermost layer, responsible for androgen production (primarily dehydroepiandrosterone \[DHEA\] and androstenedione) ## Adrenal medulla The inner portion of the gland, comprising about 10%-20% of its mass and is responsible for catecholamine production (primarily epinephrine and norepinephrine) by chromaffin cells. The adrenal glands are highly vascularized, receiving blood supply from the superior, middle, and inferior adrenal arteries.  Venous drainage occurs primarily through the central adrenal vein. # Physiology The adrenal glands produce several hormones essential for maintaining homeostasis: **Glucocorticoids (primarily cortisol)** - Regulate metabolism, immune function, and stress response - Increase blood glucose levels through gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis - Suppress inflammation and immune responses - Maintain vascular tone and cardiac contractility **Mineralocorticoids (primarily aldosterone)** -
